children.title: Uniform Finite Sums
children.top_down_role: Equal-weight component objective representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Finite Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The canonical equally weighted finite-sum objective used by component-gradient methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, and let \(f_i:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). The associated uniform finite-sum objective is
\[
F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x),\qquad x\in X.
\]
Equivalently, if \(I\) is uniformly distributed on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), then \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f_I(x)]\) whenever the displayed values are finite. At differentiability points shared by all components, \(\nabla F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla f_i(x)=\mathbb E[\nabla f_I(x)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform finite sum averages all component objectives equally; uniform component sampling gives unbiased function and gradient estimators.
assumptions_latex: For the gradient identity, every \(f_i\) is differentiable at the point considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)=\mathbb E[f_I(x)]\), and, when differentiable, \(\nabla F(x)=\mathbb E[\nabla f_I(x)]\).

notation.meaning: uniform random index in the component set

children.title: Weighted Finite Sums
children.top_down_role: Nonuniform component-weight objective representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Finite Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite sums with nonnegative component weights interpreted as a sampling distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, let \(w_i\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i=1\), and define \(J=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:w_i>0\}\). For functions \(f_i:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(i\in J\), a weighted finite-sum objective is
\[
F(x)=\sum_{i\in J}w_i f_i(x),\qquad x\in X.
\]
If \(I\) satisfies \(\mathbb P(I=i)=w_i\), then \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f_I(x)]\) whenever the displayed values are finite. Where every positively weighted component is differentiable, \(\nabla F(x)=\sum_{i\in J}w_i\nabla f_i(x)=\mathbb E[\nabla f_I(x)]\). Zero-weight indices lie outside \(J\) and do not affect \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted finite sum combines the positively weighted components using nonnegative normalized weights, equivalently taking expectation under the corresponding index distribution; zero-weight indices do not affect the objective.
assumptions_latex: For the gradient identity, every component indexed by \(J\) is differentiable at the point considered.

notation.meaning: support of the positive component weights

children.title: Weight-Normalization Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conventions governing scale, normalization, and interpretation of component weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Normalization Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion between normalized, unnormalized, and uniform finite-sum weighting conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(X\) be nonempty, let \(a_i\ge0\), and suppose \(A=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i>0\). Define \(J=\{i:a_i>0\}\), let \(f_i:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) for \(i\in J\), and set \(w_i=a_i/A\). Wherever the sums are well-defined,
\[
\frac1A\sum_{i\in J}a_i f_i(x)=\sum_{i\in J}w_i f_i(x),
\qquad \sum_{i\in J}w_i=1.
\]
Thus \(G(x)=\sum_{i\in J}a_i f_i(x)\) equals \(A F(x)\), where \(F=G/A\). Because \(A\) is constant and positive, \(F\) and \(G\) have identical minimizer sets on \(X\). Uniform averaging is the special case \(a_i=1\) for every \(i\), hence \(A=n\) and \(w_i=1/n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive unnormalized weights become a probability vector after division by their sum; positive constant scaling preserves minimizers, and uniform averaging is the all-ones special case.
assumptions_latex: The compared objectives are well-defined on a common effective domain.

notation.meaning: positive sum of the unnormalized weights

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between probability normalization and positive objective rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For real coefficients \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), let \(A=\sum_i a_i\). The coefficients \(w_i=a_i/A\) form a probability vector exactly when \(A\neq0\) and \(a_i/A\ge0\) for every \(i\). The raw objective \(G=\sum_i a_i f_i\) and normalized objective \(F=\sum_iw_i f_i\) satisfy \(G=AF\). They therefore have identical minimizers when \(A>0\); when \(A<0\), minimizing \(G\) corresponds to maximizing \(F\), and when \(A=0\), normalization is undefined. Under the standard nonnegative raw-weight convention, admissibility reduces to \(a_i\ge0\) for all \(i\) and \(A>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raw coefficients define sampling probabilities when their normalized values are nonnegative, but minimizer-preserving normalization additionally requires a positive total weight.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in\mathbb R\), \(A=\sum_i a_i\), and the compared sums are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((a_i/A)_i\in\Delta_n\iff A\neq0\text{ and }a_i/A\ge0\ \forall i\); moreover, \(\arg\min G=\arg\min F\) is guaranteed by \(A>0\), not by \(A<0\).

children.title: Empirical-Risk Objectives
children.top_down_role: Finite-sum objectives arising from samplewise losses.

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical-Risk Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample empirical risk formed from per-example losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given observations \(S=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\) in a sample space \(\mathcal Z\), a hypothesis domain \(X\), and a loss \(\ell:X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), the empirical-risk objective is
\[
\widehat R_S(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(x;z_i),\qquad x\in X.
\]
Writing \(f_i(x)=\ell(x;z_i)\) identifies empirical-risk minimization with a uniform finite-sum problem. An empirical-risk minimizer is any \(\widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\widehat R_S(x)\), provided this set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Empirical risk is the average loss over observed examples, so empirical-risk minimization is a uniform finite-sum optimization problem.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell:X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is defined on every sampled observation.

children.title: Explicit Regularization Models
children.top_down_role: Finite-sum formulations with separately represented regularizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Regularization Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularized empirical risk with a separately specified penalty and strength parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be nonempty, let \(\widehat R_S:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be an empirical risk, and let \(R:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a regularizer with a common finite point. For \(\lambda>0\), the explicit regularization model is
\[
\min_{x\in X}F_\lambda(x),
\qquad F_\lambda(x)=\widehat R_S(x)+\lambda R(x)
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(x;z_i)+\lambda R(x).
\]
The unregularized endpoint is defined separately by \(F_0=\widehat R_S\). The regularizer may encode complexity, structure, or constraints. In particular, for \(\lambda>0\), choosing \(R=\iota_C\), where \(\iota_C(x)=0\) on \(C\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(C\), restricts the effective feasible set to \(X\cap C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit regularization adds a positively scaled penalty to empirical risk; the zero-strength endpoint is the unregularized risk, and a positively scaled extended-valued indicator encodes a hard constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty and \(\widehat R_S,R:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) have a common finite point.
The regularized model uses \(\lambda>0\); the endpoint \(\lambda=0\) is defined separately by \(F_0=\widehat R_S\).
For the constraint interpretation, \(R=\iota_C\), with \(\iota_C(x)=0\) on \(C\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\lambda>0\), \(F_\lambda=\widehat R_S+\lambda R\), and \(R=\iota_C\) enforces \(x\in X\cap C\); moreover, \(F_0=\widehat R_S\).

notation.meaning: indicator function of the set C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-independent comparison of exact minimizers at two positive regularization strengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<\lambda_1<\lambda_2\), let \(F_\lambda(x)=\widehat R_S(x)+\lambda R(x)\), and choose finite-valued minimizers \(x_j\in\operatorname*{argmin}F_{\lambda_j}\) for \(j=1,2\). Then \[R(x_2)\le R(x_1),\qquad \widehat R_S(x_1)\le\widehat R_S(x_2).\] The conclusion does not require uniqueness of either minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among exact solutions, increasing the positive regularization strength cannot increase the penalty value or decrease the empirical-risk value.
assumptions_latex: Each \(F_{\lambda_j}=\widehat R_S+\lambda_jR\) attains a finite minimum at \(x_j\).

notation.meaning: An exact minimizer at regularization strength \(\lambda_j\).

children.title: Regularizer-Placement Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Alternative placements of regularization relative to component terms and aggregate objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularizer-Placement Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent objective representations that expose either a shared proximal term or regularized components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(w_i\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_iw_i=1\), and consider
\[
F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i f_i(x)+R(x).
\]
The identity
\[
F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\bigl(f_i(x)+R(x)\bigr)
\]
permits two interfaces. The shared-regularizer interface retains \(R\) outside the finite sum and exposes component oracles for \(f_i\) together with a separate oracle, commonly proximal, for \(R\). The absorbed interface defines \(g_i=f_i+R\) and exposes component oracles for \(g_i\). Objective equivalence does not imply equality of these oracle costs or update rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized weighted model can keep one shared regularizer outside the sum or absorb it into every component, yielding different oracle interfaces.
assumptions_latex: All sums are well-defined on a common effective domain.
The required component and regularizer oracles exist for the chosen interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_iw_i f_i+R=\sum_iw_i(f_i+R)\), although the two oracle interfaces need not be computationally equivalent.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise redistribution of a shared regularizer across positive-weight terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i f_i(x)+R(x)\), where \(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum_iw_i=1\), and \(J=\{i:w_i>0\}\). If \(\alpha_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_{i\in J}\alpha_i=1\), then, with the convention \(0R=0\),
\[
g_i=f_i+\frac{\alpha_i}{w_i}R\quad(i\in J)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
F=\sum_{i\in J}w_i g_i.
\]
More generally, when \(R\) is real-valued on the common domain, a representation \(g_i=f_i+\beta_iR\) preserves \(F\) whenever \(\sum_{i\in J}w_i\beta_i=1\); this condition is also necessary if \(R\) is nonzero at some point of that domain. Zero-weight components cannot contribute through the weighted sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared regularizer may be apportioned among positive-weight components, provided the weighted regularizer coefficients sum to one.
assumptions_latex: All displayed sums are well-defined on a common effective domain.
For signed redistribution coefficients, \(R\) is real-valued on that domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\sum_{i\in J}w_i(f_i+(\alpha_i/w_i)R)\) for every nonnegative \((\alpha_i)\) satisfying \(\sum_{i\in J}\alpha_i=1\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative share of the regularizer assigned to component i

review_flags: builder converse narrowed to exclude vanishing-on-domain and extended-real scaling exceptions
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Regularizer Redistribution
Composite Finite-Sum Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-sum loss combined with a proximable, possibly nonsmooth, convex term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex composite finite-sum model has the form
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb R^d}F(x),
\qquad F(x)=f(x)+R(x),
\qquad f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i f_i(x),
\]
where \(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum_iw_i=1\), every \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is convex and differentiable, and \(R:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. The standard first-order interface returns sampled component gradients \(\nabla f_i(x)\) and evaluates \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma R}(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{R(x)+\|x-v\|^2/(2\gamma)\}\) for \(\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite finite-sum model combines a smooth weighted component average with a proper closed convex term accessed through a proximal oracle.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is convex and differentiable.
\(R\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\sum_iw_i f_i+R\) admits component-gradient access to its smooth part and proximal access to \(R\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of the composite term

knowledge_statements.title: Composite First-Order and Proximal Fixed-Point Certificate
Separable Primal–Dual Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel saddle representation with one dual block for each positively weighted finite-sum component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(A_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{m_i}\) be linear, let \(\phi_i:\mathbb R^{m_i}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(R:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Let \(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i=1\), and \(J=\{i:w_i>0\}\). Fenchel biconjugacy gives, for every \(x\) at which the primal expression is well-defined,
\[
R(x)+\sum_{i\in J}w_i\phi_i(A_i x)
=\sup_{(y_i)_{i\in J}\in\prod_{i\in J}\mathbb R^{m_i}}
\left\{R(x)+\sum_{i\in J}w_i\bigl(\langle A_i x,y_i\rangle-\phi_i^*(y_i)\bigr)\right\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb R^d}\left\{R(x)+\sum_{i\in J}w_i\phi_i(A_i x)\right\}
=
\min_{x\in\mathbb R^d}\sup_{(y_i)_{i\in J}\in\prod_{i\in J}\mathbb R^{m_i}}
\left\{R(x)+\sum_{i\in J}w_i\bigl(\langle A_i x,y_i\rangle-\phi_i^*(y_i)\bigr)\right\},
\]
so the dual variables and conjugate terms are separable across positively weighted components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugacy assigns an independent dual block to each positively weighted composed component, yielding a component-separable min-sup representation without asserting interchange of minimization and maximization.
assumptions_latex: \(A_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{m_i}\) is linear for every \(i\).
Each \(\phi_i\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum_iw_i=1\), \(J=\{i:w_i>0\}\), and the primal expression is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal minimization equals the displayed \(\min_x\sup_{(y_i)_{i\in J}}\) representation with one dual block \(y_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i}\) per positively weighted component.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of component function phi_i
dual variable in R^{m_i} associated with component i
support of the positive component weights

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise and coupled inclusions characterizing attained primal–dual optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume primal and dual attainment with equal optimal values. A pair \((x^*,(y_i^*)_{i\in J})\) is primal–dual optimal if and only if
\[
y_i^*\in\partial\phi_i(A_ix^*)\quad(i\in J),
\qquad
-\sum_{i\in J}w_iA_i^*y_i^*\in\partial R(x^*).
\]
Equivalently, the component Fenchel–Young residuals
\[
\phi_i(A_ix^*)+\phi_i^*(y_i^*)-\langle A_ix^*,y_i^*\rangle
\]
and the coupled residual
\[
R(x^*)+R^*\!\left(-\sum_iw_iA_i^*y_i^*\right)+\left\langle x^*,\sum_iw_iA_i^*y_i^*\right\rangle
\]
all vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimality is certified by one Fenchel equality per component and the coupled stationarity condition for the shared primal term.
assumptions_latex: The convex primal and Fenchel dual attain equal finite optimal values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inclusions, equivalently vanishing Fenchel–Young residuals, characterize attained primal–dual optimal pairs.

notation.meaning: optimal dual block associated with component i

knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise Fenchel Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual objective and a sufficient finite-dimensional qualification for the separable Fenchel representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
P=\inf_x\left\{R(x)+\sum_{i\in J}w_i\phi_i(A_ix)\right\},
\]
where \(w_i>0\) on \(J\), the Fenchel dual is
\[
D=\sup_{(y_i)}\left\{-R^*\!\left(-\sum_{i\in J}w_iA_i^*y_i\right)-\sum_{i\in J}w_i\phi_i^*(y_i)\right\}.
\]
Weak duality gives \(D\le P\). If the primal value is finite and some \(x_0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}R)\) satisfies \(A_ix_0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}\phi_i)\) for every \(i\in J\), then \(D=P\) and the dual supremum is attained. Without an applicable qualification, zero gap and dual attainment are not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The block-separable saddle model has a coupled Fenchel dual; a relative-interior qualification ensures zero gap and dual attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) and every \(\phi_i\) are proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
The strong-duality conclusion uses the displayed relative-interior condition and finite primal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\le P\), with \(D=P\) and dual attainment under the stated qualification.
review_flags: stated relative-interior condition is sufficient and need not be necessary

children.title: Componentwise Convexity
children.top_down_role: Convexity regimes imposed on individual component objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity imposed separately on every component of a finite-sum objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), the finite-sum family \((f_i)_{i=1}^n\) is componentwise convex on \(X\) precisely when, for every \(i\), every \(x,y\in X\), and every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
f_i(tx+(1-t)y)\le t f_i(x)+(1-t)f_i(y).
\]
If \(w_i\ge0\), then the aggregate \(F=\sum_iw_i f_i\) is convex on \(X\). Componentwise convexity is stronger than merely requiring convexity of the aggregate because it forbids cancellation of negative curvature among components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every component must satisfy the convexity inequality individually; nonnegative weighting then guarantees aggregate convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Componentwise convexity implies convexity of \(F=\sum_iw_i f_i\) for all nonnegative weights.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weight-Sign Boundary for Automatic Convexity Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp coefficient-sign boundary for transferring componentwise convexity uniformly over component families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Componentwise convexity guarantees convexity of \(F=\sum_iw_if_i\) for every component family when all weights are nonnegative. If a coefficient is negative, this uniform implication fails. For example, on \(\mathbb R\), let \(f_1(x)=f_2(x)=x^2\), \(w_1=1\), and \(w_2=-2\). Both components are convex, but \(F(x)=-x^2\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative weights transfer componentwise convexity to the aggregate; allowing a negative coefficient destroys that guarantee over arbitrary component families.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise First- and Second-Order Convexity Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent convexity tests imposed separately on every differentiable component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open and convex and suppose every \(f_i\) is differentiable on \(U\). The family is componentwise convex if and only if, for every \(i\) and all \(x,y\in U\), \(f_i(y)\ge f_i(x)+\langle
abla f_i(x),y-xangle\); equivalently, \(\langle
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(y),x-yangle\ge0\) for every \(i,x,y\). If every \(f_i\in C^2(U)\), this is further equivalent to \(
abla^2f_i(x)\succeq0\) for every \(i\) and \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Componentwise convexity is equivalent to imposing the standard support, gradient-monotonicity, or Hessian test on every component separately.
assumptions_latex: The Hessian characterization additionally assumes every \(f_i\in C^2(U)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (f_i)_i\text{ is componentwise convex}\iff\forall i,\ \nabla f_i\text{ is monotone};\quad f_i\in C^2(U)\Rightarrow\bigl(\forall i,x,\nabla^2f_i(x)\succeq0\bigr).

children.title: Aggregate Convexity
children.top_down_role: Convexity regimes imposed only on the finite-sum aggregate.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity required only of the weighted aggregate finite-sum objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be convex and let \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i f_i(x)\) be well-defined on \(X\). The finite-sum model is aggregate convex when, for every \(x,y\in X\) and \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
F(tx+(1-t)y)\le tF(x)+(1-t)F(y).
\]
This condition constrains only the weighted sum. Individual \(f_i\) may be nonconvex, provided their weighted combination satisfies the displayed inequality. Thus aggregate convexity is sufficient for convexity of the optimization objective but not for componentwise convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregate convexity requires the weighted sum, but not each component, to satisfy the convexity inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is aggregate convex exactly when \(F(tx+(1-t)y)\le tF(x)+(1-t)F(y)\) on \(X\).

children.title: Convexity-Mismatch Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where component geometry differs from aggregate geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity-Mismatch Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate convexity can persist despite nonconvex components through curvature cancellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Aggregate convexity does not imply componentwise convexity. On \(X=\mathbb R\), take \(n=2\), \(w_1=w_2=1/2\),
\[
f_1(x)=-x^2,
\qquad f_2(x)=3x^2.
\]
Then \(f_1\) is nonconvex, while
\[
F(x)=\tfrac12f_1(x)+\tfrac12f_2(x)=x^2
\]
is convex and strongly convex. More generally, for twice-differentiable components, positive semidefiniteness of \(\sum_iw_i\nabla^2f_i(x)\) need not imply positive semidefiniteness of every \(\nabla^2f_i(x)\). Analyses using componentwise convex inequalities therefore do not automatically apply under aggregate convexity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonconvex component curvature can cancel in the weighted sum, so aggregate convexity alone cannot justify componentwise convexity arguments.
assumptions_latex: For the Hessian characterization, components are twice differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=x^2\) is convex although \(f_1(x)=-x^2\) is not convex.

notation.meaning: uniform aggregate of the two components

children.title: Strong-Convexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Component-level or aggregate-level strong-curvature settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Convexity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes componentwise strong convexity from strong convexity of only the aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty and convex, and extend each function under discussion by \(+\infty\) outside \(X\). A proper convex function \(h:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) with \(\operatorname{dom}h\subseteq X\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(X\), for \(\mu>0\), when
\[
h(y)\ge h(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac\mu2\lVert y-x\rVert^2
\]
for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial h\), every \(y\in X\), and every \(g\in\partial h(x)\), where \(\partial h\) is the convex subdifferential in \(\mathbb R^d\). A finite-sum model is componentwise strongly convex if every \(f_i\) satisfies this condition with a modulus \(\mu_i>0\). If \(w_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_iw_i=1\), then \(F=\sum_iw_i f_i\) is strongly convex with modulus \(\sum_iw_i\mu_i>0\). In the weaker aggregate regime, only \(F\) is required to be strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity may hold for every component or only for the normalized weighted aggregate; in the componentwise regime, the aggregate modulus is the corresponding weighted sum of component moduli.
assumptions_latex: Each component is proper and convex, with the extended-value convention outside \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every \(f_i\) is \(\mu_i\)-strongly convex and \(w_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_iw_i=1\), then \(F=\sum_iw_i f_i\) is \(\left(\sum_iw_i\mu_i\right)\)-strongly convex.

notation.meaning: ambient-space convex subdifferential of h at x

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex on a convex set \(X\), with \(\mu>0\). If \(F\) attains its minimum at \(x_\star\), then \(x_\star\) is unique and \(F(x)-F(x_\star)\ge\tfrac\mu2\|x-x_\star\|^2\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained minimum of a strongly convex function is unique and satisfies quadratic growth.

children.title: Finite-Sum Condition Measures
children.top_down_role: Condition measures relevant to finite-sum method behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Condition Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition numbers induced by component smoothness and aggregate strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where each \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) has an \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\). Define \(L_{\max}=\max_i L_i\), \(L_{\mathrm{avg}}=n^{-1}\sum_iL_i\), and let \(L_f\) be the least Lipschitz constant of \(\nabla f\). The component, average, and aggregate condition measures are respectively
\[\kappa_{\max}=\frac{L_{\max}}{\mu},\qquad \kappa_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{L_{\mathrm{avg}}}{\mu},\qquad \kappa_f=\frac{L_f}{\mu}.\]
Since \(L_f\le L_{\mathrm{avg}}\le L_{\max}\), one has \(\kappa_f\le\kappa_{\mathrm{avg}}\le\kappa_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-sum conditioning compares aggregate curvature with aggregate, average-component, or worst-component smoothness; these condition measures are ordered from aggregate to worst-component.

notation.meaning: Worst-component, average-component, and aggregate gradient-Lipschitz constants.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-to-Aggregate Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of component curvature and smoothness bounds to their uniform average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Suppose each \(f_i\) is \(\mu_i\)-strongly convex with \(\mu_i\ge 0\) and has an \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient with \(L_i\ge 0\). Define \(\mu_{\mathrm{avg}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mu_i\) and \(L_{\mathrm{avg}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nL_i\). Then \(f\) is \(\mu_{\mathrm{avg}}\)-strongly convex and \(\nabla f\) is \(L_{\mathrm{avg}}\)-Lipschitz. If \(L_f\) is the least Lipschitz constant of \(\nabla f\) and \(\mu_f\) is the supremum of the strong-convexity moduli of \(f\), then \(L_f\le L_{\mathrm{avg}}\) and \(\mu_f\ge\mu_{\mathrm{avg}}\). Consequently, when \(\mu_{\mathrm{avg}}>0\),
\[\kappa_f:=\frac{L_f}{\mu_f}\le\frac{L_{\mathrm{avg}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{avg}}}.\]
Aggregate conditioning alone does not imply the corresponding componentwise bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging transfers component smoothness and strong convexity to the objective, so the aggregate condition number is bounded by the ratio of the average component constants. Aggregate conditioning does not conversely impose those properties on every component.

notation.meaning: Supremal aggregate strong-convexity modulus and least aggregate gradient-Lipschitz constant.

children.title: Error-Bound Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Local Error Bound Need Not Be Global
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of local and global aggregate-gradient error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x^2/(1+x^2)\), the minimizer set is \(X^*=\{0\}\) and \(f'(x)=2x/(1+x^2)^2\). On \(|x|\le r\), \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\frac{(1+r^2)^2}{2}|f'(x)|.\] However, \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)/|f'(x)|=(1+x^2)^2/2\to\infty\), so no global gradient error-bound constant exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth objective can satisfy a gradient error bound near its minimizer while failing every global bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The gradient error bound holds on }[-r,r]\text{ but not globally.}

notation.meaning: radius of the local validity interval

knowledge_statements.title: A Local Error Bound Need Not Be Global

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Distance Contraction from a Gradient Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-descent consequence of an aggregate-gradient error bound on an invariant region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be convex with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\). Let \(S\) contain the gradient-descent trajectory \(x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\), and suppose \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\|\nabla f(x)\|\) for every \(x\in S\). Then \[\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},X^*)^2\le\left(1-\frac{1}{L^2\kappa^2}\right)\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*)^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On any forward-invariant region where a convex smooth gradient error bound holds, the standard gradient step contracts squared distance linearly.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
The trajectory remains in \(S\), where the error bound holds with \(\kappa>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Distance Contraction from a Gradient Error Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Quadratic Growth Implies a Gradient Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic growth as a sufficient condition for an aggregate-gradient error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and convex with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\). If, on \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), \[f(x)-f^*\ge\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{QG}}}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^2\qquad(\mu_{\mathrm{QG}}>0),\] then \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\frac{2}{\mu_{\mathrm{QG}}}\|\nabla f(x)\|\qquad(x\in S).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable convex objective, quadratic growth on a region guarantees a gradient error bound there.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Quadratic Growth Implies a Gradient Error Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local or global gradient error bounds relative to the aggregate solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, let \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}f
e\varnothing\), and let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). The gradient error-bound condition on \(S\) holds with constant \(\kappa_{\mathrm{EB}}>0\) when
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le \kappa_{\mathrm{EB}}\|
abla f(x)\|\qquad	ext{for every }x\in S.\]
The regime is global if \(S=\mathbb{R}^d\), and local if \(S\) is a specified neighborhood of \(X^*\). For a finite sum, the residual is the aggregate gradient \(
abla f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_i

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An error-bound regime controls distance to the solution set by the norm of the aggregate gradient, either globally or near that set.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from the point to the minimizer set.

children.title: Gradient-Dominance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Finite-sum settings organized by gradient-dominance structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: PL Dominance Does Not Imply Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonconvex family satisfying a global PL inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(a\in(0,1)\), let \(g(x)=x+a\sin x\), and set \(f(x)=g(x)^2\). Since \(g'(x)=1+a\cos x\ge1-a\), \[\frac12|f'(x)|^2=2g(x)^2g'(x)^2\ge2(1-a)^2f(x).\] Thus \(f\) is globally PL with \(f^*=0\). Nevertheless \(f''(x)=2(g'(x)^2+g(x)g''(x))\) is negative at suitable arbitrarily large points, so \(f\) is not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A squared nonlinear diffeomorphism can be globally PL while remaining nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is globally PL with }\mu=2(1-a)^2\text{ but is not convex.}
knowledge_statements.title: PL Dominance Does Not Imply Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationary Points Are Globally Optimal under PL Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequence of Polyak–Łojasiewicz dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) satisfies \(\tfrac12\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\ge\mu(f(x)-f^*)\) with \(\mu>0\), then \[\nabla f(\bar x)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(\bar x)=f^*.\] The condition does not imply uniqueness of minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PL objective has no nonoptimal stationary points, although it may have multiple minimizers.
assumptions_latex: The PL inequality holds at \(\bar x\) with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Stationary Points Are Globally Optimal under PL Dominance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Objective Convergence under Polyak–Łojasiewicz Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-descent consequence of PL dominance on an invariant region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and attain \(f^*\). Let \(S\) contain the trajectory \(x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\), and suppose \(\tfrac12\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\ge\mu(f(x)-f^*)\) for every \(x\in S\). Then \[f(x_{k+1})-f^*\le\left(1-\frac{\mu}{L}\right)(f(x_k)-f^*).\] Convexity is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth PL dominance on a forward-invariant region gives linear objective convergence without convexity.
assumptions_latex: The trajectory remains in \(S\), where PL holds with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Objective Convergence under Polyak–Łojasiewicz Dominance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convexity as a sufficient condition for aggregate PL dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\), and let \(f^*=\min_x f(x)\). Then \[f(x)-f^*\le\frac{1}{2\mu}\|\nabla f(x)\|^2,\] equivalently \[\frac12\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\ge\mu\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every differentiable strongly convex objective satisfies the global PL inequality with the same parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Convexity Implies Polyak–Łojasiewicz Dominance
Gradient-Dominance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyak–Łojasiewicz gradient dominance for the aggregate finite-sum objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable with finite attained minimum \(f^*=\min_x f(x)\). The Polyak–Łojasiewicz gradient-dominance condition holds on \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) with parameter \(\mu_{\mathrm{PL}}>0\) if
\[\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\ge \mu_{\mathrm{PL}}\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x\in S.\]
It is a global regime when \(S=\mathbb{R}^d\) and a local regime when \(S\) is a stated neighborhood or sublevel set. The condition does not itself require convexity or uniqueness of minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient dominance bounds aggregate objective suboptimality by the squared aggregate-gradient norm and may hold globally or only on a specified region.

notation.meaning: Region on which gradient dominance is asserted.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition is precise and the content kind fits, but its normalization and local/global formulation require a cited source.

children.title: Regime-Separation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions distinguishing error-bound behavior from gradient-dominance behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Error Bound Implies Gradient Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One direction of the convex relationship between the two regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be differentiable and convex with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\). If \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\|
abla f(x)\|\) on \(S\), then \[f(x)-f^*\le\kappa\|
abla f(x)\|^2\qquad(x\in S).\] Hence \(	frac12\|
abla f(x)\|^2\ge(2\kappa)^{-1}(f(x)-f^*)\) on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable convex objective, a gradient error bound implies PL dominance on the same region.
assumptions_latex: The gradient error bound holds on \(S\) with \(\kappa>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Error Bound Implies Gradient Dominance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex PL Dominance Implies a Gradient Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse implication under global convex differentiable geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be convex and continuously differentiable with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\). If \[\frac12\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\ge\mu(f(x)-f^*)\qquad\text{for all }x\] with \(\mu>0\), then \(f(x)-f^*\ge(\mu/2)\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^2\), and consequently \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\frac{2}{\mu}\|\nabla f(x)\|.\] Thus global convex PL dominance entails a global gradient error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex differentiable objective, global PL dominance also yields a global gradient error bound.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb R^d\).
The PL inequality holds globally with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex PL Dominance Implies a Gradient Error Bound
Regime-Separation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flat minima separate smooth nonconvex objectives from error-bound and gradient-dominance regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any integer \(p>1\), consider the one-component finite sum \(f_p(x)=x^{2p}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), with minimizer set \(X^*=\{0\}\). Although \(f_p\) is smooth and convex, no neighborhood of zero admits either a positive gradient error-bound constant or a positive Polyak–Łojasiewicz parameter. Indeed,
\[\frac{|f_p'(x)|}{\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)}=2p|x|^{2p-2}\to0,\qquad
\frac{|f_p'(x)|^2}{2(f_p(x)-f_p^*)}=2p^2|x|^{2p-2}\to0
\]
as \(x\to0\). Thus smoothness, convexity, and existence of minimizers alone do not place a finite sum in either regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth convex objectives with sufficiently flat minima can satisfy neither a gradient error bound nor gradient dominance, marking the boundary of both regimes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \(\kappa_{\mathrm{EB}}<\infty\) or \(\mu_{\mathrm{PL}}>0\) makes the respective condition hold on any neighborhood of \(0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polynomial calculations correctly separate smooth convex objectives from local error-bound and PL regimes, but this nontrivial failure-boundary claim has no cited evidence.

children.title: Interpolation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exact interpolation structure in finite-sum objectives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonconvex Failure of the Shared-Minimizer Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact component stationarity at an aggregate minimizer need not imply common component minimization without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1(x)=x^4-x^2\), \(f_2(x)=x^4+3x^2\), and \(f=(f_1+f_2)/2=x^4+x^2\). Then \(x^*=0\) is the unique aggregate minimizer and \(f_1'(0)=f_2'(0)=0\), so exact first-order interpolation holds. Nevertheless, \(0\notin\operatorname*{argmin}f_1\), and hence \(0\notin\bigcap_i\operatorname*{argmin}f_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonconvex components, every component gradient can vanish at an aggregate minimizer even though that point does not minimize every component.

notation.meaning: The aggregate minimizer at which all component gradients vanish.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Failure of the Shared-Minimizer Equivalence
Interpolation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order interpolation at an aggregate optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable. The exact interpolation condition holds if there exists \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\) such that
\[
abla f_i(x^*)=0\qquad	ext{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}.\]
If each component is convex, this is equivalent to \(x^*\in igcap_i\operatorname*{argmin}f_i\). Under random uniform component sampling, exact interpolation also gives zero component-gradient noise at \(x^*\): \(\mathbb{E}_I\|
abla f_I(x^*)-
abla f(x^*)\|^2=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact interpolation means that one aggregate optimizer is stationary for every component; for convex components, it minimizes every component simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f_i(x^*)=0\) for every \(i\), and the component-gradient variance at \(x^*\) is zero.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact interpolation condition, convex equivalence, and zero-variance consequence are coherent, but no source supports the selected finite-sum convention or equivalence.

children.title: Shared-Minimizer Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric consequences of common component minimizers.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aggregate Minimization without a Shared Component Minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of common-minimizer membership when the component minimizer sets do not intersect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1(x)=(x-1)^2\), \(f_2(x)=(x+1)^2\), and \(f=(f_1+f_2)/2=x^2+1\). Then \(\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{0\}\), whereas \(\operatorname*{argmin}f_1=\{1\}\), \(\operatorname*{argmin}f_2=\{-1\}\), and their intersection is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An average may have a minimizer even when its component minimizer sets are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Minimization without a Shared Component Minimum

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Aggregate Minimizer Set under a Shared Minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimizer-set geometry when all component minima are simultaneously attainable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\neq\varnothing\), let \(f_i:X\to\mathbb R\), and define \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\). If \(X_\cap=\bigcap_{i=1}^n\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f_i(x)\neq\varnothing\), then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)=X_\cap.\] No convexity or differentiability is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whenever all components have a common minimizer, the minimizers of their average are exactly their common minimizers.

notation.meaning: Intersection of the component minimizer sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Aggregate Minimizer Set under a Shared Minimum
Shared-Minimizer Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry induced by a nonempty intersection of component minimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), where every \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) attains its minimum, and suppose
\[X_{\cap}=\bigcap_{i=1}^n\operatorname*{argmin}f_i\ne\varnothing.\]
Then every shared minimizer minimizes the aggregate, so \(X_{\cap}\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}f\), and for \(x^*\in X_{\cap}\),
\[f(x)-f(x^*)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(x^*)\bigr)\ge0.\]
If the components are differentiable, \(\nabla f_i(x^*)=0\) for every \(i\). Aggregate minimization alone does not generally imply membership in \(X_{\cap}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common component minimizer also minimizes the average and makes every component gradient vanish when differentiable; an aggregate minimizer need not be common.

notation.meaning: Intersection of all component minimizer sets.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shared-minimizer inclusion and differentiable consequence are correct and fit a property record, but the record lacks evidence for both the property and converse failure.

children.title: Approximate-Interpolation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Near-interpolation settings with residual component incompatibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate-Interpolation Residual Can Depend on the Selected Aggregate Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of optimizer-independent residuals without additional component structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) and \(f_2(x,y)=x^2-y^2\). Their average is \(f(x,y)=x^2\), with \(X^*=\{(0,y):y\in\mathbb R\}\). At \(x_y^*=(0,y)\), \[\frac12\sum_{i=1}^2\|\nabla f_i(x_y^*)\|^2=4y^2.\] Thus the residual is zero at \((0,0)\) and arbitrarily large at other minimizers of the same aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonconvex components, different aggregate minimizers can have different and unbounded interpolation residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma_*^2(x_y^*)=4y^2,\text{ so the residual depends on the selected }x^*\in X^*.

notation.meaning: component-gradient second moment at the selected minimizer

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Interpolation Residual Can Depend on the Selected Aggregate Minimizer

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth-convex sufficient condition for a small component-gradient residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every \(f_i\) be convex and differentiable with \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient, and choose an aggregate minimizer \(x^*\). With \(f_i^*=\inf_x f_i(x)\), \[\|\nabla f_i(x^*)\|^2\le2L_i(f_i(x^*)-f_i^*),\] and hence \[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|\nabla f_i(x^*)\|^2\le\frac2n\sum_{i=1}^nL_i(f_i(x^*)-f_i^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth convex components, component value gaps at an aggregate optimizer upper-bound its interpolation residual.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f_i\) is convex with an \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Component Suboptimality Controls Interpolation Residual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Control of component-gradient noise near a selected aggregate optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}F\), where \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), and suppose \[ rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|
abla f_i(x^*)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2,\qquad  rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(y)\|^2\le L^2\|x-y\|^2.\] Then, for every \(x\), \[ rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|
abla f_i(x)\|^2\le2\varepsilon^2+2L^2\|x-x^*\|^2.\] The uniformly sampled component-gradient variance at \(x\) is therefore at most the same quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean-square component smoothness propagates a small interpolation residual at a selected optimizer into a distance-dependent component-noise bound.
assumptions_latex: The component-gradient second moment at \(x^*\) is at most \(\varepsilon^2\).
The displayed mean-square smoothness condition holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation of an Approximate-Interpolation Residual
Approximate-Interpolation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual component-gradient energy at an aggregate optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), with differentiable components, and choose \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\). For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the finite sum satisfies \(\varepsilon\)-approximate interpolation at \(x^*\) when
\[\sigma_*^2:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|\nabla f_i(x^*)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2.\]
Because \(\nabla f(x^*)=0\), \(\sigma_*^2\) is exactly the variance of a uniformly sampled component gradient at \(x^*\). Exact interpolation is the boundary case \(\varepsilon=0\); positive \(\varepsilon\) quantifies persistent component noise despite aggregate stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate interpolation bounds the mean squared component gradient at an aggregate optimizer; zero tolerance recovers exact interpolation.

notation.meaning: Component-gradient second moment at the selected optimizer.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is internally consistent for a selected aggregate optimizer, but the epsilon-squared convention and optimizer-dependent notion of approximate interpolation require a source.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Finite-Sum Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient and sampling-variance geometry without component or aggregate convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable but need not be convex, and let \(I\) be uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Then
\[
abla f(x)=\mathbb{E}_I[
abla f_I(x)]\]
and the component-gradient dispersion has the exact representation
\[\mathbb{E}_I\|
abla f_I(x)-
abla f(x)\|^2= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|
abla f_i(x)\|^2-\|
abla f(x)\|^2.\]
In this geometry, a first-order target is aggregate stationarity \(\|
abla f(x)\|=0\); it need not imply component stationarity or global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a nonconvex finite sum, the component gradient is unbiased and has an exact variance decomposition, while aggregate stationarity need not mean component stationarity or optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}_I\nabla f_I(x)=\nabla f(x)\) with the displayed variance identity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aggregate Stationarity Has Two Independent Limitations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete witnesses that aggregate stationarity need imply neither component stationarity nor optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f_1(x)=(x-1)^2\) and \(f_2(x)=(x+1)^2\), their average has \(f'(0)=0\), while \(f_1'(0)=-2\) and \(f_2'(0)=2\); aggregate stationarity therefore need not imply component stationarity. Separately, for the one-component finite sum \(h(x)=(x^2-1)^2\), \(h'(0)=0\) but \(h(0)=1>0=\min h\); aggregate stationarity therefore need not imply global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient cancellation defeats component stationarity, and a nonconvex stationary point can be globally suboptimal.
assumptions_latex: All displayed component functions are differentiable.
Equal weighting is used in the two-component example.

children.title: Component Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric structure attached to individual finite-sum components.

knowledge_statements.title: Component Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space representation of component values and gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For differentiable components \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\), define the component-value map and component-gradient operator by
\[\mathcal{F}(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_n(x)),\qquad G(x)=(
abla f_1(x),\ldots,
abla f_n(x))\in(\mathbb{R}^d)^n.\]
With the product norm \(\|G(x)\|_{\mathrm{prod}}^2=n^{-1}\sum_i\|
abla f_i(x)\|^2\), component geometry records directions, smoothness constants, curvature, and minimizer sets separately for each index. The averaging operator \(A(v_1,\ldots,v_n)=n^{-1}\sum_i v_i\) maps this product geometry to the aggregate gradient through \(A(G(x))=
abla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component geometry retains every component value and gradient in product space; averaging the gradient tuple produces the aggregate gradient.

notation.meaning: Uniform averaging operator on the gradient product space.

children.title: Aggregate Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric structure of the averaged or summed objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective, gradient, and curvature obtained by averaging component geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) with differentiable components,
\[f(x)= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x),\qquad 
abla f(x)= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
abla f_i(x).\]
If the components are twice differentiable, then \(
abla^2f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_i
abla^2f_i(x)\). Consequently, component directions or curvatures may cancel under averaging: aggregate stationarity need not imply \(
abla f_i(x)=0\) for every \(i\), and aggregate convexity need not imply component convexity. Aggregate geometry therefore concerns the averaged objective and its derivatives rather than the full component tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregate geometry is obtained by averaging component values and derivatives; cancellation means aggregate stationarity or convexity need not hold componentwise.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f_i\) is differentiable; Hessian claims additionally require twice differentiability.

children.title: Individual Component Smoothness
children.top_down_role: Smoothness controls specified component by component.

knowledge_statements.title: Individual Component Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-component Lipschitz-gradient regularity in a finite-sum model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and let \(L_i\ge0\). Component \(i\) is \(L_i\)-smooth when
\[\|\nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\|\le L_i\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d.\]
This condition implies the quadratic upper model
\[f_i(y)\le f_i(x)+\langle\nabla f_i(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L_i}{2}\|y-x\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d.\]
If \(f_i\) is additionally convex, the quadratic upper model is equivalent to \(L_i\)-Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla f_i\). The constants may vary with \(i\), and individual smoothness itself does not require convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each component may have its own gradient-Lipschitz constant. Gradient Lipschitz continuity implies the quadratic upper model without convexity; the converse holds when the component is convex.
assumptions_latex: Convexity is additionally assumed only for the converse implication.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\|\le L_i\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and this implies the displayed quadratic upper model.

children.title: Average Smoothness
children.top_down_role: Regularity controls expressed through averages across components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate and componentwise Lipschitz consequences of the mean-square component-gradient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\|
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(y)\|^2\le L_{\mathrm{av}}^2\|x-y\|^2\) and \(f=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\), then \(\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le L_{\mathrm{av}}\|x-y\|\) and \(\|
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(y)\|\le\sqrt nL_{\mathrm{av}}\|x-y\|\) for every \(i\). Both universal factors are sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average smoothness makes the average objective L_av-smooth and every component sqrt(n)L_av-smooth, with sharp factors.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable for every \(i\).
The family satisfies the average-smoothness inequality.
review_flags: Sharpness is witnessed by identical increments for the aggregate bound and by one active component for the component bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Consequences of Average Smoothness
Average Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root-mean-square aggregation of component gradient Lipschitz constants for a finite sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where every \(f_i\) is differentiable. The family has average-smoothness constant \(L_{\mathrm{av}}\ge 0\) if
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\lVert \nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\rVert^2\le L_{\mathrm{av}}^2\lVert x-y\rVert^2
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d.
\]
If each component gradient is \(L_i\)-Lipschitz, the condition holds with \(L_{\mathrm{av}}=(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n L_i^2)^{1/2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average smoothness bounds the mean squared change of component gradients by a single root-mean-square regularity constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n^{-1}\sum_i\lVert\nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\rVert^2\le L_{\mathrm{av}}^2\lVert x-y\rVert^2\) for all \(x,y\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the component gradient

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard root-mean-square component-smoothness condition used in finite-sum variance-reduction analysis
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically precise, matches the Average Smoothness leaf, and uses the correct content kind, but no inspectable source is supplied for the terminology or normalization.

children.title: Smoothness Heterogeneity
children.top_down_role: Variation among component smoothness scales and its structural consequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothness Heterogeneity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensionless dispersion measures for unequal component gradient smoothness constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(\nabla f_i\) is \(L_i\)-Lipschitz for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). Define
\[
\bar L=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n L_i,\qquad L_{\mathrm{rms}}=\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nL_i^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad H=\frac{L_{\mathrm{rms}}^2}{\bar L^2}.
\]
When \(\bar L>0\), one has \(1\le H\le n\). Moreover, \(H=1\) exactly when all \(L_i\) are equal, while large \(H\) indicates that smoothness is concentrated in relatively few components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smoothness heterogeneity compares the mean square and squared mean of component constants; it ranges from one to the number of components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\le H\le n\), with \(H=1\) if and only if \(L_1=\cdots=L_n\).

notation.meaning: arithmetic mean of component smoothness constants

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary normalized second-moment measure of component smoothness dispersion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The heterogeneity ratio and its bounds are correct for nonnegative component constants with positive mean, and property is an appropriate content kind. An authoritative source with a specific locator is still required for this particular heterogeneity convention.

children.title: Expected-Smoothness Models
children.top_down_role: Sampling-aware smoothness controls used in finite-sum analysis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimum-referenced expected-smoothness convention for sampled finite-sum gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\), and let \(g_v\) be a square-integrable unbiased sampled gradient. The model satisfies optimum-referenced expected smoothness with constant \(\mathcal L\ge0\) if
\[
\mathbb E\|g_v(x)-g_v(x_\star)\|^2\le2\mathcal L\bigl(f(x)-f(x_\star)\bigr)
\quad\text{for every }x.
\]
An all-pairs Bregman-divergence inequality implies this condition by setting \(y=x_\star\) when \(\nabla f(x_\star)=0\); the optimum-referenced condition alone asserts nothing for arbitrary pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected smoothness commonly bounds sampled gradient increments from an optimum by objective suboptimality; an all-pairs Bregman version is stronger.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and has an unconstrained minimizer \(x_\star\).
review_flags: Terminology varies: some sources reserve expected smoothness for the optimum-referenced form and treat the all-pairs Bregman inequality separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimum-Referenced Expected Smoothness
Expected-Smoothness Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise expected-smoothness condition for an unbiased sampled finite-sum gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f=\mathbb{E}[f_v]\), where \(v\) is a sampling variable and \(f_v\) is differentiable. The sampling model satisfies expected smoothness with constant \(\mathcal L\ge0\) if, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\),
\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert\nabla f_v(x)-\nabla f_v(y)\rVert^2\right]
\le 2\mathcal L\bigl(f(x)-f(y)-\langle\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\bigr).
\]
This formulation presumes the right-hand Bregman divergence is nonnegative, as occurs when \(f\) is convex, and makes the regularity constant dependent on the sampling law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected smoothness bounds the sampled gradient-difference second moment by a multiple of the objective’s Bregman divergence.
assumptions_latex: \(f_v:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable almost surely and \(\mathbb{E}[\nabla f_v(x)]=\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert\nabla f_v(x)-\nabla f_v(y)\rVert^2]\le2\mathcal L D_f(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\).

notation.meaning: sampled component or reweighted sampled objective
Bregman divergence of the differentiable convex objective

review_flags: exact expected-smoothness convention varies between pairwise and optimum-referenced formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed pairwise condition is coherent, but expected-smoothness terminology is also commonly used for an optimum-referenced condition. Without a dedicated source, the intended convention and hypotheses cannot be reliably matched to this leaf.

children.title: Expected-Residual Models
children.top_down_role: Sampling-aware residual controls for stochastic component access.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Residual Does Not Imply Expected Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict separation between centered residual control and uncentered expected smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For deterministic sampling with \(g_v(x)=
abla f(x)\), the centered residual is identically zero for every differentiable \(f\). Taking \(f(x)=x^4\) and \(x_\star=0\), no finite \(\mathcal L\) satisfies \(\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(x_\star)\|^2\le2\mathcal L(f(x)-f(x_\star))\) for all \(x\), since this would require \(16x^6\le2\mathcal Lx^4\) globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero centered residual need not give expected smoothness: deterministic sampling of the quartic objective has zero residual but no finite global expected-smoothness constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho=0\) is valid for the centered residual, while no finite optimum-referenced expected-smoothness constant exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Expected Residual Does Not Imply Expected Smoothness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation of the expected residual as a variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Delta_v(x)=g_v(x)-g_v(x_\star)\), assume \(\mathbb E\|\Delta_v(x)\|^2<\infty\), and suppose \(\mathbb E\Delta_v(x)=\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(x_\star)\). Then
\[
\mathbb E\|\Delta_v(x)-\mathbb E\Delta_v(x)\|^2
=\mathbb E\|\Delta_v(x)\|^2-\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(x_\star)\|^2.
\]
Hence an uncentered increment bound implies the corresponding centered residual bound with the same right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expected residual is the variance of the sampled gradient increment and equals its second moment minus the squared mean increment.
assumptions_latex: The sampled gradient increment is unbiased.

notation.meaning: sampled gradient increment from the reference minimizer

knowledge_statements.title: Centered-Increment Variance Identity
Expected-Residual Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Centered stochastic-gradient residual bound relative to a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin} f\), let \(g_v(x)=\nabla f_v(x)\), and assume \(\mathbb{E}[g_v(x)]=\nabla f(x)\). The sampling model satisfies an expected-residual condition with constant \(\rho\ge0\) if
\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\lVert g_v(x)-g_v(x_\star)-\bigl(\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(x_\star)\bigr)\right\rVert^2\right]
\le 2\rho\bigl(f(x)-f(x_\star)\bigr)
\]
for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\). The centering removes the mean gradient increment and isolates sampling variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expected-residual model bounds the variance of sampled gradient increments around their mean by objective suboptimality.

\(g_v\) is unbiased and square-integrable at every point considered.

children.title: Sampling-Dependent Regularity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of expectation-based regularity constants on the sampling design.

assumptions_latex: For every \(i\), \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable and \(\lVert\nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\rVert\le L_i\lVert x-y\rVert\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(L_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert g_I(x)-g_I(y)\rVert^2]\le \bigl(n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^n L_i^2/p_i\bigr)\lVert x-y\rVert^2\); if every \(L_i>0\), the coefficient is minimized over strictly positive probability vectors by \(p_i=L_i/\sum_{j=1}^nL_j\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct finite-sum importance-sampling second-moment calculation
strict-positivity qualification added for attainment of the optimal sampling distribution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity constant induced by importance sampling of component gradients, with attainment of the optimal probabilities stated only when all component constants are positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), let \(\nabla f_i\) be \(L_i\)-Lipschitz, and sample \(I=i\) with probability \(p_i>0\). For the unbiased estimator \(g_I(x)=(np_I)^{-1}\nabla f_I(x)\),
\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert g_I(x)-g_I(y)\rVert^2\right]
\le \left(\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{L_i^2}{p_i}\right)\lVert x-y\rVert^2.
\]
Thus the displayed mean-square regularity bound depends on the sampling law. If \(L_i>0\) for every \(i\), its coefficient is minimized over strictly positive probability vectors by \(p_i=L_i/\sum_{j=1}^nL_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Importance-sampling probabilities determine the mean-square Lipschitz bound of the unbiased component-gradient estimator. When every component smoothness constant is positive, probabilities proportional to those constants minimize the displayed bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Dependent Regularity
Heterogeneous Component Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise regularity model allowing distinct smoothness and convexity parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A differentiable finite-sum model \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) has heterogeneous component regularity on a convex set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) when each component is assigned constants \(L_i\ge0\) and \(\mu_i\ge0\) such that, for all \(x,y\in X\),
\[
\frac{\mu_i}{2}\lVert x-y\rVert^2
\le f_i(x)-f_i(y)-\langle\nabla f_i(y),x-y\rangle
\le\frac{L_i}{2}\lVert x-y\rVert^2.
\]
The parameter pairs may vary with \(i\); no common component constant is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heterogeneous regularity assigns each finite-sum component its own smoothness and strong-convexity constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_i\) obeys component-specific quadratic lower and upper first-order bounds with parameters \((\mu_i,L_i)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One Component Response Does Not Determine the Aggregate Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary between incremental and aggregate first-order access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R\) with \(n=2\), query component \(1\) at \(x=0\). The finite sums
\[
(f_1,f_2)=(0,0)
\quad\text{and}\quad
(\widetilde f_1,\widetilde f_2)=(0,z\mapsto z)
\]
produce the same queried value and gradient for component \(1\), but their aggregate gradients at zero are \(0\) and \(1/2\), respectively. Hence one incremental response does not generally determine the full gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two finite sums can agree on the queried component response while having different aggregate gradients.
assumptions_latex: The oracle query is restricted to component \(1\) at \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Identical single-component oracle responses need not determine \(\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: One Component Response Does Not Determine the Aggregate Gradient

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order access to one selected differentiable finite-sum component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) with differentiable components, an incremental first-order oracle accepts \((i,x)\) and returns \(\nabla f_i(x)\). A declared value–gradient variant additionally returns \(f_i(x)\). The index may be chosen deterministically, randomly, or adaptively from the past transcript. One call reveals only the queried component's response; sampling rules, importance weights, persistent memory, and aggregate access are separate interface choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incremental first-order oracle returns exact first-order information for one selected component, optionally with its value under a declared convention.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at queried points.
The response convention specifies whether component values are included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A query \((i,x)\) returns \(\nabla f_i(x)\), optionally paired with \(f_i(x)\), and exposes no unqueried component response.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental First-Order Access Contract
Incremental First-Order Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-component value-and-gradient access for differentiable finite sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) with differentiable components, an incremental first-order oracle is a map \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{IFO}}\) that, on a query \((i,x)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\times\mathbb{R}^d\), returns
\[
\mathcal O_{\mathrm{IFO}}(i,x)=\bigl(f_i(x),\nabla f_i(x)\bigr).
\]
An algorithm may choose \(i\) deterministically, adaptively, or randomly using its past transcript. One oracle call exposes information about only the queried component; aggregate quantities require additional oracle access or stored information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incremental first-order oracle returns the value and gradient of one selected finite-sum component at a query point.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Incremental Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-component proximal access for extended-real-valued finite-sum terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), where each \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and closed. A proximal incremental oracle receives \((i,x,\lambda)\) with \(\lambda>0\) and returns a point
\[
\mathcal O_{\mathrm{PIO}}(i,x,\lambda)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^d}
\left\{f_i(z)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert z-x\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
When \(f_i\) is convex, this returned point is unique. Each call accesses only the selected component’s proximal mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal incremental oracle evaluates the proximal mapping of one selected finite-sum component at a chosen point and stepsize.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i\) is proper and closed, and the displayed minimizer exists.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Component Proximal Optimality and Fixed-Point Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion and fixed-point certificates for an exact convex component proximal response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_i\) be proper, closed, and convex and let \(\lambda>0\). Then
\[
z=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f_i}(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{x-z}{\lambda}\in\partial f_i(z).
\]
In particular,
\[
x=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f_i}(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in\partial f_i(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f_i.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A component proximal response is certified by its subgradient inclusion, and its fixed points are exactly the component minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f_i}(x)\iff(x-z)/\lambda\in\partial f_i(z)\), and proximal fixed points minimize \(f_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Component Proximal Optimality and Fixed-Point Tests

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Averaged Component Proximal Maps Need Not Equal the Aggregate Proximal Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of reconstructing the proximal map of an average by averaging component responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R\), let \(f_1(z)=0\), \(f_2(z)=\tfrac12(z-a)^2\), \(f=\tfrac12(f_1+f_2)=\tfrac14(z-a)^2\), and use proximal parameter \(1\). Then
\[
\frac12\left(\operatorname{prox}_{f_1}(x)+\operatorname{prox}_{f_2}(x)\right)=\frac{3x+a}{4},
\qquad
\operatorname{prox}_{f}(x)=\frac{2x+a}{3}.
\]
They differ whenever \(x\ne a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for two convex quadratics, averaging component proximal points generally does not produce the proximal point of the averaged objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Averaged Component Proximal Maps Need Not Equal the Aggregate Proximal Map

children.title: Full-Gradient Oracles
children.top_down_role: Interfaces exposing complete aggregate-gradient evaluations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract aggregate-gradient access for a differentiable finite-sum objective, separated from implementation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) with differentiable components, an exact full-gradient oracle returns
\[
\mathcal O_{\mathrm{FG}}(x)=\nabla f(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla f_i(x).
\]
One oracle response is exact aggregate information. The abstract interface does not assign its implementation cost. If the only available primitive is uncached component-gradient evaluation and no additional structure is available, constructing the response uses one evaluation of every component at \(x\); other implementations may have different costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-gradient oracle returns the exact aggregate gradient; the cost of producing that response is a separate modeling choice.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at the query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{FG}}(x)=n^{-1}\sum_i\nabla f_i(x)\), without an intrinsic cost assignment.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Full-Gradient Access
Full-Gradient Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate gradient access for a differentiable finite-sum objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) with differentiable components, a full-gradient oracle is a map \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{FG}}\) satisfying
\[
\mathcal O_{\mathrm{FG}}(x)=\nabla f(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla f_i(x).
\]
The oracle interface treats the aggregate gradient as one query result. In an implementation using only incremental component-gradient access, evaluating this result exactly requires querying all \(n\) components at \(x\), unless reusable structure or cached exact values are available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-gradient oracle returns the exact average of all component gradients at the queried point.

children.title: Mixed Component–Aggregate Oracles
children.top_down_role: Interfaces combining component access with occasional aggregate access.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum oracle contract exposing both indexed component gradients and exact aggregate gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) with differentiable components, a mixed component–aggregate oracle supports
\[
\mathcal O_{\mathrm{mix}}(\mathrm{comp},i,x)=\nabla f_i(x),
\qquad
\mathcal O_{\mathrm{mix}}(\mathrm{full},x)=\nabla f(x).
\]
An algorithm may select and interleave these query types using its prior transcript. Availability of both responses does not prescribe their relative costs: complexity must retain separate query counts or invoke an explicitly declared cost conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed oracle exposes both component and exact aggregate gradients while leaving their relative costs to a separate cost model.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at the queried points.
The transcript and any adaptive query rule are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A transcript may contain both \(\nabla f_i(x)\) and \(\nabla f(x)\) responses, with no intrinsic conversion between their query counts.
review_flags: cost conversion intentionally excluded from the access contract
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Component–Aggregate Access Contract
Mixed Component–Aggregate Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle interface combining component-gradient and exact aggregate-gradient queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), a mixed component–aggregate oracle supports two query types:
\[
\mathcal O_{\mathrm{mix}}(\mathrm{comp},i,x)=\nabla f_i(x),
\qquad
\mathcal O_{\mathrm{mix}}(\mathrm{full},x)=\nabla f(x)=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\nabla f_j(x).
\]
An algorithm may interleave the query types adaptively. Its oracle complexity must report component and aggregate calls separately, or specify a conversion assigning an aggregate query the cost of \(n\) component-gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed oracle permits both individual component-gradient queries and exact full-gradient queries, with an explicit accounting rule for their different costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transcript may contain both \(\nabla f_i(x)\) and \(\nabla f(x)\) responses under a declared cost convention.
