knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-epoch contraction for variance-reduced mirror descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded contraction guarantee using the source-defined variance-reduced mirror-descent setting, notation, and potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(\theta_t=(1-\gamma\mu)^{-t}\) for all \(t\ge 0\), \(2L\gamma\le 1\), and \(\gamma\mu+4L_Q\gamma\le 1\). Define
\[
\Delta_s:=\gamma\mathbb E[\Psi(x^s)-\Psi(x^*)]+\mathbb E[V(x^s,x^*)]+(1-\gamma\mu-4L_Q\gamma)\mu^{-1}(\theta_T-\theta_1)\mathbb E[\Psi(\widetilde x^s)-\Psi(x^*)]
\]
and
\[
\rho:=\max\left\{\frac{1}{\theta_T},\frac{4L_Q\gamma(\theta_T-1)}{(1-\gamma\mu-4L_Q\gamma)(\theta_T-\theta_1)}\right\}.
\]
Then \(\Delta_s\le \rho\Delta_{s-1}\) for every \(s\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated weight and step-size conditions, the source-defined expected objective-and-Bregman potential for variance-reduced mirror descent contracts from epoch s−1 to epoch s by the factor rho for every s at least 1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Undersized ESO Constants Fail Even for Serial Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of the ESO majorant below the serial coordinate threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For serial sampling, choose a coordinate \(j\) with \(p_j>0\), set \(h_j=1\), and set all other entries of \(h\) to zero. If \(v_j<\|a_j\|^2\), then \[\mathbb E\left\|\sum_{i\in S}a_i h_i\right\|^2=p_j\|a_j\|^2>p_jv_j,\] so the ESO inequality fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A serial ESO vector cannot assign a coordinate a constant below its squared feature norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Undersized ESO Constants Fail Even for Serial Sampling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp ESO Constants for Serial Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialization of the ESO condition when exactly one coordinate is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(|S|=1\) almost surely and \(\mathbb P(S=\{i\})=p_i>0\), then \[\mathbb E\left\|\sum_{i\in S}a_i h_i\right\|^2=\sum_i p_i\|a_i\|^2h_i^2.\] Thus the coordinatewise minimal ESO constants are \(v_i=\|a_i\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For serial sampling, the sharp ESO constant of a coordinate is its squared feature norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp ESO Constants for Serial Sampling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matrix Characterization of the ESO Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent semidefinite form of the sampling-aware squared-norm majorant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_n]\), let \(P_{ij}=\mathbb P(i,j\in S)\), and let \(p_i=P_{ii}\). Then \[\mathbb E\left\|\sum_{i\in S}a_i h_i\right\|^2=h^{\mathsf T}\bigl(P\circ A^{\mathsf T}A\bigr)h.\] Consequently, the ESO inequality holds for every \(h\) if and only if \[P\circ A^{\mathsf T}A\preceq\operatorname{Diag}(p_1v_1,\ldots,p_nv_n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ESO inequality is exactly a semidefinite domination involving pairwise inclusion probabilities and the feature Gram matrix.
assumptions_latex: The feature vectors lie in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
First- and second-order inclusion probabilities exist.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Characterization of the ESO Condition
SDCA–Quartz Sampling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper coordinate and minibatch sampling conditions shared by SDCA–Quartz analyses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a random subset of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and define \(p_i=\mathbb{P}(i\in S)\) and \(P_{ij}=\mathbb{P}(i,j\in S)\). The sampling is proper when \(p_i>0\) for every \(i\). It is serial when \(|S|=1\) almost surely, uniform when all \(p_i\) coincide, and a fixed-size minibatch when \(|S|=\tau\) almost surely. A sampling-aware SDCA–Quartz step is admissible when its coordinate parameters are positive and the required expected-separable-overapproximation inequality \[\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\sum_{i\in S}a_i h_i\right\rVert^2\leq\sum_{i=1}^n p_i v_i h_i^2\] holds for all \(h\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with declared constants \(v_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Admissible regimes sample every coordinate with positive probability and use parameters controlling the expected squared norm of sampled coordinate combinations.
assumptions_latex: The feature vectors \(a_i\) belong to a common Euclidean space.
The random subset \(S\) has well-defined first- and second-order inclusion probabilities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The probabilities \(p_i\) and constants \(v_i\) specify a proper, sampling-compatible coordinate regime for SDCA–Quartz updates.
review_flags: A Quartz or arbitrary-sampling coordinate-descent source is required to certify the exact compatibility inequality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role is appropriate for the sampling-regime leaf, and the elementary sampling definitions are clear. The exact expected-separable-overapproximation inequality and its claim of admissibility for SDCA-Quartz updates require a Quartz or arbitrary-sampling source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased product-space representation for a sampled dual-block increment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let block \(i\) be sampled with probability \(p_i>0\), and let \(\delta_i\) be the dual increment that would be produced for block \(i\) from the current state. With \(U_i\) denoting the canonical block embedding, the probability-corrected realized increment is \(p_i^{-1}U_i\delta_i\), and \[\mathbb E[p_i^{-1}U_i\delta_i\mid\mathcal F_t]=\sum_{i=1}^nU_i\delta_i.\] Thus one sampled block can provide an unbiased estimate of the simultaneous product-space increment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dividing a sampled dual-block increment by its sampling probability makes its conditional mean equal the sum of all hypothetical block increments.
assumptions_latex: The hypothetical increments \(\delta_i\) are fixed under the pre-sampling history \(\mathcal F_t\).

notation.meaning: Canonical embedding of dual block i into the product space.
Information available before the current block draw.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uncorrected Random Block Increments Target the Wrong Product-Space Update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampling failure independent of a particular stochastic-PDHG ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let block \(i\) be sampled with probability \(p_i\), and let \(U_i\delta_i\) be its hypothetical product-space increment. Without inverse-probability correction, \[\mathbb E[U_i\delta_i\mid\mathcal F_t]=\sum_i p_iU_i\delta_i,\] which generally differs from \(\sum_iU_i\delta_i\). An algorithm claiming the latter conditional mean must use probability correction or redefine its target operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An uncorrected sampled dual-block increment averages to a probability-weighted operator, not the simultaneous block update.
assumptions_latex: The increments are fixed under the pre-sampling history.
At least one nonzero block has inclusion probability below one.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncorrected Random Block Increments Target the Wrong Product-Space Update
Random Primal–Dual Finite-Sum Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random block-coordinate primal–dual splitting for a separable finite-sum saddle problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min_{x\in X}\max_{y_i\in Y_i}\left\{g(x)+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(\langle A_i x,y_i\rangle-f_i^*(y_i)\bigr)\right\}.\] Initialize \(x_0\), dual blocks \(y_i^0\), and an aggregate \(z_0=n^{-1}\sum_iA_i^*y_i^0\). At iteration \(t\), sample \(i_t\) with probability \(p_{i_t}>0\), update \[y_{i_t}^{t+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma_{i_t}f_{i_t}^*}\bigl(y_{i_t}^t+\sigma_{i_t}A_{i_t}\bar x_t\bigr),\] leave other blocks fixed, update the aggregate incrementally, and set \(x_{t+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau g}(x_t-\tau z_{t+1})\). Return the declared averaged or terminal primal–dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random primal–dual method updates one sampled dual block, maintains its aggregate coupling, and performs a proximal primal step.
assumptions_latex: The functions \(g\) and \(f_i^*\) are proper, closed, and convex.
Every block has positive sampling probability.
Stepsizes satisfy the declared primal–dual operator-norm compatibility condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration changes one dual block and performs a coupled primal proximal update for the finite-sum saddle formulation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized single-component primal-dual method for a convex finite-sum objective. The extracted dual subproblem displays the coefficient \(\tau\), although the initialization declares a sequence \(\{\tau_t\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x^0=x^{-1}\in X\) and \(y_i^0=m^{-1}\nabla f_i(x^0)\). For \(t=1,\ldots,k\), sample \(i_t\) with \(\Pr(i_t=i)=p_i\), set
\[
\widetilde x^t=x^{t-1}+\alpha_t(x^{t-1}-x^{t-2}),
\]
and update
\[
y_i^t=\begin{cases}
\operatorname*{argmin}_{y_i\in\mathcal X_i}\{\langle-\widetilde x^t,y_i\rangle+J_i(y_i)+\tau W_i(y_i^{t-1},y_i)\},&i=i_t,\\
y_i^{t-1},&i\ne i_t.
\end{cases}
\]
Define
\[
\widetilde y_i^t=\begin{cases}
p_i^{-1}(y_i^t-y_i^{t-1})+y_i^{t-1},&i=i_t,\\
y_i^{t-1},&i\ne i_t,
\end{cases}
\]
and compute
\[
x^t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^m\widetilde y_i^t,x\right\rangle+h(x)+\mu v(x)+\eta_tV(x^{t-1},x)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, RPDG samples one finite-sum component, extrapolates the primal iterate, updates only the sampled dual block, applies an inverse-probability correction, and solves a Bregman-regularized primal subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^t,y^t)_{t=1}^k\text{ is generated by the stated randomized primal-dual updates.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Efficient implementation of randomized primal-dual gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental implementation of RPDG using cached component gradients and their maintained aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x^0=x^{-1}\in X\), \(\underline x_i^0=x^0\), \(y_i^0=m^{-1}\nabla f_i(x^0)\), and \(g^0=\sum_{i=1}^my_i^0\). For \(t=1,\ldots,k\), sample \(i_t\) with \(\Pr(i_t=i)=p_i\), set
\[
\widetilde x^t=x^{t-1}+\alpha_t(x^{t-1}-x^{t-2}),
\]
\[
\underline x_i^t=\begin{cases}(1+\tau_t)^{-1}(\widetilde x^t+\tau_t\underline x_i^{t-1}),&i=i_t,\\\underline x_i^{t-1},&i\ne i_t,\end{cases}\qquad
y_i^t=\begin{cases}m^{-1}\nabla f_i(\underline x_i^t),&i=i_t,\\y_i^{t-1},&i\ne i_t.\end{cases}
\]
Compute
\[
x^t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\{\langle g^{t-1}+p_{i_t}^{-1}(y_{i_t}^t-y_{i_t}^{t-1}),x\rangle+h(x)+\mu v(x)+\eta_tV(x^{t-1},x)\},
\]
and update
\[
g^t=g^{t-1}+y_{i_t}^t-y_{i_t}^{t-1}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The efficient RPDG implementation caches each component gradient and their sum. An iteration refreshes only the sampled component, uses its inverse-probability-corrected change in the primal subproblem, and updates the cached sum incrementally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^t,y^t,g^t)_{t=1}^k\text{ is generated with one sampled component-gradient refresh per iteration.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Initial dual-divergence bounds for randomized primal-dual finite-sum analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization bounds connecting the method's aggregate dual Bregman divergence to primal geometry and objective suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x^0\in X\), let \(y_i^0=m^{-1}\nabla f_i(x^0)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and use \(J_i'(y_i^0)=x^0\) in the definition of \(W(y^0,y)\). For every \(x\in X\) with \(y_i=m^{-1}\nabla f_i(x)\),
\[
W(y^0,y)\le \frac{L_f}{2}\|x^0-x\|^2\le L_fV(x^0,x).
\]
If \(x^*\) is an optimal solution and \(y_i^*=m^{-1}\nabla f_i(x^*)\), then
\[
W(y^0,y^*)\le \Psi(x^0)-\Psi(x^*).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the specified gradient initialization and subgradient selection, the initial aggregate dual Bregman divergence to a gradient-generated dual point is bounded by the smoothness quadratic and primal Bregman distance. At an optimum it is also bounded by the initial objective gap.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is optimal and }y_i^*=\frac1m\nabla f_i(x^*)\text{ for the second bound}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Bregman identities for a sampled dual block
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step conditional-expectation identities for the dual-coordinate update in the random primal-dual finite-sum method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y^t\), \(\widetilde y^t\), and \(\widehat y^t\) be defined by the referenced RPDG updates. For every \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(t=1,\ldots,k\),
\[
\mathbb E_t[W_i(y_i^{t-1},y_i^t)]=p_iW_i(y_i^{t-1},\widehat y_i^t).
\]
For every \(y\in\mathcal Y\),
\[
\mathbb E_t[W_i(y_i^t,y_i)]=p_iW_i(\widehat y_i^t,y_i)+(1-p_i)W_i(y_i^{t-1},y_i),
\]
where \(\mathbb E_t\) is conditional expectation with respect to \(i_t\) given \(i_1,\ldots,i_{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditioned on the sampling history, a component's expected Bregman movement equals its full-update movement times its sampling probability. Its expected divergence to a comparison component is the probability-weighted mixture of the updated and unchanged divergences.
assumptions_latex: y^t,\widetilde y^t,\widehat y^t\text{ are defined by the referenced RPDG updates}
y\in\mathcal Y\text{ for the second identity}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbiased Inner Estimates Do Not Produce an Unbiased Prox-Linear Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinearity boundary for abstract variance-reduced inner-value and Jacobian estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Separate unbiasedness of \(\widehat c\) and \(\widehat J\) does not imply unbiasedness of \(h(\widehat c+\widehat Jd)\). Let \(h(u)=u^2\), \(c=0\), \(Jd=0\), \(\widehat Jd=0\), and let \(\widehat c\) equal \(1\) or \(-1\) with equal probability. Then \(\mathbb E[\widehat c]=c\), but \[\mathbb E[h(\widehat c+\widehat Jd)]=1\ne0=h(c+Jd).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unbiased value and Jacobian estimates can become biased after passing through a nonlinear convex outer function.
assumptions_latex: The outer function is nonlinear and convex.
The random inner-value estimator is integrable.

Variance-Reduced Prox-Linear Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance-reduced prox-linear update for finite-sum composite objectives with smooth inner maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n h_i(c_i(x))+r(x)\), where each \(h_i\) is convex and each \(c_i\) is differentiable. At iteration \(t\), construct variance-reduced estimators \(\widehat c_t\) and \(\widehat J_t\) of the sampled or averaged inner-map value and Jacobian using snapshot or recursive corrections. Compute \[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x}\left\{\widehat h_t\bigl(\widehat c_t+\widehat J_t(x-x_t)\bigr)+r(x)+\frac{1}{2\eta_t}\lVert x-x_t\rVert^2\right\},\] where \(\widehat h_t\) denotes the declared sampled or aggregated outer model. Refresh the estimators according to a fixed schedule and return the prescribed iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method builds variance-reduced estimates of a composite model and minimizes its regularized linearization at each iteration.
assumptions_latex: Each outer function \(h_i\) is proper and convex, and each inner map \(c_i\) is differentiable.
The regularized prox-linear subproblem is solvable.
Estimator sampling and refresh rules are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The next iterate minimizes a variance-reduced linearized composite model stabilized by a quadratic proximal term.

The outer-model aggregation is left explicit but abstract.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epoch-based accelerated variance reduction with snapshot gradients and Bregman-proximal composite updates; notation is retained from the extraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(\widetilde x^0=x^0\). At epoch \(s\), set \(\widetilde x=\widetilde x^{s-1}\), \(\widetilde g=\nabla F(\widetilde x)\), \(x_0=x^{s-1}\), and \(\bar x_0=\widetilde x\). For \(t=1,\ldots,T_s\), sample \(i_t\sim Q\) and set
\[\underline x_t=\frac{(1+\mu\gamma_s)(1-\alpha_s-p_s)\bar x_{t-1}+\alpha_sx_{t-1}+(1+\mu\gamma_s)p_s\widetilde x}{1+\mu\gamma_s(1-\alpha_s)},\]
\[G_t=\frac{\nabla f_{i_t}(\underline x_t)-\nabla f_{i_t}(\widetilde x)}{q_{i_t}n}+\widetilde g,\]
\[x_t\in\arg\min_{x\in X}\left\{\gamma_s\left[\langle G_t,x\rangle+h(x)+\mu V(\underline x_t,x)\right]+V(x_{t-1},x)\right\},\]
\[\bar x_t=(1-\alpha_s-p_s)\bar x_{t-1}+\alpha_sx_t+p_s\widetilde x.\]
Set \(x^s=x_{T_s}\) and
\[\widetilde x^s=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T_s}\theta_t\bar x_t}{\sum_{t=1}^{T_s}\theta_t}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each epoch computes a full gradient at a snapshot, forms snapshot-corrected component-gradient estimates, performs accelerated composite Bregman-proximal updates, and returns the last inner iterate together with a weighted average.
assumptions_latex: Q=(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\text{ is a probability distribution and }q_{i_t}>0\text{ almost surely}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^s,\widetilde x^s)\text{ are generated by the displayed epochwise recursion.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restarted accelerated variance reduction: contraction and component-gradient complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded, algorithm-specific guarantee under condition (5.4.35) and the source-defined parameters. The unresolved cross-references and implicit integer conventions prevent interpretation beyond that stated setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_i=L_i/\sum_{j=1}^m L_j\), let \(\theta_t\) be defined by (5.4.12), and choose \(\{\gamma_s\},\{p_s\},\{\alpha_s\}\) as in (5.4.17) and (5.4.18). Set \(T_s=T_1 2^{s-1}\) for \(s\le s_0\) and \(T_s=T_{s_0}\) for \(s>s_0\), where \(s_0=4\), \(s=s_0+4\sqrt{L/(\bar\mu m)}\), and \(T_1=\min\{m,L/\bar\mu\}\). Under (5.4.35), for every \(x^*\in X^*\), \[\mathbb E[\psi(\widetilde x^s)-\psi(x^*)]\le \frac{5}{16}[\psi(x^0)-\psi(x^*)].\] Moreover, if Algorithm 5.7 is restarted \(k=\log((\psi(x^0)-\psi(x^*))/\varepsilon)\) times, with \(s\) iterations per restart, then \[\mathbb E[\psi(\widetilde x^{sk})-\psi(x^*)]\le \left(\frac{5}{16}\right)^k[\psi(x^0)-\psi(x^*)]\le\varepsilon,\] and its total number of component-gradient evaluations is \[\bar N=\mathcal O\!\left(\left(m+\sqrt{\frac{mL}{\bar\mu}}\right)\log\frac{\psi(x^0)-\psi(x^*)}{\varepsilon}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With sampling probabilities proportional to component smoothness constants and the source-defined acceleration parameters and stage schedule, Algorithm 5.7 reduces the expected objective gap by a factor of 5/16 under condition (5.4.35). The prescribed restart scheme reaches expected error at most epsilon with order (m plus the square root of mL divided by bar-mu) times the logarithm of the initial-gap-to-epsilon ratio component-gradient evaluations.
assumptions_latex: k=\log\frac{\psi(x^0)-\psi(x^*)}{\varepsilon}\text{ restarts are performed, each with }s\text{ iterations}

children.title: Estimate-Sequence Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Variance-reduction acceleration organized through estimate-sequence structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Estimate-Sequence Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nesterov estimate-sequence invariant used to accelerate variance-reduced first-order methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an objective \(F\) with minimum value \(F^*\), an estimate sequence is a pair \((\varphi_k,\lambda_k)\) with \(\lambda_k\geq0\), \(\lambda_k\to0\), and \[\varphi_k(x)\leq(1-\lambda_k)F(x)+\lambda_k\varphi_0(x)\qquad\text{for every }x.\] If an algorithm produces iterates satisfying \(F(x_k)\leq\varphi_k^*:=\inf_x\varphi_k(x)\), then \[F(x_k)-F^*\leq\lambda_k\bigl(\varphi_0(x^*)-F^*\bigr)\] for every minimizer \(x^*\). In a stochastic variance-reduced construction, both displayed inequalities may instead hold in expectation with respect to the algorithmic history.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An estimate sequence transfers a decaying upper model into an objective-gap bound; accelerated rates follow from making its weight decay rapidly.
assumptions_latex: The objective \(F\) attains its minimum at some \(x^*\).
The estimate functions have finite infima \(\varphi_k^*\).
The deterministic inequalities hold pointwise, or their stochastic counterparts hold in expectation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x_k)-F^*\leq\lambda_k(\varphi_0(x^*)-F^*)\), with the analogous expected bound in the stochastic case.

notation.meaning: minimum value of the estimate function

review_flags: An authoritative estimate-sequence source and a variance-reduced specialization locator are absent from the supplied inventory.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle role fits the estimate-sequence acceleration leaf, and the deterministic implication is stated precisely. No authoritative source is supplied for the estimate-sequence definition or for the proposed expectation-based variance-reduced extension, whose conditioning and placement of expectations require source-specific formulation.

children.title: Linear-Coupling Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Variance-reduction acceleration organized through linear coupling.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Coupling Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceleration by coupling a gradient step with a mirror or proximal step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be convex and differentiable, and let \(h\) generate the Bregman divergence \(D_h\). At iteration \(t\), form a coupled query point \(x_t=(1-\theta_t)y_t+\theta_t z_t\). Using a gradient or conditionally unbiased variance-reduced estimator \(v_t\), compute \[y_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t v_t,\qquad z_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z}\left\{\langle \alpha_t v_t,z\rangle+D_h(z,z_t)\right\}.\] Choose \(\theta_t\), \(\eta_t\), and \(\alpha_t\) so that the gradient-descent decrease and mirror-descent regret terms cancel in a weighted potential inequality. The declared output is \(y_T\) or a prescribed weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear coupling combines a descent step and a mirror step at one mixed query point, choosing weights so their potential terms cancel.
assumptions_latex: The objective \(F\) is convex and has Lipschitz-continuous gradient in the chosen geometry.
The mirror map \(h\) is strongly convex.
The estimator \(v_t\) is exact or conditionally unbiased with controlled second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatible parameters yield a telescoping coupled potential, which is the acceleration mechanism.
review_flags: An authoritative linear-coupling source and its variance-reduced compatibility conditions are absent from the supplied inventory.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle role fits the linear-coupling leaf, but 'compatible parameters' and the claimed potential cancellation are not mathematically specified. An authoritative linear-coupling source, plus a variance-reduced specialization when stochastic estimators are included, is required to validate the update geometry and compatibility conditions.

children.title: Coupling-Compatibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Estimator and geometry regimes supporting the respective acceleration principles.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupling-Compatibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility conditions for coupling accelerated and variance-reduced updates on a composite finite sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)+\psi(x)\), where every \(f_i\) is convex and \(L_i\)-smooth and \(\psi\) is proper, closed, and convex. A coupling regime is compatible when its mixing coefficients satisfy \(\tau_1>0\), \(\tau_2\ge 0\), and \(\tau_1+\tau_2\le 1\); its estimator satisfies \(\mathbb E_k[g_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\); and its proximal step size \(\eta\) obeys the estimator-dependent stability restriction \(\eta V\le c\tau_1\), where \(V\) is a valid conditional variance constant and \(c>0\) is the coupling lemma's numerical constant. Under these conditions, the gradient, mirror, and snapshot contributions can share one nonnegative Lyapunov descent inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupling is compatible when mixing weights are convex, the gradient estimator is conditionally unbiased, and its variance-scaled step size fits the acceleration weight.
assumptions_latex: A conditional variance bound with constant \(V\) is available.

notation.meaning: constant in the applicable conditional variance bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits, but f is not explicitly defined, V and c are formulation-dependent, and the asserted common Lyapunov inequality cannot be validated without a specific coupling lemma and locator.

children.title: Catalyst Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Catalyst wrappers for finite-sum variance-reduced methods.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer–inner tradeoff governing the Catalyst regularization parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Increasing \kappa decreases the inner condition number (L+\kappa)/(\mu+\kappa), but also decreases q=\mu/(\mu+\kappa). In the strongly convex Catalyst regime, the outer-stage factor scales as q^{-1/2}=\sqrt{(\mu+\kappa)/\mu}, up to logarithmic accuracy factors. Thus inner conditioning alone does not justify arbitrarily large \kappa.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: More regularization improves each inner problem but increases the required number of outer stages.
assumptions_latex: The strongly convex Catalyst estimate-sequence regime is used.
knowledge_statements.title: Catalyst Regularization Tradeoff

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature transformation caused by Catalyst quadratic regularization in the smooth strongly convex regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If F is L-smooth and \mu-strongly convex, then H_y(x)=F(x)+\frac{\kappa}{2}\lVert x-y\rVert^2 is (L+\kappa)-smooth and (\mu+\kappa)-strongly convex. Consequently, \chi_\kappa=(L+\kappa)/(\mu+\kappa)\le L/\mu.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Catalyst regularization improves inner-problem conditioning by adding the same curvature to smoothness and strong convexity.
assumptions_latex: F is differentiable, L-smooth, and \mu-strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Catalyst Subproblem Conditioning

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion between subproblem objective gap and gradient residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is differentiable, \(L\)-smooth, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex, then \(H_k\) is \((L+\kappa)\)-smooth and \((\mu+\kappa)\)-strongly convex. Hence every inner point \(x\) satisfies \[\frac{1}{2(L+\kappa)}\|\nabla H_k(x)\|^2\le H_k(x)-H_k^*\le\frac{1}{2(\mu+\kappa)}\|\nabla H_k(x)\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth strongly convex Catalyst subproblems, gradient residuals and objective gaps are quantitatively interchangeable certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Catalyst Subproblem Residual Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-gap interface between the Catalyst outer recurrence and an inner solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(H_k(x)=F(x)+\frac\kappa2\|x-y_k\|^2\), an inner output \(x_{k+1}\) has absolute accuracy \(\varepsilon_k\) when \[H_k(x_{k+1})-\min_xH_k(x)\le\varepsilon_k.\] If \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, then, writing \(x_k^*=\arg\min H_k\), \[\|x_{k+1}-x_k^*\|\le\sqrt{\frac{2\varepsilon_k}{\mu+\kappa}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified Catalyst subproblem objective gap controls distance to the exact proximal point.

notation.meaning: Exact minimizer of the kth Catalyst subproblem.

knowledge_statements.title: Catalyst Absolute Inner-Accuracy Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uncontrolled Inner Solves Can Stagnate Catalyst
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a Catalyst-style approximate proximal wrapper when inner outputs obey no accuracy condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(y_0=x_0\), \(x_{k+1}\) is an unrestricted output for \(H_k(x)=F(x)+\frac{\kappa}{2}\|x-y_k\|^2\), and \(y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+\beta_k(x_{k+1}-x_k)\). If the inner procedure always returns \(x_{k+1}=y_k\), then \(x_k=y_k=x_0\) for every \(k\). Hence, if \(x_0\notin\operatorname*{argmin}F\), the wrapper stagnates away from the optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without an enforceable inner-accuracy rule, a Catalyst-style wrapper can return its center forever and stagnate.
assumptions_latex: The inner procedure may return \(x_{k+1}=y_k\) without an accuracy certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Inner Solves Can Stagnate Catalyst
Catalyst Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Catalyst outer acceleration with approximate solutions of strongly convex proximal subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a \(\mu\)-strongly convex function \(F\), choose \(\kappa>0\), set \(q=\mu/(\mu+\kappa)\), \(y_0=x_0\), and \(\alpha_0=\sqrt q\). At outer iteration \(k\), approximately minimize \(H_k(x)=F(x)+\frac{\kappa}{2}\lVert x-y_k\rVert^2\) to obtain \(x_{k+1}\). Choose \(\alpha_{k+1}\in(0,1)\) satisfying \(\alpha_{k+1}^2=(1-\alpha_{k+1})\alpha_k^2+q\alpha_{k+1}\), define \(\beta_k=\alpha_k(1-\alpha_k)/(\alpha_k^2+\alpha_{k+1})\), and set \(y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+\beta_k(x_{k+1}-x_k)\). Stop when the prescribed outer criterion holds and return the latest \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Catalyst accelerates a base solver by approximately solving regularized proximal subproblems and extrapolating their successive solutions.
assumptions_latex: The inner method can meet the prescribed subproblem tolerances.

children.title: Proximal-Point Acceleration
children.top_down_role: Acceleration frameworks based on proximal-point outer structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Point Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nesterov acceleration applied to exact proximal-point evaluations in a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be proper, closed, and convex on a real Hilbert space. Choose \(\lambda>0\), initialize \(x_0=y_0\) and \(t_0=1\), and iterate \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(y_k)\), \(t_{k+1}=(1+\sqrt{1+4t_k^2})/2\), and \(y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+((t_k-1)/t_{k+1})(x_{k+1}-x_k)\). Equivalently, this is accelerated gradient descent on the Moreau envelope because \(\nabla F_\lambda(y)=\lambda^{-1}(y-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(y))\). Stop under a stated residual or iteration criterion and return the latest proximal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerated proximal point applies Nesterov extrapolation between exact proximal evaluations, equivalently accelerating gradient descent on the Moreau envelope.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, convex, and has a minimizer.
Exact evaluations of \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}\) are available.

Thus \lVert r_\lambda(y)\rVert\le\varepsilon certifies \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\le\varepsilon, and r_\lambda(y)=0 exactly when y=x is a minimizer of F.

children.title: Inner-Solver Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Variance-reduced solver families suitable for accelerated outer frameworks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual conversions for a strongly convex proximal subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H be proper, closed, and m-strongly convex with minimizer x_H^*. For x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial H and g\in\partial H(x), \lVert x-x_H^*\rVert\le\lVert g\rVert/m and H(x)-H^*\le\lVert g\rVert^2/(2m). Hence \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial H(x))\le\delta certifies distance error at most \delta/m and objective error at most \delta^2/(2m).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient residual certifies distance and objective error for a strongly convex inner problem.
assumptions_latex: H is proper, closed, and m-strongly convex with m>0.
A subgradient residual of H is computable.
knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Inner-Solve Certificates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal output interface between an inexact accelerated outer method and an inner solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compatibility is determined by the certificate required by the outer inexactness theorem, not by the inner estimator class. A deterministic, biased, or randomized inner method is admissible whenever its returned point satisfies the prescribed deterministic or conditional subproblem certificate at the required tolerance. Conditional unbiasedness is needed only when invoked by the particular inner convergence theorem used to establish that certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal acceleration wrapper requires a certified subproblem approximation, not universally an unbiased inner estimator.
assumptions_latex: The outer theorem specifies an enforceable subproblem certificate and tolerance.
Randomized guarantees are conditioned on the allowed outer history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Required certified error}\Longrightarrow\text{outer-interface compatibility, independently of estimator type}.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Agnostic Compatibility Principle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a strongly convex inner objective-gap certificate into pointwise subproblem accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H be proper, closed, and m-strongly convex with minimizer x_H^*. If H(x)-H^*\leq\varepsilon, then \lVert x-x_H^*\rVert\leq\sqrt{2\varepsilon/m}. Thus an outer method requiring point error at most r may accept the certificate H(x)-H^*\leq mr^2/2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity converts a certified inner objective gap into a distance-to-solution guarantee.
assumptions_latex: H is proper, closed, and m-strongly convex with m>0.
H attains its minimum at x_H^*.

notation.meaning: unique minimizer of the inner problem

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Gap-to-Distance Inner Certificate
Inner-Solver Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient interface conditions for an inexact solver used inside accelerated proximal-point outer iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subproblems \(H_k(x)=F(x)+\frac{\kappa}{2}\lVert x-y_k\rVert^2\), an inner solver is compatible if it accepts the warm start supplied by the outer method and returns \(x_{k+1}\) with a verifiable bound \(\mathbb E[H_k(x_{k+1})-H_k^*\mid\mathcal F_k]\le\varepsilon_k\). The tolerance sequence must satisfy the summability requirement imposed by the outer estimate sequence; a standard sufficient choice is \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)\sqrt{\varepsilon_k}<\infty\). For finite sums, each inner call must also preserve unbiasedness of its stochastic estimator conditional on \(\mathcal F_k\). These conditions prevent accumulated inner error from dominating accelerated outer convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible inner solver supplies conditional subproblem-error guarantees, preserves estimator unbiasedness, and meets a weighted summability schedule for its errors.
assumptions_latex: The outer method exposes its center, warm start, and tolerance.
Inner randomness is conditionally measurable relative to \(\mathcal F_k\).

notation.meaning: minimum value of the kth proximal subproblem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility-condition role fits, but the weighted summability rule depends on the outer inexact-acceleration theorem. Conditional estimator unbiasedness is not universally necessary for compatible deterministic or biased inner solvers, so a scoped source is needed.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Momentum Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Snapshot-directed negative momentum in accelerated finite-sum variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widetilde x\) be a snapshot at which a full gradient or control variate is stored. In a three-sequence variance-reduced method, form \(x_{k+1}=\tau_1 z_k+\tau_2\widetilde x+(1-\tau_1-\tau_2)y_k\), where \(\tau_1>0\), \(\tau_2>0\), and \(\tau_1+\tau_2\le1\). Relative to the evolving pair \((y_k,z_k)\), the fixed snapshot term acts as negative momentum: it repeatedly pulls the query point toward the estimator's reference point. Consequently, distances controlling estimator variance enter the same Lyapunov relation as the acceleration energy, allowing variance reduction without discarding the accelerated coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative momentum pulls each gradient query toward the control-variate snapshot, coupling variance control with accelerated movement of the other iterates.
assumptions_latex: A snapshot-based unbiased variance-reduced estimator is used.
The mixing coefficients form a convex combination.
The component functions are convex and smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=\tau_1z_k+\tau_2\widetilde x+(1-\tau_1-\tau_2)y_k\) includes a positive snapshot weight \(\tau_2\) that controls estimator variance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind and snapshot-directed interpretation match the node, but the claim that the snapshot term controls variance within a shared accelerated Lyapunov relation requires a specific Katyusha theorem or analysis locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected component-gradient complexity of classical Katyusha for strongly convex composite finite sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)+\psi(x)\), where every \(f_i\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth, \(\psi\) is proper, closed, convex, and proximable, and \(F\) is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex. With the prescribed classical Katyusha parameters, uniform component sampling, and output rule, an output \(x\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[F(x)-F(x^*)]\leq\varepsilon\) is obtained in \[O\!\left(\left(n+\sqrt{\frac{nL}{\sigma}}\right)\log\frac{F(x_0)-F(x^*)}{\varepsilon}\right)\] component-gradient-equivalent evaluations, counting a full gradient as \(n\) component evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classical strongly convex Katyusha has complexity n plus the square root of n times the condition number, multiplied by a logarithmic accuracy factor.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is convex with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
\(\psi\) is proper, closed, convex, and proximable.
The classical Katyusha parameter restrictions and output rule are used.

notation.meaning: strong-convexity modulus of the composite objective

review_flags: A primary Katyusha theorem locator remains desirable for source-sensitive publication.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected component-gradient complexity of classical uniform-sampling Katyusha without strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)+\psi(x), where every f_i is convex and L-smooth and \psi is proper, closed, convex, and proximable. Let x^* be a minimizer, \Delta_0=F(x_0)-F(x^*), and 0<\varepsilon<\Delta_0. With the prescribed convex-regime classical Katyusha parameters and output rule, \mathbb E[F(x)-F(x^*)]\leq\varepsilon is attainable in \[O\!\left(n\log\frac{\Delta_0}{\varepsilon}+\sqrt{\frac{nL\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert^2}{\varepsilon}}\right)\] component-gradient-equivalent evaluations, counting a full gradient as n component evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the convex composite regime, classical Katyusha uses logarithmically many full-pass terms plus an accelerated square-root inverse-accuracy term.
assumptions_latex: Each f_i is convex with an L-Lipschitz gradient.
\psi is proper, closed, convex, and proximable.
The classical uniform-sampling convex-regime parameters and prescribed output rule are used.

After the prescribed inner length, replace \(\widetilde x\) by the specified weighted average of inner \(y\)-iterates; return the latest snapshot.

children.title: KatyushaX
children.top_down_role: The core KatyushaX acceleration family.

knowledge_statements.title: KatyushaX
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epoch-level acceleration wrapper around a variance-reduced finite-sum solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal T\) denote one prescribed epoch of a variance-reduced method for minimizing \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)+\psi(x)\). Initialize two outer points \(x_0=z_0\). At epoch \(s\), form an extrapolated input \(y_s\) from the current and preceding outer states using the KatyushaX momentum parameter, run one randomized epoch \(x_{s+1}=\mathcal T(y_s;\xi_s)\), and update the momentum state \(z_{s+1}\) using the resulting displacement. The epoch map must be analyzed through its expected one-epoch progress inequality rather than through individual inner iterates. Stop after the chosen number of epochs or at a certified residual and return \(x_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KatyushaX accelerates a variance-reduced epoch map by extrapolating outer states and applying momentum at epoch boundaries.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a convex composite finite sum.
\(\mathcal T\) satisfies the required expected one-epoch progress inequality.
Epoch random variables \(\xi_s\) are conditionally sampled as prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{s+1}=\mathcal T(y_s;\xi_s)\), with KatyushaX extrapolation and momentum performed between epochs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record describes only a generic epoch-level momentum wrapper. Without the actual KatyushaX recurrence, momentum coefficients, and specified variance-reduced epoch map, it is not a complete or reliably identifiable KatyushaX algorithm.

children.title: KatyushaX Variants
children.top_down_role: Direct modifications of the KatyushaX framework.

knowledge_statements.title: KatyushaX Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant interface defining admissible variants of the KatyushaX epoch wrapper.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a randomized epoch map \(\mathcal T_s\) and an outer momentum recurrence. A KatyushaX variant is acceleration-compatible when, conditional on the epoch history \(\mathcal F_s\), its output satisfies a one-epoch inequality \(\mathbb E[F(\mathcal T_s(y))-F^*\mid\mathcal F_s]\le a_s(F(y)-F^*)+b_s\lVert y-x^*\rVert^2\), with nonnegative constants accepted by the outer estimate sequence. Changes to sampling, epoch length, regularization, or the inner variance-reduced solver are admissible only if this inequality remains valid and the momentum coefficients keep the outer Lyapunov weights nonnegative. The output is the final outer iterate or its prescribed average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KatyushaX variants may alter the inner epoch or sampling only while preserving the progress inequality required by the outer momentum analysis.
assumptions_latex: Each epoch map is measurable relative to fresh conditional randomness.
The outer momentum recurrence has a stated Lyapunov function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[F(\mathcal T_s(y))-F^*\mid\mathcal F_s]\le a_s(F(y)-F^*)+b_s\lVert y-x^*\rVert^2\) with compatible nonnegative outer weights.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inequality is a generic sufficient interface rather than a sourced account of KatyushaX variants. Primary sources are needed to identify the covered variants, their actual epoch inequalities, and whether a condition is the correct role for this leaf.

children.title: Post-KatyushaX Relatives
children.top_down_role: Closely related accelerated methods derived from KatyushaX design ideas.

knowledge_statements.title: Post-KatyushaX Relatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A mathematical criterion for methods descended from epoch-map momentum acceleration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal T_s\) be a stochastic variance-reduced epoch operator and let \(u_s\) denote an auxiliary momentum state. An epoch-accelerated relative forms \(y_s=A_sx_s+B_su_s+C_s\widetilde x_s\), applies \(x_{s+1}=\mathcal T_s(y_s)\), and updates \(u_{s+1}\) from \(u_s\) and the epoch displacement, with \(A_s+B_s+C_s=1\). Fixed points are preserved whenever \(x^*=u_s=\widetilde x_s\) and \(\mathcal T_s(x^*)=x^*\). To inherit an accelerated guarantee, the modified epoch operator and coefficients must additionally satisfy the same estimate-sequence or Lyapunov contraction used by the outer momentum construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Post-KatyushaX relatives retain an accelerated epoch-map wrapper, while changing the inner solver, snapshot mechanism, sampling, or momentum state.
assumptions_latex: The epoch operator has a common minimizer as a fixed point.
A one-epoch progress inequality is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_s=A_sx_s+B_su_s+C_s\widetilde x_s\), \(x_{s+1}=\mathcal T_s(y_s)\), and \(A_s+B_s+C_s=1\) preserve the common fixed point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle is mathematically plausible but does not establish that any method is a post-KatyushaX relative. Named descendant methods and lineage-supporting primary sources are required before the local title can be filled reliably.

children.title: Loopless Katyusha
children.top_down_role: Katyusha variants using randomized refresh without explicit outer loops.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at which loopless snapshot renewal disappears.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the snapshot changes only on a Bernoulli refresh and the refresh probability is \(p=0\), then \(w_k=w_0\) for every \(k\). Unless component-gradient differences relative to \(w_0\) satisfy an additional global variance bound, the standard refresh-based loopless Katyusha contraction theorem is inapplicable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At zero refresh probability the snapshot never changes, so the standard loopless Katyusha contraction mechanism is unavailable.
assumptions_latex: The snapshot changes only on a Bernoulli refresh event.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p=0\implies w_k=w_0\ \forall k,\quad\text{and the standard refresh-based contraction theorem does not apply}.
knowledge_statements.title: No-Refresh Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric Snapshot Age and Refresh Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional and component-oracle consequences of independent Bernoulli snapshot refresh.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a snapshot is independently refreshed after each iteration with probability \(p\in(0,1]\). In stationarity, let \(A_k\) be the number of consecutive nonrefresh iterations since the latest refresh. Then \(\mathbb P(A_k\geq t)=(1-p)^t\) for integers \(t\geq0\) and \(\mathbb E[A_k]=(1-p)/p\). If a refresh computes a full gradient at a cost of \(n\) component gradients, its expected refresh cost per iteration is \(pn\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bernoulli refresh produces geometric snapshot age with mean (1−p)/p and costs pn component gradients per iteration in expectation.
assumptions_latex: Refresh indicators are independent Bernoulli variables with success probability \(p\in(0,1]\).
A refresh computes one full gradient using \(n\) component-gradient evaluations.
The snapshot-age distribution is evaluated in stationarity.

notation.meaning: consecutive nonrefresh count since the latest refresh
component-gradient refresh cost at an iteration

Loopless Katyusha
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Katyusha with Bernoulli snapshot refreshes replacing deterministic epoch boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Maintain coupled iterates \(y_k,z_k\) and a snapshot \(w_k\) with stored full gradient \(
abla f(w_k)\). Form \(x_{k+1}=	au_1z_k+	au_2w_k+(1-	au_1-	au_2)y_k\), sample \(i_k\) uniformly, and set \(g_k=
abla f_{i_k}(x_{k+1})-
abla f_{i_k}(w_k)+
abla f(w_k)\). Apply the prescribed Katyusha proximal updates to obtain \(y_{k+1},z_{k+1}\). Independently draw \(B_k\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\); if \(B_k=1\), refresh \(w_{k+1}\) from the prescribed current iterate and compute \(
abla f(w_{k+1})\), otherwise set \(w_{k+1}=w_k\). Return the latest iterate or specified average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Loopless Katyusha replaces fixed epochs by independent Bernoulli snapshot refreshes while retaining coupled proximal updates and a control-variate estimator.
assumptions_latex: The composite finite sum satisfies the Katyusha smoothness and convexity assumptions.
Refresh and component-sampling randomness follow the stated conditional law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_{k+1}\) is refreshed with probability \(p\) and otherwise retained, eliminating deterministic epoch boundaries.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, and Bernoulli snapshot refresh captures the loopless idea, but the refresh iterate, proximal recurrences, independence conditions, and parameter restrictions are essential variant-specific details requiring a primary source.

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary-Sampling Katyusha
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Katyusha using a Horvitz–Thompson control variate for nonuniform subset sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a random subset \(S_k\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) have inclusion probabilities \(p_i=\mathbb P(i\in S_k)>0\). At snapshot \(w_k\), form the unbiased estimator \(g_k=
abla f(w_k)+n^{-1}\sum_{i\in S_k}p_i^{-1}(
abla f_i(x_k)-
abla f_i(w_k))\). Use \(g_k\) in the gradient and mirror proximal updates of Katyusha, with step sizes and coupling weights chosen from the sampling-dependent expected-smoothness or variance constants. Refresh the snapshot according to the selected epoch or loopless rule. Stop under the prescribed iteration or residual criterion and return the designated iterate or weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary-sampling Katyusha corrects subset gradients by their inclusion probabilities and tunes acceleration to sampling-dependent variance constants.
assumptions_latex: The subset law admits a finite sampling-dependent variance bound.
The component functions satisfy the required convexity and smoothness assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_k[g_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\), and Katyusha uses sampling-dependent stability parameters.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Horvitz–Thompson estimator is unbiased under positive inclusion probabilities, but identifying the full method as Arbitrary-Sampling Katyusha requires sourced sampling-dependent smoothness constants, coupling parameters, proximal updates, and refresh rules.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic support obstruction for inverse-probability subset estimators proposed here but canonically owned by sampling-interface theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), suppose an estimator observes component differences only for indices in a random subset \(S\). If \(p_j=\mathbb P(j\in S)=0\) and component \(j\)'s gradient difference is not reconstructible from the other observations, then an estimator based only on \(S\) cannot be unbiased for the full gradient difference for every admissible component family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonredundant component with zero inclusion probability prevents generally unbiased recovery of the full gradient difference.
assumptions_latex: The estimator observes component-gradient differences only for indices in \(S\).
Component \(j\)'s gradient difference is not reconstructible from other observations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_j=0\implies\text{unbiased full-gradient-difference estimation is impossible in general}.

notation.meaning: marginal inclusion probability of component j

review_flags: This is a generic arbitrary-sampling support theorem already represented by probability-weighting and sampling-interface topics, not primarily a Katyusha theorem.

children.title: Katyusha Sampling–Acceleration Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interactions between sampling design and accelerated Katyusha structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Katyusha Sampling–Acceleration Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Estimator contract connecting a sampling law to valid Katyusha acceleration parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a snapshot estimator \(g(x,w,S)\), the sampling law is acceleration-compatible if \(\mathbb E[g(x,w,S)\mid x,w]=\nabla f(x)\) and there exists a finite constant \(V_S\) such that \(\mathbb E[\lVert g(x,w,S)-\nabla f(x)\rVert^2\mid x,w]\le V_S\mathcal D(x,w)\), where \(\mathcal D(x,w)\ge0\) is the Bregman or function-gap quantity used by the Katyusha Lyapunov analysis. Coupling weights and proximal step sizes must be selected using the same \(V_S\); parameters derived from uniform sampling are invalid unless they also satisfy the resulting stability inequality. Snapshot refresh probabilities must likewise be included in the Lyapunov balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling interfaces with acceleration through unbiasedness, a compatible variance bound, and parameters tuned to that same variance and refresh law.
assumptions_latex: The estimator is defined for every admissible query and snapshot.
\(\mathcal D(x,w)\) is nonnegative and vanishes when \(x=w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[g\mid x,w]=\nabla f(x)\) and \(\mathbb E[\lVert g-\nabla f(x)\rVert^2\mid x,w]\le V_S\mathcal D(x,w)\), with acceleration parameters tuned to \(V_S\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the interface leaf, but the generic variance bound does not specify the discrepancy, constants, or stability inequality used by a particular Katyusha analysis. Those details and the refresh-probability balance require a scoped source.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Prox-SVRG
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic momentum-coupled proximal SVRG template; exact published variants differ in momentum and snapshot rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)+\psi(x)\). At epoch \(s\), choose a snapshot \(\widetilde x_s\), compute \(g_s=n^{-1}\sum_i
abla f_i(\widetilde x_s)\), and initialize \(z_0=x_s\). For \(t=0,\ldots,m-1\), sample \(i_t\) uniformly and set \(y_t=(1-	heta)\widetilde x_s+	heta z_t\), \(v_t=
abla f_{i_t}(y_t)-
abla f_{i_t}(\widetilde x_s)+g_s\), and \(z_{t+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta\psi}(z_t-\eta v_t)\). Output an admissible average or randomly selected inner iterate as \(x_{s+1}\), and update \(\widetilde x_{s+1}\) according to the chosen accelerated Prox-SVRG variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each epoch combines a full snapshot gradient, an unbiased component-gradient correction, a proximal step, and momentum coupling between the snapshot and current iterate.

The function \(\psi:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex with computable proximal map.
Parameters \(m\in\mathbb N\), \(\eta>0\), and \(\theta\in(0,1]\) satisfy the stability conditions of the selected variant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditionally on \(y_t\), the estimator satisfies \(\mathbb E[v_t\mid y_t]=\nabla(n^{-1}\sum_i f_i)(y_t)\).

Named-method source with an algorithm locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Acceleration Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strongly convex smooth finite-sum regime shared by accelerated proximal variance-reduction schemes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)+\psi(x)\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, every \(f_i\) is convex and smooth with constant at most \(L\), and \(\kappa=L/\mu\). The \(n\) term pays for snapshot gradients, while \(\sqrt{n\kappa}\) is the accelerated stochastic-conditioning term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the strongly convex regime, both families target a linear rate with component-gradient cost proportional to sample size plus the square root of sample size times condition number.
assumptions_latex: The finite-sum objective is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(0<\mu\leq L\).
Component-gradient and proximal evaluations are counted in the standard finite-sum first-order oracle model.
Algorithm parameters use the relevant method’s theoretically admissible tuning.

Logarithmic factors and proximal-oracle accounting may vary by published variant.

Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i(x)+\psi(x)\). Choose positive weights \(a_t\), let \(A_t=\sum_{j=1}^t a_j\), and maintain a snapshot \(\widetilde x\) with full gradient \(g=n^{-1}\sum_i
abla f_i(\widetilde x)\). At step \(t\), form an extrapolated point \(y_t\), sample \(i_t\), and set \(v_t=
abla f_{i_t}(y_t)-
abla f_{i_t}(\widetilde x)+g\). Accumulate \(s_t=s_{t-1}+a_t v_t\) and compute \[z_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\left\{\langle s_t,xangle+A_t\psi(x)+	frac12\lVert x-x_0Vert^2ight\}.\] The output and subsequent snapshot are weighted combinations prescribed by the selected VRADA variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: VRADA combines snapshot-based unbiased gradients with accelerated dual averaging, accumulating weighted gradients before solving a regularized proximal subproblem.

children.title: Point-SAGA Family
children.top_down_role: Accelerated proximal-point methods associated with Point-SAGA.

knowledge_statements.title: Point-SAGA Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit component-proximal SAGA template with a table of subgradient memories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), maintain memory vectors \(g_i\in\partial f_i(\phi_i)\) and their mean \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_i g_i\). Given \(x_k\), sample \(i_k\) uniformly and set \(u_k=x_k+\gamma(g_{i_k}-\bar g)\) and \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f_{i_k}}(u_k)\). Define the implicit subgradient \(g_{i_k}^{+}=\gamma^{-1}(u_k-x_{k+1})\in\partial f_{i_k}(x_{k+1})\), replace only that table entry, and update \(\bar g^{+}=\bar g+n^{-1}(g_{i_k}^{+}-g_{i_k})\). Return the latest iterate or a prescribed average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Point-SAGA performs a randomly selected component proximal-point step corrected by a SAGA memory table, then updates only the selected component’s stored subgradient.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
Every component proximal map \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f_i}\) is computable for the selected \(\gamma>0\).
The initialization satisfies \(g_i\in\partial f_i(\phi_i)\) for every component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proximal optimality condition certifies \(g_{i_k}^{+}\in\partial f_{i_k}(x_{k+1})\), while unselected memory entries remain unchanged.

The precise published update requires confirmation from a primary source.

children.title: Cross-Family Acceleration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objective and oracle regimes distinguishing VRADA from Point-SAGA.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Family Acceleration Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-complexity regime used to compare VRADA- and Point-SAGA-type acceleration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite sum of \(n\) convex component functions whose average is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and whose relevant smoothness or proximal regularity scale is \(L\), set \(\kappa=L/\mu\). In the standard randomized component-oracle model, the accelerated benchmark is \[N(\varepsilon)=O\!\left((n+\sqrt{n\kappa})\log\frac{\Delta_0}{\varepsilon}\right),\qquad \Delta_0=F(x_0)-F_\star.\] A VRADA or Point-SAGA theorem belongs to the same acceleration regime only when its stated oracle accounting reduces to this dependence, up to universal constants and explicitly declared logarithmic factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: VRADA and Point-SAGA variants share an acceleration regime only when their oracle bounds reduce to the same sample-size and condition-number scaling under comparable assumptions.
assumptions_latex: The objective is strongly convex and admits the component oracle required by the compared methods.
The same accuracy criterion \(\mathbb E[F(x)-F_\star]\leq\varepsilon\) is used for both families.
Full passes, component gradients, and component proximal calls are converted to a common oracle accounting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-family accelerated comparability requires leading dependence \(n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\) under matched assumptions and resource units.
review_flags: Exact VRADA and Point-SAGA bounds must be sourced before asserting cross-family equivalence.
Component-proximal and component-gradient oracle costs are not automatically interchangeable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the cross-family regime leaf. However, component-gradient and component-proximal calls are distinct resources, and no cited theorems establish the asserted common scaling under a justified conversion.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Primal–Dual Finite-Sum Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic variance-reduced accelerated primal–dual scheme for separable finite-sum saddle problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x\max_{y_1,\ldots,y_n}\{\psi(x)+n^{-1}\sum_i(\langle K_i x,y_i\rangle-h_i^*(y_i))\}\). Maintain primal state \(x_k\), dual blocks \(y_i^k\), and their aggregate \(q_k=n^{-1}\sum_iK_i^*y_i^k\). Sample \(i_k\), update only that block by \(y_{i_k}^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma h_{i_k}^*}(y_{i_k}^k+\sigma K_{i_k}\bar x_k)\), update \(q_{k+1}\) incrementally, and set \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau\psi}(x_k-\tau q_{k+1})\). Form \(\bar x_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+\theta_k(x_{k+1}-x_k)\), with sampling corrections and parameters chosen by the particular accelerated variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These methods randomly update a dual component, maintain its aggregate contribution, apply a primal proximal step, and extrapolate the primal iterate to obtain acceleration.
assumptions_latex: The spaces are finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and every \(K_i\) is linear and bounded.
The functions \(\psi\) and \(h_i^*\) are proper, closed, convex, and proximable.
Step sizes, sampling corrections, and extrapolation weights satisfy the selected method’s stability condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration uses one component dual proximal oracle, one primal proximal oracle, and an incremental update of \(q_k\).

notation.meaning: adjoint of the component linear map
aggregate dual contribution to the primal update

children.title: Sample-Size Transitions
children.top_down_role: Acceleration regimes organized by finite-sum size.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Term-dominance transition of the classical strongly convex Katyusha benchmark as sample size varies at fixed condition number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let B(n,\kappa)=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}. For fixed \kappa\geq1, the two terms agree at n=\kappa. If 1\leq n\leq\kappa, then B(n,\kappa)=\Theta(\sqrt{n\kappa}); if n\geq\kappa, then B(n,\kappa)=\Theta(n).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed condition number, the Katyusha benchmark changes from conditioning sensitive to full-pass dominated when sample size crosses the condition number.
assumptions_latex: The applicable component-gradient complexity has leading factor B(n,\kappa)=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}, as in the accepted strongly convex classical Katyusha bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Condition Sample-Size Transition
Sample-Size Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition in the benchmark accelerated complexity as sample size varies at fixed condition number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B(n,\kappa)=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\) denote the nonlogarithmic part of an accelerated finite-sum oracle bound. For fixed \(\kappa\geq1\), the two terms are equal precisely when \(n=\kappa\). If \(1\leq n\leq\kappa\), then \(\sqrt{n\kappa}\geq n\) and \(B(n,\kappa)=\Theta(\sqrt{n\kappa})\). If \(n\geq\kappa\), then \(n\geq\sqrt{n\kappa}\) and \(B(n,\kappa)=\Theta(n)\). Thus increasing the sample size crosses from a conditioning-sensitive regime to a data-pass-dominated regime at \(n\asymp\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed condition number, the accelerated stochastic term dominates below sample size κ, while the full-pass term dominates above κ; the transition occurs at n comparable to κ.
assumptions_latex: The relevant complexity has leading factor \(B(n,\kappa)=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sample-size transition boundary is \(n=\kappa\), with regimes \(B=\Theta(\sqrt{n\kappa})\) for \(n\leq\kappa\) and \(B=\Theta(n)\) for \(n\geq\kappa\).

children.title: Condition-Number Transitions
children.top_down_role: Acceleration regimes organized by conditioning.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Term-dominance transition of the classical strongly convex Katyusha benchmark as conditioning varies at fixed sample size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \kappa=L/\sigma and B(n,\kappa)=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}. For fixed n\geq1, the two terms agree at \kappa=n. If 1\leq\kappa\leq n, then B(n,\kappa)=\Theta(n); if \kappa\geq n, then B(n,\kappa)=\Theta(\sqrt{n\kappa}).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed sample size, the Katyusha benchmark changes from full-pass dominated to conditioning dominated when the condition number crosses the sample size.
assumptions_latex: The applicable component-gradient complexity has leading factor B(n,\kappa)=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}, as in the accepted strongly convex classical Katyusha bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Sample Condition-Number Transition
Condition-Number Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition in the benchmark accelerated complexity as conditioning varies at fixed sample size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B(n,\kappa)=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\) and fixed \(n\geq1\), the full-pass and accelerated conditioning terms coincide at \(\kappa=n\). When \(1\leq\kappa\leq n\), one has \(\sqrt{n\kappa}\leq n\), hence \(B(n,\kappa)=\Theta(n)\). When \(\kappa\geq n\), one has \(\sqrt{n\kappa}\geq n\), hence \(B(n,\kappa)=\Theta(\sqrt{n\kappa})\). Therefore worsening conditioning moves the method from a sample-limited region into a conditioning-limited region when \(\kappa\) becomes comparable to \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed sample size, full-pass cost dominates for κ below n, while accelerated conditioning cost dominates for κ above n; the transition is κ comparable to n.
assumptions_latex: The method’s leading oracle complexity is proportional to \(B(n,\kappa)\), up to logarithmic accuracy factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condition-number transition boundary is \(\kappa=n\), separating \(B=\Theta(n)\) from \(B=\Theta(\sqrt{n\kappa})\).

children.title: Sample–Condition Phase Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Joint parameter regions where the preferred accelerated complexity regime changes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint term-dominance diagram for the classical strongly convex Katyusha benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For B(n,\kappa)=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}, \[B(n,\kappa)=\begin{cases}\Theta(\sqrt{n\kappa}),&n\leq\kappa,\\\Theta(n),&n\geq\kappa.\end{cases}\] The diagonal n=\kappa is the equality boundary: the square-root term dominates for n<\kappa, the full-pass term dominates for n>\kappa, and both equal n on the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The line n=κ separates the conditioning-dominated and full-pass-dominated regions of the Katyusha benchmark.
assumptions_latex: The applicable component-gradient complexity has leading factor B(n,\kappa)=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}, as in the accepted strongly convex classical Katyusha bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Katyusha Sample–Condition Phase Boundary
Sample–Condition Phase Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-region phase diagram induced by the accelerated finite-sum benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The leading factor \(B(n,\kappa)=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\) admits the piecewise-equivalent representation \[B(n,\kappa)=\begin{cases}\Theta(\sqrt{n\kappa}),&n\leq\kappa,\\ \Theta(n),&n\geq\kappa.\end{cases}\] Consequently, the diagonal \(n=\kappa\) partitions the positive \((n,\kappa)\)-plane into a conditioning-dominated region \(n<\kappa\) and a sample-pass-dominated region \(n>\kappa\). On the boundary, both contributions equal \(n=\kappa\), so neither term can be discarded in a constant-sensitive comparison.

children.title: Restart Policies
children.top_down_role: Scheduled or adaptive restart organizations for accelerated methods.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic complexity consequence of a certified restart block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If each restart block costs at most W charged operations and contracts a nonnegative error by E_{r+1}\le\rho E_r with \rho\in(0,1), then R=\left\lceil\log(E_0/\varepsilon)/\log(1/\rho)\right\rceil blocks suffice for E_R\le\varepsilon, with total work at most WR.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed contraction per restart block yields geometric convergence and logarithmically many blocks.
assumptions_latex: Every block costs at most W in the declared resource.
knowledge_statements.title: Block-Contraction Complexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-reset requirement for restarting an accelerated variance-reduced routine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a restart boundary, every state variable whose invariant or estimate-sequence guarantee is tied to the previous block must be reinitialized consistently at the accepted reference point. The inertial displacement and coupled estimate-sequence weights must be reset. A variance-reduction table, snapshot gradient, or control variate may be retained only if the next-block theorem remains valid conditional on that state; otherwise it must be refreshed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restarting momentum is insufficient when the proof also couples acceleration to finite-sum estimator state.
assumptions_latex: The base routine exposes its acceleration and variance-reduction state.
Each restarted block must satisfy the same declared base guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Restart validity}\Longrightarrow\text{all theorem-coupled state is reset or revalidated}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Restart State Condition
Restart Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic restart of a convex accelerated method under known strong curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an accelerated base routine \(\mathcal A_T\) satisfy \(F(\mathcal A_T(x))-F_\star\leq cL\lVert x-x_\star\rVert^2/T^2\) for convex \(L\)-smooth objectives. If \(F\) is also \(\mu\)-strongly convex, choose \(T\geq\lceil2\sqrt{cL/\mu}\rceil\), set \(x^{(0)}=x_0\), and recursively define \(x^{(r+1)}=\mathcal A_T(x^{(r)})\), resetting all momentum and epoch state after each block. Stop after \(R\) blocks or when a prescribed verifiable residual tolerance is met. Then each completed block contracts the objective gap by at least one half.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run the accelerated routine for a curvature-dependent block length, erase its momentum state, and repeat; strong convexity converts each block’s sublinear guarantee into geometric contraction.
assumptions_latex: The base routine has the displayed \(O(T^{-2})\) objective guarantee.
The objective is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and smooth with constant \(L\).
Each restart reinitializes every acceleration and variance-reduction state required by the base guarantee.

children.title: Unknown-Curvature Policies
children.top_down_role: Acceleration policies used when curvature parameters are unavailable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of positive-curvature search when no positive strong-convexity modulus exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat\mu_j>0\) be every finite trial curvature. If the true strong-convexity modulus is \(\mu=0\), then \(\widehat\mu_j\leq\mu\) fails for every finite \(j\). Hence a restart guarantee activated only after finding \(0<\widehat\mu_j\leq\mu\) cannot be certified in the merely convex regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive curvature guesses can never become valid lower guesses when the true strong-convexity modulus is zero.

notation.meaning: positive trial curvature at stage j

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Curvature Search Boundary
Unknown-Curvature Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric search over curvature guesses with certified acceptance of restart blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume a base accelerated routine can be restarted using a trial curvature \(\widehat\mu>0\). Choose \(\widehat\mu_0\leq L\). At search stage \(j\), run one block of length \(T_j=\lceil C\sqrt{L/\widehat\mu_j}\rceil\), starting from the last accepted point. Accept the block only when an available computable certificate verifies the prescribed contraction; otherwise discard its candidate endpoint, set \(\widehat\mu_{j+1}=\widehat\mu_j/2\), and repeat. After acceptance, continue restarting with that guess while the certificate remains valid, reducing the guess again upon failure. The policy never requires the true curvature \(\mu\) as input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When curvature is unknown, try geometrically decreasing curvature estimates, lengthen restart blocks accordingly, and accept a block only after a computable contraction certificate succeeds.
assumptions_latex: The smoothness scale \(L>0\) is known or safely upper-bounded.
A computable certificate soundly verifies the contraction required by the base restart theorem.
Failed trial blocks can be discarded without changing the last accepted algorithmic state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After at most \(\lceil\log_2(\widehat\mu_0/\mu)\rceil_+\) failed guesses, the policy reaches \(\widehat\mu_j\leq\mu\), provided \(\mu>0\).
review_flags: The applicable contraction certificate is method-dependent and unspecified by the node path.
A sourced unknown-curvature restart theorem is required to fix acceptance rules and overhead.

children.title: Curvature-Misspecification Responses
children.top_down_role: Policy responses to inaccurate curvature information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar counterexample showing that restart cannot repair an unsafe base step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For F(x)=\frac{L}{2}x^2, a gradient step with scale 1/\widehat L gives x^+=(1-L/\widehat L)x. It is contractive exactly when |1-L/\widehat L|<1, equivalently \widehat L>L/2. If \widehat L\le L/2, even the nonaccelerated step is noncontractive; a response policy must increase the smoothness scale or reject the step before an acceleration guarantee can apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A severe smoothness underestimate destroys contraction even without momentum, so restart alone is insufficient.
assumptions_latex: The trial step size is 1/\widehat L.
knowledge_statements.title: Smoothness Underestimate Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of restart guarantees calibrated with an excessive strong-convexity estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a restart theorem requires T\ge C\sqrt{L/\mu}. If \widehat\mu>\mu and one instead chooses T=C\sqrt{L/\widehat\mu}, then T<C\sqrt{L/\mu}, so the theorem does not certify the claimed contraction. Conversely, 0<\widehat\mu\le\mu gives a conservative block length and preserves the implication, at the cost of longer blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overestimating strong convexity can make restart blocks too short; underestimating it is conservative but slower.
assumptions_latex: The underlying restart theorem requires T\ge C\sqrt{L/\mu}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Curvature Overestimate Boundary
Curvature-Misspecification Responses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive restart for accelerated variance reduction when strong convexity is unknown or incorrectly estimated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) be \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly convex, with unknown \(\mu>0\). Choose \(\widehat\mu_0\in(0,L]\), a reduction factor \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), and a prescribed contraction test. At stage \(s\), run an accelerated variance-reduced inner method using curvature estimate \(\widehat\mu_s\) for its scheduled stage length. If the resulting reference point fails the contraction test, discard the acceleration state, set \(\widehat\mu_{s+1}=\gamma\widehat\mu_s\), and restart from the last accepted reference point; otherwise accept the point and retain \(\widehat\mu_s\). Stop when the chosen verifiable accuracy criterion is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run acceleration with a curvature estimate; when its prescribed contraction test fails, reduce the estimate, erase momentum, and restart from the last accepted point.
assumptions_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly convex for some unknown \(\mu>0\).
The inner method and contraction test are specified for each estimate \(\widehat\mu_s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\mu_{s+1}=\gamma\widehat\mu_s\) after a failed test, with acceleration state restarted.
