children.title: Ineffective Acceleration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where acceleration provides no material complexity improvement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regime where a common full-data term masks an improved condition-dependent term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C_A=(n+a)\ell(\varepsilon) and C_B=(n+b)\ell(\varepsilon), with a,b\ge0 and \ell(\varepsilon)>0. On any regime where a=O(n) and b=O(n), both complexities are \Theta(n\ell(\varepsilon)). Hence reducing the condition-dependent term does not produce an asymptotic improvement while the common data-size floor dominates both bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When full-data work dominates both bounds, improving the condition-dependent term cannot change their asymptotic order.
assumptions_latex: Both bounds use the same component-oracle and accuracy convention.
The constants hidden in O(n) are uniform in the declared regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Floor Dominance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between numerical speedup and asymptotic acceleration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If positive complexity bounds satisfy 0<c\le C_B(\theta)/C_A(\theta)\le C'<\infty throughout a declared asymptotic regime, then C_B=\Theta(C_A). Method B may be faster by a constant factor, but it has no asymptotic complexity acceleration in that regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded, nonvanishing complexity ratio permits constant-factor speedup but not asymptotic acceleration.
assumptions_latex: Both complexities charge the same resource and certify the same output event.
knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Factor-Only Regime
Ineffective Acceleration Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-complexity boundary for standard strongly convex finite-sum acceleration rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a strongly convex finite sum with condition number \(\kappa=L/\mu\). Suppose a baseline variance-reduced method uses \(O((n+\kappa)\log(1/\varepsilon))\) component-gradient evaluations, while its accelerated counterpart uses \(O((n+\sqrt{n\kappa})\log(1/\varepsilon))\). If \(\kappa\le n\), then \(n\le n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\le 2n\) and \(n\le n+\kappa\le2n\). Thus both bounds are \(\Theta(n\log(1/\varepsilon))\); acceleration changes constants at most. A strict asymptotic improvement in this comparison can occur only in the regime \(\kappa>n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the standard finite-sum rates, acceleration gives no asymptotic component-gradient improvement when the condition number does not exceed the sample size.
assumptions_latex: The compared bounds use the same component-gradient oracle and the same accuracy criterion.

notation.meaning: condition number L divided by mu

review_flags: The two benchmark complexity bounds require an authoritative accelerated-variance-reduction source.

children.title: False Acceleration Claims
children.top_down_role: Apparent acceleration caused by incomparable baselines or accounting choices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary comparison conditions for a finite-sum acceleration claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A claim that B accelerates A must fix a common instance class, oracle, output criterion, success probability, initialization convention, and charged-resource function C. It must then demonstrate an asymptotic improvement in a declared joint parameter regime, or explicitly limit the claim to a constant-factor improvement. Omitting a changing parameter can turn a regime-specific result into a false uniform claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid acceleration claim fixes the full comparison model and declares the regime where charged complexity improves.
assumptions_latex: Both algorithms are evaluated under one declared computational model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{An acceleration claim requires a common comparison model and an explicitly quantified improvement regime}.

notation.meaning: charged complexities under the common convention

knowledge_statements.title: Valid Acceleration Comparison Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample to inferring work acceleration from iteration count alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose A reaches a common target in n iterations using one component-gradient evaluation per iteration, while B reaches it in \sqrt n iterations but evaluates all n components per iteration. Then B uses fewer iterations but n^{3/2} component evaluations, versus n for A. Thus an iteration-count speedup by \sqrt n coexists with an oracle-work slowdown by \sqrt n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fewer iterations can mean more total work when each accelerated iteration is more expensive.
assumptions_latex: Both methods solve the same instances to the same accuracy event.
A full-component iteration costs n component evaluations.
knowledge_statements.title: Iteration-Count False Acceleration
False Acceleration Claims
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample to inferring oracle acceleration solely from an improved epoch count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let one epoch require exactly \(n\) component-gradient evaluations. An algorithm reported to need \(O(\sqrt\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon))\) epochs therefore needs \(O(n\sqrt\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon))\) component-gradient evaluations. On the family \(\kappa=n\), this is \(O(n^{3/2}\log(1/\varepsilon))\), whereas a variance-reduced baseline with complexity \(O((n+\kappa)\log(1/\varepsilon))\) uses \(O(n\log(1/\varepsilon))\). Hence the smaller-looking dependence on \(\kappa\) in epoch units does not establish acceleration in component-oracle complexity and can conceal an asymptotically worse method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An improved epoch count can hide an extra factor of the dataset size and therefore need not imply improved component-gradient complexity.
assumptions_latex: Each reported epoch evaluates all \(n\) component gradients.
Both methods use the same accuracy convention.
review_flags: The counterexample is algebraically self-contained, but the benchmark rate comparison lacks a supplied finite-sum acceleration source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample role fits the leaf and the epoch-to-oracle conversion is algebraically correct. However, the comparison relies on an uncited variance-reduced baseline rate, so the claimed asymptotic comparison lacks the required evidence.

children.title: Complexity-Metric Mismatches
children.top_down_role: Discrepancies among iteration, oracle, gradient, and wall-clock comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Complexity-Metric Mismatches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on comparing acceleration claims expressed in different computational resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an algorithm \(A\), let \(N_g^A(\varepsilon)\), \(N_{m pass}^A(\varepsilon)\), and \(T^A(\varepsilon)\) denote component-gradient count, data-pass count, and wall-clock time. A bound on one resource does not order another unless a conversion bound is supplied. In particular, \(N_g^A<N_g^B\) does not imply \(T^A<T^B\) when gradient costs, synchronization, memory traffic, or parallelism differ. Likewise, \(N_{m pass}=N_g/n\) is valid only when a pass is defined as exactly \(n\) comparable component evaluations. Therefore an acceleration claim is well-posed only when both methods share the resource metric, oracle model, accuracy criterion, and cost accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complexity bounds cannot establish acceleration across different metrics unless explicit, valid cost conversions and common accuracy conventions are supplied.
assumptions_latex: The compared algorithms target the same optimization problem and accuracy event.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling with Replacement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent component selection for stochastic finite-sum oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), sampling with replacement draws an index sequence \((I_t)_{t\ge0}\) independently from a fixed distribution \(p\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), so that \(\mathbb P(I_t=i)=p_i\) and repeated indices are allowed. If every \(p_i>0\), the importance-corrected component-gradient estimator at a query point \(x_t\) is \(G_t=\nabla f_{I_t}(x_t)/(np_{I_t})\). Conditional on \(x_t\), it satisfies \(\mathbb E[G_t\mid x_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\). Uniform sampling is the special case \(p_i=1/n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each oracle call independently selects a component, permits repeats, and uses inverse-probability weighting when nonuniform probabilities are used.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is differentiable at the query point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp support requirement for universally unbiased with-replacement component estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\in\mathbb R^d\), let \(p_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_i p_i=1\), and draw \(I\sim p\). Define \(G=g_I/(np_I)\) on sampled indices. Then \[\mathbb E[G]=\frac1n\sum_{i:p_i>0}g_i.\] Thus \(G\) is unbiased for \(n^{-1}\sum_i g_i\) exactly when \(\sum_{i:p_i=0}g_i=0\); unbiasedness for every component family requires \(p_i>0\) for all \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-probability components are omitted from the expectation, so full support is necessary for universal unbiasedness.
assumptions_latex: \(G=g_I/(np_I)\) is evaluated only on sampled indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[G]=n^{-1}\sum_{i:p_i>0}g_i\), and universal unbiasedness holds if and only if every \(p_i>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), stepsizes \(\eta_{s,j}>0\), and \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), epoch \(s\) independently draws a uniformly random permutation \(\pi_s\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Set \(x_{s,0}=x_s\) and update \(x_{s,j}=x_{s,j-1}-\eta_{s,j}\nabla f_{\pi_s(j)}(x_{s,j-1})\) for \(j=1,\ldots,n\). Then set \(x_{s+1}=x_{s,n}\). Stop after a prescribed number of epochs or when a specified stopping rule holds, and output the final iterate. Within an epoch every component is used exactly once, so the component indices are dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each epoch, draw a fresh uniform permutation and process every component exactly once in that order.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Conditional Unbiasedness Within an Epoch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence created after part of a random permutation has been revealed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\in\mathbb R^d\), let \(\pi\) be a uniform random permutation of \([n]\), and let \(\mathcal F_{j-1}=\sigma(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(j-1))\). Then \[\mathbb E[g_{\pi(j)}\mid\mathcal F_{j-1}]=\frac{1}{n-j+1}\sum_{i\notin\{\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(j-1)\}}g_i.\] Every position is marginally uniform, but for \(j>1\) this conditional mean generally differs from \(n^{-1}\sum_i g_i\). For example, if \(n=2\), \(g_1=0\), and \(g_2=2\), observing \(\pi(1)=1\) forces \(g_{\pi(2)}=2\), while the full mean is \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reshuffled component is marginally uniform, but conditional on the revealed prefix its mean is the mean of the remaining components rather than generally the full mean.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi\) is uniformly distributed over all permutations of \([n]\).
The vectors \(g_i\) are fixed before the permutation is drawn.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[g_{\pi(j)}\mid\mathcal F_{j-1}]\) is the remaining-population mean and need not equal \(n^{-1}\sum_i g_i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic deterministic traversal of finite-sum component indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an ordered list \((i_1,\ldots,i_n)\) containing every element of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) exactly once. A cyclic component order is the infinite deterministic sequence \(I_t=i_{1+(t\bmod n)}\) for \(t=0,1,\ldots\). Thus each block of \(n\) consecutive updates aligned with a cycle uses every component once, and the same order is repeated in every cycle. For incremental gradient descent, the associated update is \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t\nabla f_{I_t}(x_t)\). No conditional unbiasedness identity is implied for the individual update directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed ordering of all components is repeated periodically, using every component once per aligned cycle without randomization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-sum traversals specified by one or more fixed permutations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi=(\pi_s)_{s\ge 0}\) be a predetermined sequence of permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A deterministic permutation-order method selects component \(I_{sn+j-1}=\pi_s(j)\) at position \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) of epoch \(s\ge 0\). Every epoch therefore visits each component exactly once, but neither \(\pi_s\) nor the selected indices are random. A fixed cyclic order is the special case \(\pi_s=\pi\) for all \(s\); allowing a predetermined varying sequence gives a broader permutation-order family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each epoch follows a predetermined permutation, visiting every component once; the permutation may stay fixed or vary deterministically across epochs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Commuting Update Maps Eliminate Permutation Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient structural condition for one-pass endpoints to be independent of deterministic component order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1,\ldots,T_n:X\to X\) satisfy \(T_i\circ T_j=T_j\circ T_i\) for all \(i,j\). Then, for any permutations \(\pi,\sigma\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \[T_{\pi(n)}\circ\cdots\circ T_{\pi(1)}=T_{\sigma(n)}\circ\cdots\circ T_{\sigma(1)}.\] Thus every one-pass permutation has the same epoch map. Failure of pairwise commutativity permits, but does not by itself guarantee, distinct endpoints at a given initial point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise commuting component-update maps make every one-pass permutation produce the same epoch map; noncommutativity alone does not guarantee different endpoints at every initial point.
assumptions_latex: \(T_i:X\to X\) is a well-defined deterministic component-update map for each \(i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-component example showing that an epoch endpoint depends on deterministic component order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), let \(f_1(x)=\tfrac12(x-1)^2\), \(f_2(x)=\tfrac12(x+1)^2\), and start incremental gradient descent at \(x_0=0\) with constant \(\eta\in(0,1)\). Processing order \((1,2)\) gives \(x_1=\eta\) and \(x_2=-\eta^2\). Processing order \((2,1)\) gives \(x_1=-\eta\) and \(x_2=\eta^2\). Both orders use each component exactly once and have the same average objective \(F=(f_1+f_2)/2\), whose minimizer is \(0\), yet their epoch endpoints differ by \(2\eta^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even when every component is used once, reversing a deterministic two-component order changes the epoch endpoint.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\) and write \(g_i=\nabla f_i(x)\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Draw \(I\) with probabilities \(p_i>0\), where \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\), and set \(G=g_I/(np_I)\). Then \(\mathbb E[G]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i=\nabla F(x)\) and \(\mathbb E\lVert G\rVert^2=n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^n\lVert g_i\rVert^2/p_i\). If \(\lVert g_i\rVert>0\) for every \(i\), this second moment is minimized over positive probability vectors by \(p_i=\lVert g_i\rVert/\sum_{j=1}^n\lVert g_j\rVert\). If some component gradients vanish, the infimum over strictly positive probability vectors is approached by assigning vanishing probability to the zero gradients and probability proportional to \(\lVert g_i\rVert\) on the nonzero gradients; an imposed positive-probability floor changes the constrained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse-probability weighting preserves unbiasedness, while probabilities proportional to nonzero component-gradient norms minimize the estimator's second moment when strictly positive probabilities are feasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper sampling design on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is a random subset \(S\) whose marginal inclusion probabilities \(p_i=\mathbb P(i\in S)\) satisfy \(p_i>0\) for every \(i\). Dependence among inclusion indicators is unrestricted. For vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\) in a real Hilbert space, the Horvitz--Thompson-type estimator \(G_S=n^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}g_i/p_i\) is well-defined and satisfies \(\mathbb E[G_S]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i\). Properness is the positivity condition needed for every component to be recoverable through inverse-probability weighting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random-subset design is proper when every component has positive inclusion probability, enabling an unbiased inverse-probability estimator.
knowledge_statements.title: Proper Sampling Designs

source_witnesses.locator: 5 Randomized coordinate update methods p. 113

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact second moment of the inverse-inclusion estimator for an arbitrary proper subset law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq[n]\) be a proper sampling with \(p_i=\mathbb P(i\in S)>0\) and \(p_{ij}=\mathbb P(i,j\in S)\), using \(p_{ii}=p_i\). For fixed vectors \(g_i\), set \(G_S=n^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}g_i/p_i\) and \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_i g_i\). Then \[\mathbb E\|G_S-\bar g\|^2=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{p_{ij}-p_ip_j}{p_ip_j}\langle g_i,g_j\rangle.\] Thus marginal inclusion probabilities determine unbiasedness, while pairwise inclusion probabilities determine the covariance of this linear estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any proper subset design, inverse-inclusion weighting is unbiased and its exact variance is determined by first- and second-order inclusion probabilities.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i\) are fixed vectors in a real Hilbert space.

notation.meaning: joint inclusion probability of indices i and j

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An independent inclusion design chooses \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) by mutually independent indicators \(Z_i=\mathbf 1_{\{i\in S\}}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i)\), with \(p_i\in(0,1]\). Hence \(\mathbb P(S=C)=\prod_{i\in C}p_i\prod_{i\notin C}(1-p_i)\) for every \(C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For fixed vectors \(g_i\), define \(G_S=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i g_i/p_i\) and \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i\). Then \(\mathbb E[G_S]=\bar g\) and \(\mathbb E\lVert G_S-\bar g\rVert^2=n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^n(1-p_i)\lVert g_i\rVert^2/p_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each component is included by an independent Bernoulli trial; inverse-probability weighting is unbiased and has an additive variance formula.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Inclusion Designs

source_witnesses.locator: 5 Randomized coordinate update methods p. 113

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal Bernoulli inclusion probabilities under a prescribed expected batch size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let nonzero fixed vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\) be sampled by mutually independent indicators with probabilities \(0<p_i\leq1\), subject to \(\sum_i p_i=\tau\in(0,n]\). The variance of the inverse-probability mean estimator is \(n^{-2}\sum_i(1-p_i)\|g_i\|^2/p_i\). Its unique minimizing probability vector is \[p_i^\star=\min\{1,\|g_i\|/\lambda\},\] where \(\lambda>0\) is any threshold producing \(\sum_i p_i^\star=\tau\); the threshold is unique when \(\tau<n\). Thus unsaturated probabilities are norm-proportional and sufficiently large components are always included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a fixed expected Bernoulli batch size, variance-optimal inclusion probabilities follow a capped norm-proportional water-filling rule.
assumptions_latex: The inclusion indicators are mutually independent.

notation.meaning: threshold in the capped proportional rule

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Optimal Independent Inclusion Probabilities

children.title: Dependent Proper Designs
children.top_down_role: Proper subset distributions featuring coupled inclusion events.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pairwise Independence Does Not Certify an Independent Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Higher-order inclusion dependence invisible to first- and second-order inclusion probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U,V\) be independent \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) variables and define \(Z_1=U\), \(Z_2=V\), and \(Z_3=U\oplus V\), where \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. Each \(Z_i\) is fair Bernoulli and every pair is independent, so \(p_{ij}=p_ip_j=1/4\). Nevertheless \(Z_3=Z_1\oplus Z_2\) almost surely, so the three indicators are not mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper inclusion indicators can be pairwise independent yet jointly dependent, so pairwise inclusion data do not certify mutual independence.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(V\) are independent fair Bernoulli variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_{ij}=p_ip_j\text{ for every pair, but }(Z_1,Z_2,Z_3)\text{ are not mutually independent}.
knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Independence Does Not Certify an Independent Design

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical negatively dependent proper design obtained by uniform sampling without replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq2\) and let \(S\) be uniform over all subsets of \([n]\) of size \(\tau\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Then \(p_i=\tau/n\) and, for \(i\ne j\), \(p_{ij}=\tau(\tau-1)/(n(n-1))\), which is less than \(p_ip_j\) when \(\tau<n\). For fixed vectors \(g_i\), with \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_i g_i\), the sample mean \(G_S=\tau^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}g_i\) satisfies \[\mathbb E[G_S]=\bar g,\qquad \mathbb E\|G_S-\bar g\|^2=\frac{n-\tau}{\tau(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|g_i-\bar g\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform fixed-size sampling is a negatively dependent proper design whose sample mean has the finite-population variance correction.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is uniform among all \(\tau\)-subsets of \([n]\), with \(1\leq\tau\leq n\).
\(g_1,\ldots,g_n\) are fixed vectors in a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Fixed-Size Sampling Variance
Dependent Proper Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper random-subset sampling whose inclusion indicators are not mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a random subset of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and define inclusion indicators \(Z_i=\mathbf 1_{\{i\in S\}}\), first-order inclusion probabilities \(p_i=\mathbb P(i\in S)\), and second-order inclusion probabilities \(p_{ij}=\mathbb P(i,j\in S)\). The design is proper when \(p_i>0\) for every \(i\in[n]\). It is a dependent proper design when \((Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\) are not mutually independent. For vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\in\mathbb R^d\), the estimator \(\widehat g=n^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}g_i/p_i\) is unbiased for \(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i\); its second moment depends on the pairwise covariance terms \(p_{ij}-p_ip_j\), which need not detect higher-order dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper design gives every index positive inclusion probability. It is dependent when its inclusion indicators are not mutually independent. Importance correction preserves the population mean, while the estimator variance uses pairwise inclusion covariances and may not reveal purely higher-order dependence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i\), and the pairwise covariance terms are \(p_{ij}-p_ip_j\).

notation.meaning: first-order inclusion probability of index i
joint inclusion probability of indices i and j

A source is needed to determine the intended support score or weighting formula.

children.title: Curvature-Aware Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampling policies shaped by component smoothness or local curvature variation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal distribution for the worst importance-corrected component smoothness bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_i>0\), and let \(p\) range over positive probability vectors. Define \(C(p)=\max_i L_i/(np_i)\). Then \[\min_{p_i>0,\,\sum_i p_i=1}C(p)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nL_i,\] and the unique minimizer is \(p_i=L_i/\sum_jL_j\). At this choice every corrected bound \(L_i/(np_i)\) equals \(\bar L=n^{-1}\sum_jL_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling proportionally to component smoothness uniquely minimizes the worst importance-corrected smoothness constant and equalizes all corrected constants.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimax-Optimal Curvature-Proportional Probabilities
Curvature-Aware Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Importance sampling based on component smoothness constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where each \(f_i\) has an \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(L_i>0\). Define \(p_i=L_i/\sum_{j=1}^n L_j\). Then the importance-corrected component gradient \(G(x;i)=\nabla f_i(x)/(n p_i)\), for \(i\sim p\), is unbiased. Moreover, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^d\), \(\|G(x;i)-G(y;i)\|\le \bar L\|x-y\|\) for every sampled index, where \(\bar L=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n L_j\). Thus curvature-proportional sampling equalizes the corrected component Lipschitz bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling components proportionally to their smoothness constants preserves unbiasedness and equalizes the Lipschitz bounds of importance-corrected gradients.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable with \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient.

notation.meaning: arithmetic mean of the component smoothness constants

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard importance sampling by component smoothness
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unbiasedness and equalized corrected Lipschitz bound are mathematically correct for positive component smoothness constants, and property is an appropriate kind. No inspectable citation supports the claim.

children.title: Joint Structural Weighting
children.top_down_role: Sampling priorities that combine support information with curvature information.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Structural Weighting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampling probabilities combining curvature and support information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose component \(f_i\) has positive curvature proxy \(L_i\) and known gradient support \(T_i\subseteq[d]\). Let \(s_i>0\) be a prescribed support score computed from the family \((T_j)_{j=1}^n\), and let \(\Psi:(0,\infty)^2\to(0,\infty)\) be a fixed aggregation rule. Joint structural weighting assigns \(w_i=\Psi(L_i,s_i)\) and \(p_i=w_i/\sum_{j=1}^n w_j\). For \(i\sim p\), the corrected estimator \(G(x;i)=\nabla f_i(x)/(n p_i)\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[G(x;i)]=\nabla F(x)\), independently of the particular positive aggregation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint structural weighting combines curvature and support scores into positive sampling weights, with importance correction ensuring an unbiased gradient estimate.

notation.meaning: positive rule aggregating curvature and support scores

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The importance-correction identity is correct for any positive weights, but the unrestricted aggregation map does not identify the intended joint structural weighting method. A source is needed for the support score and aggregation formula.

children.title: Independent Batches
children.top_down_role: Mini-batches formed through independent component draws or inclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Batches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: With-replacement mini-batches formed from independent component draws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_1,\ldots,I_b\) be independent draws from probabilities \(p_i>0\) on \([n]\), and let \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\in\mathbb R^d\). Define \(\widehat g_b=b^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^b g_{I_r}/(n p_{I_r})\) and \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i\). Then \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_b]=\bar g\), and independence gives \(\mathbb E\|\widehat g_b-\bar g\|^2=b^{-1}\mathbb E\|g_I/(n p_I)-\bar g\|^2\), where \(I\sim p\). Thus the mean-square sampling variance is reduced by the factor \(1/b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A batch of independent importance-weighted samples is unbiased, and its mean-square sampling variance equals the single-sample variance divided by batch size.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i\in\mathbb R^d\) are deterministic conditional on the current iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_b]=\bar g\) and \(\mathbb E\|\widehat g_b-\bar g\|^2=b^{-1}\mathbb E\|g_I/(n p_I)-\bar g\|^2\).

notation.meaning: number of independent draws in the batch

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: variance identity for an average of independent unbiased samples
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The independent-sample variance identity is correct and property fits the leaf. The batch size should explicitly be a positive integer, and no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Without-Replacement Batches
children.top_down_role: Mini-batches formed from distinct components within each sampling round.

knowledge_statements.title: Without-Replacement Batches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform fixed-size mini-batches sampled without replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be uniformly distributed over all subsets of \([n]\) having cardinality \(b\), where \(1\le b\le n\), and let \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\in\mathbb R^d\). With \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i\), define \(\widehat g_S=b^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}g_i\). Then \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_S]=\bar g\) and \[\mathbb E\|\widehat g_S-\bar g\|^2=\frac{n-b}{b(n-1)}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\|g_i-\bar g\|^2.\] The factor \((n-b)/(n-1)\) is the finite-population correction relative to independent uniform draws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform batch sampled without replacement is unbiased and enjoys the finite-population variance correction, vanishing when the full population is selected.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a uniform cardinality-\(b\) subset of \([n]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_S]=\bar g\) with variance factor \((n-b)/(b(n-1))\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical finite-population sampling variance identity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-size uniform without-replacement estimator and finite-population variance formula are correct for n greater than one. Property fits the leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Batch-Size Saturation
children.top_down_role: Transitions where finite-population effects materially alter batch efficiency.

knowledge_statements.title: Batch-Size Saturation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance and information saturation as a mini-batch approaches the dataset size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For uniform sampling without replacement from \(n>1\) vectors, the batch-mean variance multiplier is \(q_b=(n-b)/(b(n-1))\) for \(1\le b\le n\). Hence \(q_n=0\): at batch size \(n\), the estimator equals the full mean deterministically, so additional sampling cannot reduce data-access variance. By contrast, for independent sampling with replacement, the multiplier is \(1/b\), which is positive for every finite \(b\) whenever the single-sample variance is nonzero. Thus exact finite-size saturation is specific to exhaustive without-replacement coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without-replacement variance reaches zero at a full batch; independent with-replacement batching only approaches zero and does not saturate at dataset size.
assumptions_latex: The single-sample variance is nonzero when comparing with-replacement sampling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_n=0\) without replacement, whereas \(1/b>0\) for every finite with-replacement batch size \(b\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct boundary consequence of finite-population variance formulas
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated saturation boundary correctly distinguishes exhaustive without-replacement sampling from finite with-replacement batching, and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. No inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Stratified Batches
children.top_down_role: Batch construction using predefined component strata with controlled representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vector Covariance of a Stratified Batch Mean
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-population covariance decomposition for vector-valued component gradients sampled independently within strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stratified design with disjoint nonempty strata H_h, sizes N_h, and independent uniform without-replacement samples A_h of sizes 1\le b_h\le N_h, let g_i\in\mathbb R^d, \bar g_h=N_h^{-1}\sum_{i\in H_h}g_i, and \Sigma_h=(N_h-1)^{-1}\sum_{i\in H_h}(g_i-\bar g_h)(g_i-\bar g_h)^\top for N_h>1, with \Sigma_h=0 for N_h=1. For \widehat g=\sum_h(N_h/n)b_h^{-1}\sum_{i\in A_h}g_i, \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat g)=\sum_h\left(\frac{N_h}{n}\right)^2\left(1-\frac{b_h}{N_h}\right)\frac{\Sigma_h}{b_h}. Consequently, the estimator is exact whenever every stratum is fully sampled or has zero within-stratum covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For vector gradients, independent stratified sampling yields a sum of finite-population-corrected within-stratum covariance matrices; census or internally constant strata contribute no error.
assumptions_latex: Within each stratum, sampling is uniform without replacement with fixed size b_h.
Samples from different strata are independent.

notation.meaning: finite-population covariance matrix within stratum h

knowledge_statements.title: Vector Covariance of a Stratified Batch Mean
Stratified Batches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased mini-batches sampled separately within disjoint data strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \([n]\) into nonempty strata \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\) of sizes \(N_h\). For each \(h\), let \(A_h\subseteq H_h\) be a uniformly sampled subset of size \(b_h\), with the subsets sampled independently across strata, and define \(\bar g_h=N_h^{-1}\sum_{i\in H_h}g_i\). The estimator \(\widehat g=\sum_{h=1}^m(N_h/n)b_h^{-1}\sum_{i\in A_h}g_i\) is unbiased for \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i\). For scalar \(g_i\), define \(\sigma_h^2=(N_h-1)^{-1}\sum_{i\in H_h}(g_i-\bar g_h)^2\) when \(N_h>1\), and set \(\sigma_h^2=0\) when \(N_h=1\). Then \[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat g)=\sum_{h=1}^m\left(\frac{N_h}{n}\right)^2\left(1-\frac{b_h}{N_h}\right)\frac{\sigma_h^2}{b_h}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stratified batching samples each stratum separately and combines the sampled stratum means using population shares. The estimator is unbiased, and for scalar data its variance is the sum of finite-population-corrected within-stratum contributions.
assumptions_latex: \((H_h)_{h=1}^m\) is a partition of \([n]\) into nonempty strata.
Each \(A_h\) is a uniform size-\(b_h\) subset of \(H_h\), sampled independently across strata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g]=\bar g\), with scalar variance \(\sum_{h=1}^m(N_h/n)^2(1-b_h/N_h)\sigma_h^2/b_h\).

notation.meaning: sampled subset of the h-th stratum

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical stratified random-sampling estimator and variance decomposition

children.title: Partitioned Batches
children.top_down_role: Batch construction using disjoint component blocks or worker-local partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Partitioned Batches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mini-batch design based on a fixed partition of component indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((B_r)_{r=1}^M\) be a partition of \([n]\) into nonempty deterministic blocks, and assign block-selection probabilities \(q_r>0\) with \(\sum_{r=1}^M q_r=1\). After drawing \(R\sim q\), access all indices in \(B_R\) and form \(\widehat g=(n q_R)^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_R}g_i\). Because each index belongs to exactly one block, \(\mathbb E[\widehat g]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i\). If all blocks have common size and \(q_r=1/M\), the estimator is simply the arithmetic mean over the selected block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partitioned batch selects one fixed index block and weights its aggregate by the block-selection probability to estimate the full mean unbiasedly.

children.title: Cross-Stratum Allocation
children.top_down_role: Allocation choices controlling how batch capacity is distributed across strata.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Integer Allocation by Marginal Gains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact allocation of an integer batch budget for a separable reciprocal variance objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_h>0\), integer capacities \(N_h\ge1\), and integer budget \(m\le b\le\sum_hN_h\). To minimize \(\sum_hA_h/b_h\) over integers \(1\le b_h\le N_h\) with \(\sum_hb_h=b\), initialize \(b_h=1\). Repeatedly assign the next sample to an uncapped stratum maximizing \[\Delta_h(b_h)=\frac{A_h}{b_h}-\frac{A_h}{b_h+1}=\frac{A_h}{b_h(b_h+1)}\] until the budget is exhausted. The resulting allocation is globally optimal; ties may yield multiple optimal allocations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integer allocations, repeatedly place the next sample where it produces the largest remaining variance reduction, subject to stratum capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The marginal-gain allocation minimizes \(\sum_hA_h/b_h\) over all feasible integer allocations.

notation.meaning: objective decrease from increasing stratum h from k to k+1 samples

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Integer Allocation by Marginal Gains

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous variance-minimizing allocation when each stratum has finite sampling capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_h>0\), capacities \(N_h>0\), and \(0<b<\sum_{h=1}^mN_h\). For \[\min_{0<b_h\le N_h,\;\sum_hb_h=b}\sum_{h=1}^m\frac{A_h}{b_h},\] the unique minimizer satisfies \[b_h^*=\min\!\left\{N_h,\sqrt{A_h/\lambda}\right\},\] where the unique \(\lambda>0\) is chosen so that \(\sum_hb_h^*=b\). For stratified mean estimation, \(A_h=(N_h/n)^2S_h^2\), so uncapped strata receive allocations proportional to \(N_hS_h\). The uncapped Neyman allocation is feasible exactly when none of its entries exceeds its capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An over-capacity Neyman allocation is capped, and the remaining continuous budget is redistributed in square-root proportion among uncapped strata.
assumptions_latex: Allocations are continuous; integer restrictions are excluded.

notation.meaning: coefficient of the allocation-dependent variance term

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Constrained Continuous Allocation
Cross-Stratum Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance-minimizing allocation of a fixed batch budget across strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scalar stratified sampling with stratum sizes \(N_h\), standard deviations \(S_h>0\), and total batch budget \(b\), ignore integer and upper-bound constraints and minimize the allocation-dependent variance term \(\sum_{h=1}^m (N_h/n)^2S_h^2/b_h\) over \(b_h>0\) subject to \(\sum_{h=1}^m b_h=b\). The unique minimizer is the Neyman allocation \[b_h^*=b\,\frac{N_hS_h}{\sum_{k=1}^m N_kS_k}.\] With unequal per-sample costs \(c_h>0\) and constraint \(\sum_h c_hb_h=b\), the continuous optimum is proportional to \(N_hS_h/\sqrt{c_h}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed sampling budget is allocated across strata proportionally to stratum size and variability, with a square-root cost adjustment when costs differ.
assumptions_latex: Each stratum has size \(N_h>0\) and scalar standard deviation \(S_h>0\).
Allocations are treated as positive real numbers before integer rounding.
The total allocation budget is fixed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The continuous Neyman allocation and square-root cost adjustment are correct under the stated relaxation, and property fits the leaf. An inspectable source is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unbiasedness when batch size depends on observations included in the same ordinary average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_1,X_2\) be independent with \(\mathbb P(X_r=1)=\mathbb P(X_r=-1)=1/2\). Set \(N=1\) if \(X_1=1\) and \(N=2\) if \(X_1=-1\), and return \(\widehat\mu=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N X_r\). Then \[\mathbb E[\widehat\mu]=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12\mathbb E[(-1+X_2)/2]=\tfrac14\ne0.\] Thus pre-batch predictability cannot generally be replaced by a stopping rule that observes samples entering the same uncorrected average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing the batch size after seeing samples in that batch can bias the ordinary sample mean even though every sample is unbiased.
assumptions_latex: The estimator is the uncorrected average through the data-dependent stopping time \(N\).
knowledge_statements.title: Bias from Within-Batch Adaptive Stopping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive with-replacement batch sizing from a predictable conditional-variance bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let Z_t be a single importance-corrected component-gradient draw at x_t such that \mathbb E[Z_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=
abla F(x_t) and \mathbb E[\lVert Z_t-
abla F(x_t)Vert^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le v_t, where v_t and a target \delta_t>0 are \mathcal F_t-measurable. Choose b_t=\max\{1,\lceil v_t/\delta_tceil\}, draw b_t conditionally independent copies Z_{t,r}, and set G_t=b_t^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{b_t}Z_{t,r}. Then \mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=
abla F(x_t) and \mathbb E[\lVert G_t-
abla F(x_t)Vert^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le\delta_t. Through iteration T, the production component-gradient cost is \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}b_t.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the next batch from a past-measurable variance bound so the averaged gradient meets a requested conditional mean-square-error target; production work is the sum of the selected sizes.
assumptions_latex: v_t and \delta_t>0 are measurable before the production batch is drawn.
Conditional on \mathcal F_t, the production draws are independent and have common conditional mean \nabla F(x_t).
The single-draw conditional mean-square error is at most v_t.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla F(x_t),\qquad \mathbb E[\lVert G_t-\nabla F(x_t)\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le\delta_t,\qquad C_T=\sum_{t<T}b_t.

notation.meaning: predictable upper bound on single-draw conditional mean-square error
target conditional mean-square error for the batch estimator

knowledge_statements.title: Predictable Variance-Targeted Batch Sizing

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid adaptation when batch size is selected using information independent of the samples entering the reported average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At iteration t, let P_t be pilot information and define \mathcal G_t=\mathcal F_t\vee\sigma(P_t). Choose an integer b_t\ge1 measurable with respect to \mathcal G_t. Conditional on \mathcal G_t, draw production gradients Z_{t,1},\ldots,Z_{t,b_t} independently with \mathbb E[Z_{t,r}\mid\mathcal G_t]=
abla F(x_t), and return G_t=b_t^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{b_t}Z_{t,r}. Then \mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal G_t]=
abla F(x_t), hence \mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=
abla F(x_t). Pilot cost must be counted separately from production cost b_t.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pilot may choose the production batch size without biasing the reported gradient when production samples are conditionally fresh after that choice; pilot queries still count as work.
assumptions_latex: b_t is measurable with respect to the pre-production information \mathcal G_t.
Production draws are conditionally independent of the selection mechanism given \mathcal G_t.
Every production draw has conditional mean \nabla F(x_t).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal G_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\Longrightarrow\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla F(x_t).

notation.meaning: pilot information used to select the production batch size
information available after the pilot and before production sampling

knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Pilot Adaptation Preserves Production Unbiasedness
Adaptive Batch Sizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predictable iteration-dependent mini-batch sizes with conditionally unbiased estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\), a stepsize sequence \((\eta_t)\), and a filtration \((\mathcal F_t)\), choose at iteration \(t\) an \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable batch size \(b_t\ge1\). Conditional on \(\mathcal F_t\), draw indices \(I_{t,1},\ldots,I_{t,b_t}\) independently from fixed positive probabilities \((p_i)_{i=1}^n\), form \(G_t=b_t^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{b_t}\nabla f_{I_{t,r}}(x_t)/(n p_{I_{t,r}})\), and update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tG_t\). Stop under a prescribed budget or accuracy test and output the final iterate. Predictability of \(b_t\) yields \(\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose each batch size from past information, then sample and importance-correct the batch so the gradient estimate remains conditionally unbiased.
assumptions_latex: Conditional batch draws are independent with \(p_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\) for every iteration \(t\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component-gradient accounting for deterministic full-reference refreshes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a reference refresh costs \(n\) component-gradient evaluations and each inner update costs \(c\) component-gradient evaluations. An epoch of \(m\) updates costs \(n+cm\), so its amortized cost per update is \(c+n/m\). Through \(K\) updates, the cost is at most \[C_K\le cK+n\lceil K/m\rceil.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refreshing a full reference every m updates contributes n divided by m component-gradient evaluations per inner update, apart from a terminal partial epoch.
assumptions_latex: Each full reference costs \(n\) component-gradient evaluations.
Each inner update costs \(c\) component-gradient evaluations.
The first relevant epoch includes one full refresh.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_K\le cK+n\lceil K/m\rceil\), with completed-epoch cost per update \(c+n/m\).

notation.meaning: component-gradient cost through K inner updates

knowledge_statements.title: Amortized Full-Reference Cost

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic Reference Age Under Fixed Epochs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact freshness profile induced by deterministic epoch boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a reference is refreshed at iterations \(0,m,2m,\ldots\), its age at iteration \(k\) is \[a_k=k-m\lfloor k/m\rfloor=k\bmod m.\] Hence \(0\le a_k\le m-1\), every completed epoch contains one refresh, and the mean age over an epoch is \((m-1)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-epoch refreshing produces a periodic reference age bounded by one less than the epoch length.
assumptions_latex: Refreshes occur exactly at nonnegative integer multiples of \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_k=k\bmod m\), \(\max a_k=m-1\), and the epoch mean is \((m-1)/2\).

notation.meaning: number of updates since the latest refresh

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Reference Age Under Fixed Epochs
Fixed-Epoch Refresh
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SVRG-type reference gradient refreshed at deterministic epoch boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), choose epoch length \(m\ge1\), stepsize \(\eta>0\), and snapshot \(\widetilde x_0\). At epoch \(s\), compute \(\mu_s=
abla F(\widetilde x_s)\), initialize \(x_{s,0}=\widetilde x_s\), and for \(k=0,\ldots,m-1\) draw \(I_{s,k}\) uniformly from \([n]\), set \(v_{s,k}=
abla f_{I_{s,k}}(x_{s,k})-
abla f_{I_{s,k}}(\widetilde x_s)+\mu_s\), and update \(x_{s,k+1}=x_{s,k}-\eta v_{s,k}\). Set \(\widetilde x_{s+1}=x_{s,m}\); stop after a prescribed number of epochs and output the last snapshot.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each fixed epoch boundary, recompute a full reference gradient and use it for variance-reduced component updates throughout the next epoch.
assumptions_latex: Indices are sampled uniformly and conditionally independently during each epoch.
The epoch length \(m\) and stepsize \(\eta\) are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[v_{s,k}\mid x_{s,k},\widetilde x_s]=\nabla F(x_{s,k})\), and the reference pair is refreshed every \(m\) inner updates.

notation.meaning: snapshot at the start of epoch s
full gradient at the epoch snapshot
