intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the leaf, but the exact contraction factor depends on the snapshot-selection convention, which is not fully defined or supported by a theorem-level citation.

children.title: Table-Method Linear Convergence
children.top_down_role: Linear convergence results for methods maintaining component-indexed historical information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Linear Convergence Fails Without a Growth Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a uniform geometric table-method rate over merely convex smooth finite sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n=1\), a SAGA table update reduces to gradient descent. Define the convex \(12\)-smooth function \[f(x)=\begin{cases}x^4,&|x|\le1,\\1+4(|x|-1)+6(|x|-1)^2,&|x|>1.\end{cases}\] For any fixed \(0<\eta<1/4\) and sufficiently small \(x_0\ne0\), the iterates remain in \((-1,1)\) and satisfy \(x_{k+1}=x_k-4\eta x_k^3\). Hence \(x_{k+1}/x_k\to1\) and \(f(x_{k+1})/f(x_k)\to1\), excluding a uniform contraction factor below one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-component smooth convex table method need not converge geometrically when no strong-convexity, quadratic-growth, or comparable error-bound condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Linear Convergence Fails Without a Growth Condition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Conditional Variance Identity for a Table Estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic variance representation for a fixed component-gradient table.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), fix a table \((\alpha_i)_{i=1}^n\), set \( ar\alpha=n^{-1}\sum_i\alpha_i\), and sample \(i\) uniformly. For \(v=
abla f_i(x)-\alpha_i+ ar\alpha\), define \(\delta_i=
abla f_i(x)-\alpha_i\) and \( ar\delta=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_i\). Conditional on \(x\) and the table, \(\mathbb E_i[v]=
abla F(x)\) and \(\mathbb E_i\|v-
abla F(x)\|^2=n^{-1}\sum_i\|\delta_i- ar\delta\|^2\le n^{-1}\sum_i\|\delta_i\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed SAGA-style table gives an unbiased estimator whose variance is exactly the empirical variance of its component-gradient discrepancies.
assumptions_latex: The table is fixed before the uniform index is sampled.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Conditional Variance Identity for a Table Estimator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fully specified gradient-table update with initialization and component-oracle accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\). Initialize \(x_0\), set \(\alpha_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)\) for every \(i\), and maintain \(\bar\alpha_k=n^{-1}\sum_i\alpha_i^k\). At iteration \(k\), sample \(I_k\) uniformly, evaluate \(g_k=\nabla f_{I_k}(x_k)\), form \(v_k=g_k-\alpha_{I_k}^k+\bar\alpha_k\), set \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta v_k\), replace \(\alpha_{I_k}^{k+1}=g_k\), leave other entries unchanged, and update \(\bar\alpha_{k+1}=\bar\alpha_k+(g_k-\alpha_{I_k}^k)/n\). Initialization plus \(K\) iterations uses \(n+K\) component-gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SAGA initializes a component-gradient table, uses one fresh component to form an unbiased corrected direction, and then replaces that component's stored gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(I_k\) is conditionally uniform given the pre-sampling history.
The old table value is used before replacement.
Stored gradients and their average are retained exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Initialized Single-Index SAGA Method
Table-Method Linear Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SAGA-type linear convergence with a component-gradient memory table.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), where every \(f_i\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth and \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex. A SAGA iteration samples \(i_k\) uniformly, forms \[v_k=\nabla f_{i_k}(x_k)-\alpha_{i_k}^k+\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_j^k,\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta v_k,\] replaces \(\alpha_{i_k}^k\) by \(\nabla f_{i_k}(x_k)\), and leaves other table entries unchanged. There exist universal constants \(c,c'>0\) such that, for \(0<\eta\leq c/L\), a standard iterate-and-table Lyapunov function satisfies \[\mathbb E[V_k]\leq\left(1-c'\min\{n^{-1},\mu/L\}\right)^kV_0.\] Hence the component-gradient complexity is \(O((n+L/\mu)\log(V_0/\varepsilon))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A SAGA gradient table yields geometric Lyapunov decay and component-gradient complexity proportional to n plus the condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(i_k\) is sampled uniformly and independently conditional on the past.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the leaf, but the Lyapunov function is undefined and the universal constants and resulting complexity require a precise SAGA theorem citation.

children.title: Reference-Structure Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural contrasts between global snapshots and component tables in linear regimes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Table-Update Timing Can Destroy Conditional Unbiasedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Timing boundary distinguishing a correction based on a pre-sampling fixed table from an estimator formed after same-sample replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the pre-sampling table be \((\alpha_j)_{j=1}^n\) with mean \( ar\alpha\). Sample \(i\) uniformly, replace \(\alpha_i\) by \(
abla f_i(x)\), and use the resulting table mean \(v_i= ar\alpha+n^{-1}(
abla f_i(x)-\alpha_i)\), where \(\alpha_i\) on the right denotes the old entry. Conditional on the old table, \(\mathbb E_i[v_i]=(1-n^{-1}) ar\alpha+n^{-1}
abla F(x)\), which differs from \(
abla F(x)\) unless \( ar\alpha=
abla F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing the sampled table entry before using the updated mean as the estimator generally produces bias; unbiasedness depends on the estimator and update order.
assumptions_latex: The sampled index is uniform conditional on the old table.

notation.meaning: mean of the old gradient table
updated table mean used as an estimator

knowledge_statements.title: Table-Update Timing Can Destroy Conditional Unbiasedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage, synchronization, and representation comparison for the two stored-reference families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), the snapshot estimator \(v=
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(\widetilde x)+
abla F(\widetilde x)\) stores \(\widetilde x\) and \(
abla F(\widetilde x)\), using \(O(d)\) additional persistent storage and a synchronized \(n\)-component refresh. A gradient-table estimator \(v=
abla f_i(x)-\alpha_i+ ar\alpha\), \( ar\alpha=n^{-1}\sum_j\alpha_j\), stores \(n\) gradient references and their mean, using \(O(nd)\) storage under an explicit dense representation, and can refresh one entry without a periodic synchronized full gradient. Point tables also use \(O(nd)\) storage. For generalized-linear components whose gradients are scalar multiples of fixed data vectors, a gradient table may instead be represented by \(n\) scalars plus the maintained \(d\)-vector mean. Conditional on the stored state and uniform sampling, both displayed estimators are unbiased.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Snapshots use one synchronized global reference and little additional memory; tables use componentwise references, usually more memory, and asynchronous one-entry refreshes, with scalar-memory specializations for structured components.
assumptions_latex: The sampled index is uniform conditional on the stored reference state.
Storage costs use explicit dense-vector representations unless a structural specialization is stated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_i[v]=\nabla F(x)\) for both displayed estimators; snapshot storage is \(O(d)\), dense table storage is \(O(nd)\), and structured scalar tables can use \(O(n+d)\) additional storage.
knowledge_statements.title: Snapshot and Table Reference Structures

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Temporal representation of snapshot and component-table reference states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Index component-gradient evaluations by iteration. A snapshot has reference times \(\tau_1=\cdots=\tau_n=\tau\) and references \(r_i=\nabla f_i(x_\tau)\); refreshing it replaces all reference times simultaneously. A one-entry table has \(r_i=\nabla f_i(x_{\tau_i})\) with generally unequal \(\tau_i\), and refreshing index \(j\) changes only \(\tau_j\) and \(r_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Snapshot references have one common age, whereas table references generally have heterogeneous componentwise ages.
assumptions_latex: Each stored reference is a component gradient evaluated at a previously generated iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_1=\cdots=\tau_n\) for a snapshot, while one-entry table refreshes permit heterogeneous \((\tau_i)_{i=1}^n\).

notation.meaning: iteration at which component i's stored reference was evaluated

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Age versus Heterogeneous-Age References
Reference-Structure Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares snapshot and gradient-table control variates for smooth finite sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\). A snapshot estimator stores \((\widetilde x,
abla F(\widetilde x))\) and uses \(v=
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(\widetilde x)+
abla F(\widetilde x)\), requiring \(O(d)\) persistent storage and periodic full-gradient evaluations. A table estimator stores points or gradients \((\alpha_i)_{i=1}^n\) and uses \(v=
abla f_i(x)-\alpha_i+n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_j\), requiring \(O(nd)\) storage but no periodic synchronized full gradient. Under uniform sampling, both displayed estimators satisfy \(\mathbb E_i[v]=
abla F(x)\) when the stored quantities are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Snapshot control variates use little memory but periodically compute full gradients; table methods use linear-in-sample memory and update one stored reference per iteration. Both displayed estimators are conditionally unbiased.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_i[v]=\nabla F(x)\), with snapshot storage \(O(d)\) and table storage \(O(nd)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the comparison leaf, and the displayed conditional-unbiasedness identities are standard. However, no citation supports the storage, synchronization, or update-structure claims; moreover, the plain statement says that one table entry is updated per iteration, which the mathematical statement does not specify.

children.title: Recursive-Method Linear Convergence
children.top_down_role: Linear convergence regimes based on recursively updated variance-reduced estimators.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Error Propagation in a Recursive Estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-mean identity showing why a SARAH-type recursive estimator is not generally conditionally unbiased at every inner step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_t=v_{t-1}+
abla f_{i_t}(x_t)-
abla f_{i_t}(x_{t-1})\), where \(i_t\) is uniform and independent of the pre-sampling history \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\), and suppose \(x_{t-1},x_t,v_{t-1}\) are \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable. For \(F=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\) and \(e_t=v_t-
abla F(x_t)\), one has \(\mathbb E[v_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=v_{t-1}+
abla F(x_t)-
abla F(x_{t-1})\) and \(\mathbb E[e_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=e_{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recursive gradient difference carries the preceding estimator error forward and is not generally conditionally unbiased at every inner iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(i_t\) is uniform and independent of \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Error Propagation in a Recursive Estimator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fully timed recursive method with exact-gradient epoch initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given epoch input \widetilde x_s, set x_0=\widetilde x_s and v_0=
abla F(x_0), where F=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i. For t=1,\ldots,m, set x_t=x_{t-1}-\eta v_{t-1}, sample i_t uniformly and independently, and set v_t=v_{t-1}+
abla f_{i_t}(x_t)-
abla f_{i_t}(x_{t-1}). Draw 	au_s uniformly from \{0,\ldots,m\}, independently of the epoch samples, and set \widetilde x_{s+1}=x_{	au_s}. An implementation that separately evaluates both component terms and stores no component-gradient table uses n+2m component-gradient calls per epoch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each epoch starts with a full gradient, performs recursive same-index differences, and passes a uniformly selected inner iterate to the next epoch.
assumptions_latex: The indices i_t are independent and uniform.
Both component terms are separately evaluated and no component-gradient table is cached.
knowledge_statements.title: Epochwise Uniform-Output SARAH Recursion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Gradient-Step Boundary in the One-Component Recursive Limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary step-size boundary inherited on a scalar quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take n=1 and f_1(x)=Lx^2/2. Then v_t=Lx_t exactly and x_{t+1}=(1-\eta L)x_t. If \eta=2/L and x_0\ne0, the iterates alternate between x_0 and -x_0; if \eta>2/L, their magnitudes diverge. Thus no general convergence theorem for this recursion can permit \eta\ge2/L.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with an exact recursive estimator, the scalar quadratic oscillates at 2/L and diverges above it.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Gradient-Step Boundary in the One-Component Recursive Limit

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Mean-Square Error Accumulation in Recursive Estimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conditional second-moment recursion for the estimator error in the accepted SARAH-type update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under \(v_t=v_{t-1}+
abla f_{i_t}(x_t)-
abla f_{i_t}(x_{t-1})\), define \(e_t=v_t-
abla F(x_t)\) and \(\zeta_t=
abla f_{i_t}(x_t)-
abla f_{i_t}(x_{t-1})-[
abla F(x_t)-
abla F(x_{t-1})]\). If \(i_t\) is uniform and independent of \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\), while \(x_{t-1},x_t,v_{t-1}\) are \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable, then \(e_t=e_{t-1}+\zeta_t\), \(\mathbb E[\zeta_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0\), and \[\mathbb E[\|e_t\|^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\|e_{t-1}\|^2+\mathbb E[\|\zeta_t\|^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recursive estimator carries its preceding squared error forward and adds the conditional variance of the sampled gradient difference.
assumptions_latex: \(i_t\) is uniform and independent of \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\).

notation.meaning: history before sampling the current component

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Mean-Square Error Accumulation in Recursive Estimation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle Complexity from a Recursive-Epoch Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional conversion of a contraction for the accepted uniform-output recursion into component-gradient complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the accepted uniform-output recursive method satisfies \(\mathbb E[F(\widetilde x_s)-F^*]\le\rho^s\Delta_0\) for \(\rho\in(0,1)\). If each epoch costs \(n+2m\) component-gradient evaluations, then \[S=\left\lceil\frac{\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)}{\log(1/\rho)}\right\rceil\] epochs suffice and \[N_{\mathrm{grad}}\le(n+2m)\left\lceil\frac{\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)}{\log(1/\rho)}\right\rceil.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified epoch contraction converts into component-gradient complexity by multiplying the required epoch count by the declared epoch cost.
assumptions_latex: The specified uniform-output recursion contracts the expected objective gap by \(\rho\in(0,1)\).
Each epoch costs exactly \(n+2m\) component-gradient calls.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Complexity from a Recursive-Epoch Contraction
Recursive-Method Linear Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strongly convex SARAH-type recursion with periodic exact-gradient initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth and \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex. Initialize each epoch with \(v_0=
abla F(x_0)\), and iterate \(x_t=x_{t-1}-\eta v_{t-1}\) and \(v_t=
abla f_{i_t}(x_t)-
abla f_{i_t}(x_{t-1})+v_{t-1}\). For suitable universal choices \(\eta=\Theta(L^{-1})\) and epoch length \(m=\Theta(L/\mu)\), an appropriately selected epoch output satisfies \(\mathbb E[F(x^{s})-F^*]\leq ho^s(F(x^0)-F^*)\) for some \(ho\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A periodically restarted recursive gradient estimator converges geometrically on smooth strongly convex finite sums when its step size and epoch length scale with smoothness and condition number.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
Indices \(i_t\) are sampled uniformly and independently within each epoch.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the linear-convergence leaf, but the precise SARAH-type variant, epoch transition, selected output, admissible step size, epoch length, and contraction claim require a method-specific theorem citation.

children.title: Refresh-Method Linear Convergence
children.top_down_role: Linear convergence regimes based on randomized or scheduled estimator renewal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Snapshot Estimator Unbiasedness and Variance Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural control-variate property supporting refresh-method convergence analyses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) and \(v=
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(w)+
abla F(w)\), where \(i\) is uniform conditional on fixed \(x,w\). Then \(\mathbb E_i[v]=
abla F(x)\) and \(\mathbb E_i\|v-
abla F(x)\|^2\leq n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n\|
abla f_j(x)-
abla f_j(w)\|^2\). If every \(f_j\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth, the latter is at most \(2L igl(F(x)-F(w)-\langle
abla F(w),x-wangle igr)\), and the variance vanishes when \(x=w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The snapshot control-variate estimator is conditionally unbiased, and its variance is controlled by current-to-snapshot separation and vanishes when the points coincide.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is differentiable for the unbiasedness identity.
For the final variance bound, every \(f_i\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth.
The sampled index is uniform conditional on fixed \(x,w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_i[v]=\nabla F(x)\) with the displayed variance bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Snapshot Estimator Unbiasedness and Variance Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fully timed loopless snapshot algorithm with declared oracle accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize w_0=x_0 and g_0=
abla F(w_0). At iteration k, sample i_k uniformly, form v_k=
abla f_{i_k}(x_k)-
abla f_{i_k}(w_k)+g_k, and set x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta v_k. Independently draw B_k\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p). If B_k=1, set w_{k+1}=x_{k+1} and compute g_{k+1}=
abla F(w_{k+1}); otherwise retain (w_{k+1},g_{k+1})=(w_k,g_k). An implementation that separately evaluates both component terms uses n+2K+n\sum_{k<K}B_k calls through K iterations, with expectation n+K(2+np).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the old snapshot for the current step, then refresh to the new iterate for subsequent steps.
assumptions_latex: B_k is Bernoulli(p) and independent of i_k and the pre-decision history.
The two component terms are separately evaluated and no component-gradient table is cached.
knowledge_statements.title: Post-Step Loopless Snapshot Method

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strongly convex finite sum showing failure of exact mean-square convergence without renewal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let n=2, f_1(x)=0, f_2(x)=x^2, and F(x)=x^2/2. Fix w\ne0 and p=0. The estimator is v_k=w for i_k=1 and v_k=2x_k-w for i_k=2. Hence \mathbb E[v_k\mid x_k]=x_k and, for x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta v_k, \mathbb E[x_{k+1}\mid x_k]=(1-\eta)x_k and \mathbb E[x_{k+1}^2\mid x_k]=(1-2\eta+2\eta^2)x_k^2-2\eta^2wx_k+\eta^2w^2. For 0<\eta<1, \mathbb E[x_k]\to0 and \mathbb E[x_k^2]\to\eta w^2/(2(1-\eta))>0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed nonoptimal snapshot leaves persistent variance at the optimum and creates a positive constant-step mean-square floor.
knowledge_statements.title: No-Refresh Snapshot Noise Floor

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Oracle Complexity from a Loopless Snapshot Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional conversion of a Lyapunov contraction into expected component-gradient complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the accepted post-step loopless snapshot method has a nonnegative Lyapunov function satisfying \(\mathbb E\Phi_K\le(1-\gamma)^K\Phi_0\), where \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), and \(\mathbb E[F(x_K)-F^*]\le C\mathbb E\Phi_K\). With expected cost \(n+K(2+np)\), \[K=\left\lceil\frac{\log(C\Phi_0/\varepsilon)}{-\log(1-\gamma)}\right\rceil\] suffices, and \[\mathbb E N_{\mathrm{grad}}\le n+(2+np)\left\lceil\frac{\log(C\Phi_0/\varepsilon)}{-\log(1-\gamma)}\right\rceil.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified loopless Lyapunov contraction combines with the exact expected refresh cost to give total expected oracle work.
assumptions_latex: A declared nonnegative Lyapunov function contracts by \(1-\gamma\).
The objective gap is bounded by \(C\mathbb E\Phi_K\).
The nonreusing implementation has expected cost \(n+K(2+np)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Expected Oracle Complexity from a Loopless Snapshot Contraction
Refresh-Method Linear Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loopless snapshot refresh under smooth strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), with convex \(L\)-smooth components and \(\mu\)-strongly convex \(F\). Given a reference \(w_k\), sample \(i_k\) uniformly and set \(v_k=
abla f_{i_k}(x_k)-
abla f_{i_k}(w_k)+
abla F(w_k)\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta v_k\). Independently set \(w_{k+1}=x_k\) with probability \(p\), recomputing \(
abla F(w_{k+1})\), and otherwise set \(w_{k+1}=w_k\). For \(\eta=\Theta(L^{-1})\), a standard Lyapunov function \(\Phi_k\) obeys \(\mathbb E\Phi_k\leq (1-c\min\{\mu/L,p\})^k\Phi_0\) for a universal \(c>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Loopless snapshot variance reduction contracts geometrically; its iteration rate is governed by the slower of conditioning and probabilistic reference refresh.
assumptions_latex: Component sampling and Bernoulli refresh decisions are independent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the leaf, but the Lyapunov function is not defined and no source certifies the stated update convention or contraction rate with universal constants.

children.title: Recursion-to-Refresh Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Complexity and stability tradeoffs between estimator recursion and explicit renewal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal Refresh Probability under the Stated Cost Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimization of the conditional refresh-cost model used by this comparison leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\kappa\geq1\), \(c>0\), and \(p\in(0,1]\). If \(G(p)=(c+np)\max\{\kappa,p^{-1}\}\), then \(G\) is strictly decreasing on \((0,\kappa^{-1}]\), strictly increasing on \([\kappa^{-1},1]\), and is uniquely minimized at \(p=\kappa^{-1}\), with \(G(\kappa^{-1})=n+c\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stipulated contraction and cost model, balancing refresh frequency with conditioning gives refresh probability 1/κ and work n+cκ before the logarithmic accuracy factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Refresh Probability under the Stated Cost Model

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Refresh-Cost Minimization Is Invalid without a Rate Law
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that cost alone cannot determine refresh frequency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the expected iteration cost be c+np for p\in(0,1]. If the contraction factor is independent of p, total certified work is strictly increasing in p and has no minimizer in (0,1]. Under the distinct conditional model (c+np)\max\{\kappa,p^{-1}\}, the accepted optimizer is p=\kappa^{-1}. Thus refresh cost alone does not identify an optimal p.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rule p=1/κ is model-dependent; without a refresh-dependent rate, the same cost accounting favors arbitrarily rare refreshes.
assumptions_latex: The target relative error is fixed.
In the first model, the iteration count is independent of p.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{0<p\le1}(c+np)=c\text{ is approached as }p\downarrow0\text{ and is not attained.}
knowledge_statements.title: Refresh-Cost Minimization Is Invalid without a Rate Law

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison after both methods supply certified contraction and cost pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a\in\{r,f\} satisfies \mathbb E[\Phi_k^{(a)}]\le\rho_a^k\Phi_0^{(a)} with 0<\rho_a<1 and has expected per-iteration component cost c_a>0. Excluding separately declared initialization costs, a sufficient work bound for relative reduction \varepsilon\in(0,1) is W_a(\varepsilon)=c_a\left\lceil\log(1/\varepsilon)/(-\log\rho_a)\right\rceil. The recursive bound is smaller exactly when W_r(\varepsilon)<W_f(\varepsilon).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recursion-versus-refresh comparison combines each method's certified contraction with its component cost.
assumptions_latex: Both contractions use the same relative-error convention.
c_r,c_f>0 are expected costs under declared accounting.
Initialization costs are excluded and must be added separately when nonzero.
knowledge_statements.title: Certified-Pair Work Crossover
Recursion-to-Refresh Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-cost tradeoff between recursive propagation and probabilistic exact-reference refresh.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a dynamic-reference variance-reduction method refreshes an exact finite-sum gradient with probability \(p\) per iteration and otherwise performs a constant number of component-gradient evaluations. If its Lyapunov contraction factor is \(1-\Theta(\min\{\kappa^{-1},p\})\), then reaching relative error \(\varepsilon\) requires \(O(\max\{\kappa,p^{-1}\}\log(1/\varepsilon))\) iterations and expected component-gradient cost \(O((1+np)\max\{\kappa,p^{-1}\}\log(1/\varepsilon))\). Recursive estimators remove the \(np\) refresh charge between restarts, but propagate estimator error and generally require a recursion-length or restart control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Frequent refresh improves estimator fidelity but costs full gradients; infrequent refresh slows contraction. Recursive updates avoid frequent full gradients but accumulate estimator error.
assumptions_latex: Nonrefresh iterations have constant component-gradient cost.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the tradeoff leaf. The refresh-cost calculation follows conditionally from the assumed contraction and cost model, but those premises and the broad claim about recursive-estimator error propagation lack authoritative support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-Deficient Least Squares Is PL without Strong Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum example separating the PL error-bound regime from strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\frac1{2n}\|Ax-b\|^2\) attain its minimum and let \(\lambda_{\min}^+(A^\top A)>0\) be the smallest positive eigenvalue of \(A^\top A\). Then \(\|\nabla F(x)\|^2\ge 2\mu(F(x)-F^*)\) for every \(x\), where \(\mu=\lambda_{\min}^+(A^\top A)/n\). If \(A\) is not of full column rank, \(F\) is not strongly convex on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-sum least squares with a column-rank-deficient design satisfies a global PL inequality while failing to be strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla F(x)\|^2\ge2[\lambda_{\min}^+(A^\top A)/n](F(x)-F^*)\); lack of full column rank precludes strong convexity.

notation.meaning: smallest positive eigenvalue of the Gram matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Least Squares Is PL without Strong Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective error bound defining the principal non-strongly-convex linear regime of this leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A differentiable function \(F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) with attained minimum value \(F^*\) satisfies the Polyak--Łojasiewicz inequality with constant \(\mu>0\) on a set \(\mathcal X\) if \(\frac12\|\nabla F(x)\|^2\ge \mu(F(x)-F^*)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\). The condition implies that every stationary point in \(\mathcal X\) is globally minimizing, but does not imply convexity or uniqueness of minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PL inequality controls objective error by squared gradient norm and makes stationary points globally optimal without requiring strong convexity or unique minimizers.

notation.meaning: region on which the PL bound is asserted

knowledge_statements.title: Polyak–Łojasiewicz Error-Bound Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: PL Objective-Gap Certificate from an Inexact Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori objective-gap certificate combining a PL bound with a certified gradient-estimation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(F\) satisfies \( rac12\|
abla F(x)\|^2\ge\mu(F(x)-F^*)\) at \(x\), with \(\mu>0\). If a computable vector \(v\) has a certified error bound \(\|v-
abla F(x)\|\le\delta\), then \[F(x)-F^*\le rac{\|
abla F(x)\|^2}{2\mu}\le rac{(\|v\|+\delta)^2}{2\mu}.\] Consequently, \(\|v\|+\delta\le\sqrt{2\mu\varepsilon}\) certifies \(F(x)-F^*\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a PL inequality, an estimator norm plus a certified estimator-error radius bounds objective suboptimality.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) satisfies the PL inequality with constant \(\mu>0\) at the tested point.
knowledge_statements.title: PL Objective-Gap Certificate from an Inexact Gradient

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-growth condition distinct from PL without additional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}F
e\varnothing\). The function \(F\) has quadratic growth with constant \(\alpha>0\) on \(\mathcal X\) if \[F(x)-F^*\ge rac\alpha2\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^2\qquad(x\in\mathcal X).\] If \(F\) is differentiable and convex on a convex region containing \(x\) and a nearest minimizer, then \[\|
abla F(x)\|^2\ge rac\alpha2[F(x)-F^*],\] hence \( rac12\|
abla F(x)\|^2\ge rac\alpha4[F(x)-F^*]\). Without the stated regularity, quadratic growth and PL are not asserted to be equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth controls distance to the solution set; under convex differentiability it implies a conservative PL bound, but not unconditionally.
assumptions_latex: Convexity and differentiability are required for the displayed PL implication.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Growth Error-Bound Regime
Error-Bound Linear-Convergence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic linear convergence induced by a gradient-dominance error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with finite minimum \(F^*\), and suppose the Polyak--Łojasiewicz error bound \(\|\nabla F(x)\|^2\geq2\mu(F(x)-F^*)\) holds for all iterates. If a variance-reduced method satisfies the conditional descent relation \(\mathbb E[F(x_{k+1})-F^*\mid x_k]\leq F(x_k)-F^*-a\|\nabla F(x_k)\|^2\) for some \(a>0\) with \(2a\mu<1\), then \(\mathbb E[F(x_k)-F^*]\leq(1-2a\mu)^k(F(x_0)-F^*)\). Strong convexity is sufficient but not necessary for this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variance-reduced method with expected gradient-based descent converges linearly whenever the objective satisfies a Polyak–Łojasiewicz error bound, even without strong convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) satisfies the Polyak--Łojasiewicz inequality with constant \(\mu>0\).
The stated conditional descent inequality holds with \(0<2a\mu<1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role is appropriate, and the contraction follows directly from the two displayed assumptions. Nevertheless, the record has no citation for the PL regime or for a variance-reduced method satisfying the stipulated conditional descent relation, so its placement as finite-sum variance-reduction knowledge remains unsupported.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Uniform Linear Convergence without a PL Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed deterministic gradient-descent example rather than a finite-sum variance-reduction result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=x^4\), \(x_0\in(0,1]\), and \(x_{k+1}=x_k-4\eta x_k^3\) with \(0<\eta\leq1/4\). Then \(F(x_{k+1})/F(x_k)=(1-4\eta x_k^2)^4\to1\), while no positive PL constant holds near zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient descent on x⁴ lacks a uniform geometric objective contraction because the PL ratio degenerates near the minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no \(q<1\) such that \(F(x_{k+1})\leq qF(x_k)\) for all \(k\).
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Uniform Linear Convergence without a PL Error Bound

abla F(x_k)\), and \(\mathbb E[\|v_k\|^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le C\|

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-specific nonaccelerated finite-sum upper complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth and \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, with \(\kappa=L/\mu\). Standard SAGA, with a valid fixed stepsize and its gradient table initialized at \(x_0\), has a geometric Lyapunov contraction. Consequently, \[N_{\mathrm{IFO}}=O\!\left((n+\kappa)\log\frac{C_0}{\varepsilon}\right)\] component-gradient evaluations suffice for an output \(x_k\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[F(x_k)-F^*]\le\varepsilon\), where \(C_0>0\) is determined by the initialized iterate-and-table Lyapunov value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard SAGA attains the nonaccelerated sample-plus-condition complexity with logarithmic accuracy dependence in the smooth strongly convex finite-sum regime.
assumptions_latex: SAGA uses uniform component sampling, a theorem-admissible fixed stepsize, and a gradient table initialized at \(x_0\).

Nonaccelerated Condition-Dependent Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental-oracle complexity for nonaccelerated strongly convex variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth and \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex. Standard nonaccelerated variance-reduced methods admit an incremental first-order oracle bound \(N_{\mathrm{IFO}}=O((n+\kappa)\log((F(x_0)-F^*)/\varepsilon))\), where \(\kappa=L/\mu\), to produce an output \(\widehat x\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[F(\widehat x)-F^*]\leq\varepsilon\). One oracle call returns \((f_i(x),\nabla f_i(x))\) for a chosen component index and point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonaccelerated variance reduction reaches expected objective error epsilon using order sample-size plus condition-number oracle calls, multiplied by a logarithmic accuracy factor.
assumptions_latex: Complexity counts component incremental first-order oracle calls.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf, but no cited theorem identifies which nonaccelerated method attains the stated IFO complexity under exactly these assumptions and oracle conventions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-specific accelerated upper scale for convex-component, strongly convex finite sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth and \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, with \(\kappa=L/\mu\). A standard strongly convex Katyusha-type accelerated variance-reduced method admits a parameterization and output rule for which \[N_{\mathrm{IFO}}=O\!\left((n+\sqrt{n\kappa})\log\frac{C_0}{\varepsilon}\right)\] component-gradient evaluations suffice to obtain an output \(\widehat x\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[F(\widehat x)-F^*]\le\varepsilon\), where \(C_0>0\) is the method's initialized Lyapunov scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Katyusha-type accelerated variance-reduced method reaches expected objective error epsilon with the sample-plus-square-root-condition finite-sum scale, times a logarithmic accuracy factor.
assumptions_latex: Work is counted in component-gradient evaluations under the method's standard initialization and randomized output convention.

children.title: Sample-Size-Dominated Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity regions primarily controlled by the number of finite-sum components.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Size-Dominated Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase where the mandatory finite-sum pass dominates condition dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the nonaccelerated complexity scale \(C_{\mathrm{na}}=n+\kappa\) and accelerated scale \(C_{\mathrm{acc}}=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\), the regime \(n\geq\kappa\) is sample-size dominated. Indeed, \(n\leq C_{\mathrm{na}}\leq2n\) and \(n\leq C_{\mathrm{acc}}\leq2n\). Consequently, apart from the common logarithmic accuracy factor, both scales are \(\Theta(n)\), and acceleration cannot improve their leading order in this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the sample size is at least the condition number, both accelerated and nonaccelerated finite-sum bounds are order n, so the full-pass cost dominates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the phase-regime leaf, and the inequalities are algebraically correct given the two complexity scales. Those scales, however, are inherited from unsourced candidate bounds, so the optimization interpretation lacks evidence.

children.title: Condition-Dominated Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity regions primarily controlled by problem conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Condition-Dominated Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase where conditioning determines the excess over one full pass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C_{\mathrm{na}}=n+\kappa\) and \(C_{\mathrm{acc}}=n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\), assume \(\kappa\geq n\). Then \(\kappa\leq C_{\mathrm{na}}\leq2\kappa\), while \(\sqrt{n\kappa}\leq C_{\mathrm{acc}}\leq2\sqrt{n\kappa}\). Hence the nonaccelerated scale is \(\Theta(\kappa)\), the accelerated scale is \(\Theta(\sqrt{n\kappa})\), and their condition-dependent ratio is \(\Theta(\sqrt{\kappa/n})\), apart from the shared logarithmic accuracy factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the condition number exceeds the sample size, nonaccelerated cost scales as kappa while accelerated cost scales as the square root of n times kappa.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the phase-regime leaf, and the asymptotic comparisons are algebraically correct under kappa at least n. The underlying accelerated and nonaccelerated complexity scales remain unsupported by citations.

children.title: Crossover Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Threshold regions where sample-size dominance gives way to condition dominance.

knowledge_statements.title: Crossover Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic boundaries separating sample- and condition-dominated finite-sum complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the nonaccelerated scale \(n+\kappa\), equality of the sample and condition terms occurs when \(n=\kappa\). For the accelerated scale \(n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\), equality occurs when \(n=\sqrt{n\kappa}\), which for \(n>0\) is again equivalent to \(n=\kappa\). Thus the common crossover boundary is \(n=\kappa\); the half-plane \(n\geq\kappa\) is sample-size dominated, whereas \(\kappa\geq n\) is condition dominated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both accelerated and nonaccelerated finite-sum complexity formulas cross from sample domination to condition domination at sample size equal to condition number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n=\kappa\) is the crossover boundary for both scales.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role is appropriate and the common boundary n equals kappa is algebraically correct for the stated scales. Because both scales come from uncited complexity claims, the boundary cannot yet be accepted as sourced optimization knowledge.

knowledge_statements.title: Snapshot-Method Stationarity Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex SVRG-type snapshot complexity under average smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) be bounded below, with differentiable components satisfying average smoothness \(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\|
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(y)\|^2\leq L^2\|x-y\|^2\). A suitably tuned nonconvex snapshot variance-reduction method, using periodic full gradients and minibatched inner updates, returns a randomized iterate \(\widehat x\) with \(\mathbb E\|
abla F(\widehat x)\|^2\leq\varepsilon\) after \(N_{\mathrm{IFO}}=O(n+n^{2/3}L(F(x_0)-F_*)/\varepsilon)\) component-gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tuned nonconvex snapshot variance-reduction method reaches squared-gradient tolerance epsilon in order n plus n to the two-thirds divided by epsilon component gradients.
assumptions_latex: The components satisfy the displayed average-smoothness inequality.
The output iterate is sampled according to the method's prescribed randomized rule.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the stationarity leaf, but the exact snapshot algorithm, minibatch and epoch parameters, randomized-output rule, average-smoothness convention, and n-to-the-two-thirds bound require a specific theorem citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive-Estimator Stationarity Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum recursive-estimator complexity for expected first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) be bounded below and satisfy average smoothness \(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\|
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(y)\|^2\leq L^2\|x-y\|^2\). A suitably tuned recursive variance-reduced estimator with periodic exact-gradient initialization returns a randomized iterate \(\widehat x\) satisfying \(\mathbb E\|
abla F(\widehat x)\|^2\leq\varepsilon\) using \(N_{\mathrm{IFO}}=O(n+\sqrt n\,L(F(x_0)-F_*)/\varepsilon)\) component-gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive variance reduction improves nonconvex finite-sum stationarity complexity to order n plus square-root n divided by the squared-gradient tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The components satisfy the displayed average-smoothness inequality.
The recursive estimator is periodically initialized by an exact finite-sum gradient.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the stationarity leaf, but a method-specific source is required to certify the recursive estimator, initialization and restart schedule, output rule, average-smoothness assumptions, and square-root-n oracle bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic-Refresh Stationarity Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PAGE-type probabilistic full-refresh recursion for smooth nonconvex finite sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), where \(F\) is bounded below, \(F(x_0)-\inf F\leq \Delta\), and the component gradients satisfy average \(L\)-smoothness. A probabilistic-refresh estimator replaces itself by \(\nabla F(x_t)\) with a fixed refresh probability and otherwise uses a minibatch gradient-difference update. With refresh probability and minibatch size balanced at order \(n^{-1/2}\) and \(n^{1/2}\), respectively, a uniformly sampled iterate \(x_R\) can satisfy \(\mathbb E\|\nabla F(x_R)\|^2\leq \varepsilon^2\) using \[O\!\left(n+\frac{\sqrt n\,L\Delta}{\varepsilon^2}\right)\] component-gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced probabilistic-refresh variance-reduced method reaches expected first-order stationarity in order n plus square-root-n times LΔ divided by ε² component gradients.
assumptions_latex: The output is sampled according to the method's stationarity analysis.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf, but the PAGE-type refresh rule, average-smoothness hypothesis, parameter balancing, output sampling, and stated component-gradient bound require a specific theorem citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Nonconvex Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-gradient stationarity for a smooth nonconvex term plus a proper closed convex term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi(x)=F(x)+r(x)\) on \(\mathbb R^d\), where \(F\) is differentiable and possibly nonconvex, while \(r\) is proper, closed, and convex. For \(\eta>0\), define the proximal-gradient mapping by \[G_\eta(x)=\eta^{-1}\!\left(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\eta r}\bigl(x-\eta\nabla F(x)\bigr)\right).\] A point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}r\) is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary when \(\|G_\eta(x)\|\leq\varepsilon\). Moreover, \(G_\eta(x)=0\) holds exactly when \(0\in\nabla F(x)+\partial r(x)\), so the mapping extends gradient-norm stationarity to composite objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composite stationarity is measured by the proximal-gradient mapping; its zeros are exactly points satisfying the smooth-plus-subgradient first-order inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(r:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex

Finite-Sum Complexity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonconvex finite-sum regime with reusable component gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), assume \(F(x_0)-\inf F\leq\Delta\) and average \(L\)-smoothness of the component gradients. In the finite-sum regime, indices and previously computed reference information may be reused, and a recursive variance-reduced method can return \(x_R\) with \(\mathbb E\|\nabla F(x_R)\|^2\leq\varepsilon^2\). Its component-gradient complexity has the characteristic form \[O\!\left(n+\frac{\sqrt n\,L\Delta}{\varepsilon^2}\right),\] where the \(n\) term accounts for an exact-gradient refresh and the second term accounts for variance-reduced incremental updates.

children.title: Online Complexity Regime
children.top_down_role: Complexity behavior under streaming or effectively fresh stochastic observations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic information model without a persistent, exhaustible component collection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the online regime, \(F(x)=\mathbb E_\xi[f(x;\xi)]\) is accessed through fresh stochastic samples. A stochastic first-order call returns information such as \(g(x,\xi)=\nabla f(x;\xi)\), commonly satisfying \(\mathbb E[g(x,\xi)\mid x]=\nabla F(x)\). Every minibatch element counts as one sample, and no finite full-data pass generically reconstructs the exact population gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Online optimization uses fresh stochastic observations, charges every sampled gradient, and generally has no exact full-data refresh.
assumptions_latex: Samples follow the declared data-generating distribution
Each sampled gradient is charged separately
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{No finite full-data pass generically returns the exact population gradient.}
knowledge_statements.title: Fresh-Sample Online Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary preventing direct import of finite-sum exact-refresh rates into fresh-sample access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-sum bound containing an \(n\)-cost exact-gradient refresh cannot be transferred to the online model by treating a fresh minibatch as a persistent dataset. Conditional on the query point, a minibatch average may be an unbiased estimator of \(\nabla F(x)\), but its realized value is generally not the exact population gradient. Online guarantees must retain their dependence on noise, batch size, and success mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fresh minibatch can be unbiased without being exact, so finite-sum n-based refresh accounting does not transfer unchanged.
assumptions_latex: The population oracle is not a finitely exhaustible component collection
Refresh batches contain fresh random samples

Online Complexity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online stochastic nonconvex regime without persistent finite component reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\mathbb E_\xi[f(x;\xi)]\), with \(F(x_0)-\inf F\leq\Delta\), an unbiased stochastic-gradient oracle, bounded gradient variance, and mean-square \(L\)-smooth sample gradients. Recursive variance reduction with periodically refreshed minibatch estimates can produce \(x_R\) satisfying \(\mathbb E\|\nabla F(x_R)\|^2\leq\varepsilon^2\). For fixed problem constants, the stochastic-gradient complexity is \[O\!\left(\varepsilon^{-3}\right).\] Unlike the finite-sum regime, the refresh uses fresh samples rather than an exact pass over a persistent collection of \(n\) components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without reusable components, recursive stochastic variance reduction reaches expected ε-stationarity using order ε⁻³ stochastic-gradient samples for fixed problem constants.
assumptions_latex: Sample gradients satisfy a mean-square smoothness condition

notation.meaning: number of stochastic first-order oracle calls

children.title: Reuse-to-Streaming Transition
children.top_down_role: Boundaries where finite-data reuse ceases to provide the dominant complexity advantage.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which finite-sum and streaming complexity guarantees may be combined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C_{\mathrm{reuse}} and C_{\mathrm{stream}} be guarantees under reusable indexed-component and fresh-sample access, respectively. The bound C\leq\min\{C_{\mathrm{reuse}},C_{\mathrm{stream}}\} is operationally valid only when the same problem instance belongs to both theorem classes, the accuracy and unit-cost conventions agree, and the implementation may choose either oracle. If only one interface is available, only its guarantee is attainable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The better of reuse and streaming bounds is attainable only when both compatible oracle interfaces are available.
assumptions_latex: The problem instance satisfies both guarantee classes.
Accuracy criteria and oracle-cost units are compatible.
Either oracle interface may be selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\leq\min\{C_{\mathrm{reuse}},C_{\mathrm{stream}}\}\text{ only under joint oracle availability and compatible conventions.}

Reuse-to-Streaming Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossover between reusable finite-sum and fresh-sample stationarity costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose both indexed reuse and fresh independent sampling are available for a smooth nonconvex objective with fixed smoothness, gap, and variance constants. Comparing the finite-sum cost \(n+\sqrt n\,\varepsilon^{-2}\) with the online cost \(\varepsilon^{-3}\), the preferable oracle regime is described by \[N(\varepsilon,n)=O\!\left(\min\left\{n+\sqrt n\,\varepsilon^{-2},\;\varepsilon^{-3}\right\}\right).\] The two leading expressions balance at scale \(n\asymp\varepsilon^{-2}\): below this scale, component reuse is advantageous, while above it a fresh-sample implementation avoids paying for a full pass through all components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The crossover occurs near n equal to ε⁻²; below it finite-sum reuse wins, while above it streaming can avoid a full pass.
assumptions_latex: Both indexed component access and independent fresh sampling are admissible
Problem-dependent smoothness, gap, and variance factors are treated as constants

notation.meaning: best available oracle cost between the two regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If F\in C^2 near an unconstrained local minimizer x_\star, then 
abla F(x_\star)=0 and 
abla^2F(x_\star)\succeq0. Conversely, 
abla F(x_\star)=0 and 
abla^2F(x_\star)\succ0 imply that x_\star is a strict local minimizer. Positive semidefiniteness alone is not sufficient.

x_\star	ext{ local minimum}\Rightarrow

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation of the semidefinite-Hessian stationarity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For F(x)=x^3, F'(0)=F''(0)=0, yet every neighborhood of 0 contains x<0 with F(x)<F(0). Thus exact second-order stationarity under the nonnegative-Hessian criterion does not imply local minimality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F'(0)=F''(0)=0\quad\text{and}\quad 0\text{ is not a local minimizer}.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Incremental Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic indexed first-order oracle lower bound for smooth strongly convex finite sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(n\geq2\), smoothness \(L>0\), and strong-convexity parameter \(\mu>0\), with \(\kappa=L/\mu\). In the deterministic incremental first-order oracle model, there exist convex component functions \(f_i\) whose average \(F=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and smooth such that any deterministic method accessing one indexed component value and gradient per call requires \[\Omega\!\left(\left(n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\right)\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)\] oracle calls to guarantee \(F(x)-F^*\leq\varepsilon\bigl(F(x_0)-F^*\bigr)\), subject to the dimension and parameter range of the resisting instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Some smooth strongly convex finite sums force every deterministic incremental-gradient method to use order (n plus √nκ) log(1/ε) component calls.
assumptions_latex: Each oracle call reveals information from one chosen component
The dimension is sufficiently large for the lower-bound construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits, but the logarithmic factor, component smoothness, oracle information, parameter range, dimension requirement, and placement of the n term require an exact deterministic lower-bound theorem.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Incremental Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected indexed-oracle lower bound for randomized smooth strongly convex finite-sum optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(n\geq2\) and \(\kappa=L/\mu\). There exists a distribution over finite sums \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i\), with convex smooth components and a smooth \(\mu\)-strongly convex average, such that any randomized incremental first-order method using one indexed component oracle per call requires \[\Omega\!\left(\left(n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\right)\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)\] expected calls before producing \(x\) with \(\mathbb E[F(x)-F^*]\leq\varepsilon\bigl(F(x_0)-F^*\bigr)\). The expectation is jointly over the hard-instance distribution and the algorithm's internal randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomization does not remove the n plus √nκ logarithmic worst-case barrier for smooth strongly convex finite sums in the incremental oracle model.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm receives one indexed component value-gradient response per call
The hard-instance dimension and parameter range are sufficiently large

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-bound role fits, but the hard-instance distribution, expectation convention, oracle class, parameter range, and exact logarithmic formula require a primary theorem citation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A dimension-dependent lower bound for randomized incremental gradient methods on problem (5.1.79).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) be an optimal solution of problem \((5.1.79)\), and define \[q:=\frac{\sqrt{\mathrm Q}-1}{\sqrt{\mathrm Q}+1}.\] The iterates generated by any randomized incremental gradient method satisfy \[\frac{\mathbb E\!\left[\|x^k-x^*\|_2^2\right]}{\|x^0-x^*\|_2^2}\ge\frac12\exp\!\left(-\frac{4k\sqrt{\mathrm Q}}{m(\sqrt{\mathrm Q}+1)^2-4\sqrt{\mathrm Q}}\right)\] for every \[n\ge\underline n(m,k):=\frac{m\log\!\left(\left(1-\frac{1-q^2}{m}\right)^k/2\right)}{2\log q}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On problem (5.1.79), every randomized incremental gradient method has the displayed normalized expected squared-error lower bound whenever the dimension meets the stated threshold.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is an optimal solution of problem }(5.1.79)
\{x^k\}\text{ is generated by a randomized incremental gradient method}

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Incremental Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound for incremental proximal-oracle optimization of strongly convex composite finite sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\Phi(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)+r(x)\), where the smooth components are convex and the total objective is \(\mu\)-strongly convex. In an incremental proximal first-order model, one call may query one component value-gradient pair and apply the proximal map of \(r\). Because the admissible class contains the subclass \(r\equiv0\), there are instances for which any such method requires at least \[\Omega\!\left(\left(n+\sqrt{n\kappa}\right)\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)\] calls to attain relative expected objective error at most \(\varepsilon\), whenever the corresponding smooth incremental lower bound applies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing proximal steps cannot beat the smooth finite-sum lower bound, because the composite class includes instances with a zero regularizer.
assumptions_latex: One oracle call accesses at most one smooth component and one proximal evaluation
The smooth subclass has condition number \(\kappa=L/\mu\)

notation.meaning: incremental component and proximal oracle calls

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Restriction to r=0 is a plausible lower-bound transfer and the content kind fits, but the base smooth lower bound and the precise incremental-proximal oracle cost convention are unsourced.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Finite-Sum Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized first-order lower bound for smooth nonconvex finite-sum stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For suitable \(n\), dimension, and accuracy range, there exist differentiable components \(f_i\) such that \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i\) is bounded below, has initial gap at most \(\Delta\), and satisfies an average \(L\)-smoothness condition. Any randomized linear-span incremental first-order method must make \[\Omega\!\left(n+\frac{\sqrt n\,L\Delta}{\varepsilon^2}\right)\] component-gradient queries before it can guarantee an output \(x\) with \(\mathbb E\|\nabla F(x)\|\leq\varepsilon\). The bound is worst-case and depends on the precise oracle class, dimension, and relation among \(n\), \(L\Delta\), and \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hard smooth nonconvex finite sums require order n plus √n LΔ/ε² component gradients to find an expected ε-stationary point in the stated oracle class.
assumptions_latex: The method belongs to the randomized linear-span incremental oracle class

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-bound role fits, but the exact rate depends on the randomized linear-span model, dimension and accuracy ranges, average-smoothness definition, and whether stationarity uses E||∇F|| or E||∇F||²; a primary theorem is required.

children.title: Component-Gradient Complexity
children.top_down_role: Work accounting based on individual component-gradient evaluations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy-dependent worst-case cost under an explicit deterministic or probabilistic guarantee convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), one component-gradient query returns \(\nabla f_i(x)\) for a declared pair \((i,x)\). Fix a problem class \(\mathcal P\) and a deterministic, expected, or \((1-\delta)\)-probability accuracy requirement \(\mathsf G_\varepsilon\). The fixed-budget component-gradient complexity is \[N_{\rm grad}^{\mathsf G}(\varepsilon;\mathcal P):=\inf\{N\in\mathbb N_0:\exists A\ \forall P\in\mathcal P,\ A\text{ uses at most }N\text{ component-gradient queries and satisfies }\mathsf G_\varepsilon(P)\}.\] Batch members and repeated requests count with multiplicity; an assembled full gradient costs \(n\) queries unless a separate primitive is declared. Expected or tail bounds on a random stopping-time cost are different conventions and must be labeled separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component-gradient complexity is the least uniform query budget achieving a declared deterministic, expected, or high-probability accuracy guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The finite-sum problem class, accuracy criterion, and probability convention are fixed.
No separate unit-cost full-gradient primitive is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\rm grad}^{\mathsf G}\) is a worst-case fixed query budget; batches, repetitions, and assembled full gradients are charged by their component counts.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Budget Component-Gradient Complexity
Component-Gradient Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost measure for algorithms querying indexed gradients of a finite-sum objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), a component-gradient evaluation is one oracle request returning \(
abla f_i(x)\) for a specified pair \((i,x)\). The component-gradient complexity \(N_{\mathrm{grad}}(\varepsilon)\) is the worst-case number of such requests made before the algorithm outputs a point satisfying its declared \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy criterion. A full gradient \(
abla F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_i
abla f_i(x)\) costs \(n\) component-gradient evaluations unless the model explicitly supplies it as a separate primitive. Repeated queries and minibatch members are counted with multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component-gradient complexity counts every indexed gradient request; an explicitly assembled full gradient costs n such requests, and minibatch requests count individually.
assumptions_latex: The objective has an indexed finite-sum representation
No separate unit-cost full-gradient primitive is available
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{grad}}(\varepsilon)=\sum_t |B_t|\), and an exact assembled \(\nabla F(x)\) contributes \(n\) evaluations.

children.title: General Oracle Complexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic, Expected, and High-Probability Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-budget black-box query complexity with explicit randomized guarantee semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a problem class \(\mathcal P\), oracle \(\mathcal O\), nonnegative output error \(e_P(x)\), and algorithms accessing \(P\) only through \(\mathcal O\). Define \[N_{\mathcal O}^{\rm det}(\varepsilon):=\inf\{N:\exists A\ \forall P,\ A\text{ uses at most }N\text{ calls and }e_P(X_A)\le\varepsilon\},\] \[N_{\mathcal O}^{\rm exp}(\varepsilon):=\inf\{N:\exists A\ \sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E[e_P(X_A)]\le\varepsilon,\ A\text{ uses at most }N\text{ calls}\},\] and \[N_{\mathcal O}^{\rm hp}(\varepsilon,\delta):=\inf\{N:\exists A\ \sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb P(e_P(X_A)>\varepsilon)\le\delta,\ A\text{ uses at most }N\text{ calls}\}.\] The oracle response and all separately charged primitives must be declared. Expected-cost or tail-cost stopping-time complexity is a distinct convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General oracle complexity has separate deterministic, expected-error, and high-probability fixed-budget definitions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\), \(\mathcal O\), the admissible algorithm class, and \(e_P\) are fixed.
Algorithms receive instance information only through the declared oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deterministic, expected, and high-probability oracle complexities are distinct fixed-budget minimax quantities.

notation.symbol_latex: \(N_{\mathcal O}^{\rm det},N_{\mathcal O}^{\rm exp},N_{\mathcal O}^{\rm hp}\)

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic, Expected, and High-Probability Oracle Complexity
General Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case query count relative to an explicitly specified optimization oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an oracle \(\mathcal O\) map each admissible query \(q\) to a response \(\mathcal O(q)\), which may contain values, gradients, proximal points, Hessian-vector products, or stochastic samples according to the model. For a problem class \(\mathcal P\) and accuracy predicate \(C_\varepsilon(P,x)\), the oracle complexity is \[N_{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon;\mathcal P)=\inf_A\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\inf\{T:\ C_\varepsilon(P,x_T^A)\text{ holds}\}.\] For randomized algorithms, the predicate or stopping requirement must state whether accuracy and cost are in expectation, with high probability, or almost surely; incomparable oracle responses must not be treated as equal-cost units without an explicit reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General oracle complexity is the best algorithm's worst-case number of specified oracle calls needed to meet an explicit accuracy criterion under a declared probability convention.
assumptions_latex: The problem class \(\mathcal P\), oracle \(\mathcal O\), and accuracy predicate are fixed
Every admissible algorithm accesses the instance only through the declared oracle

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Unit Comparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for comparing finite-sum complexity claims expressed in different oracle units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\). Two complexity bounds are oracle-unit comparable only after assigning each reported operation a common cost: one component-gradient evaluation has cost \(1\), a batch evaluation on \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) has cost \(|B|\), and a full-gradient evaluation has cost \(n\). If an execution uses batches \(B_1,\ldots,B_T\) and \(q\) additional full gradients, its normalized component-oracle cost is \(N_{\mathrm{IFO}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}|B_t|+qn\). Bounds may be compared directly only when they use the same accuracy criterion, count reused or jointly returned quantities consistently, and include the same initialization and refresh costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complexity claims are comparable only after all batch and full-gradient work is converted to component-gradient units under matching accuracy and accounting conventions.
assumptions_latex: Each requested \(\nabla f_i(x)\) has unit cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Pass Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization of component accesses by the finite-sum size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-sum problem with \(n\) components, suppose an execution accesses component indices with total multiplicity \(N_{\mathrm{data}}\), counting repeated indices repeatedly and counting a batch \(B_t\) by \(|B_t|\). Its data-pass complexity is \[P_{\mathrm{data}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{data}}}{n}.\] Thus one complete traversal of all \(n\) components costs one pass, while a partial or randomized traversal may contribute a fractional pass. This quantity measures component-data accesses, not necessarily gradient evaluations: the two coincide only when every counted access computes exactly one component gradient and no additional component-level work is omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Data-pass complexity is total component-data accesses divided by dataset size; it equals gradient-equivalent passes only under matching access and computation conventions.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) is the number of finite-sum components.

children.title: Normalization Mismatches
children.top_down_role: Cases where pass counts and full-gradient equivalents yield materially different comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Mismatches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of direct comparisons when pass and oracle normalizations differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\) be the number of components. If one report gives component-gradient complexity \(N_{\nabla}\) and another gives full-gradient-equivalent passes \(P=N_{\nabla}/n\), comparing their displayed numerical values without conversion introduces a factor \(n\). Moreover, data passes \(N_{\mathrm{data}}/n\) need not equal gradient-equivalent passes when an access computes multiple derivatives, reuses cached gradients, or performs no gradient evaluation. Hence direct comparison fails unless the numerator, batch multiplicities, full-gradient charges, preprocessing, refreshes, and terminal certificate costs are normalized identically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unconverted component counts and pass counts differ by a factor of dataset size, and data passes may differ from gradient-equivalent passes.
assumptions_latex: The compared reports use at least two distinct cost normalizations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Direct numerical comparison is invalid until all reported costs are converted to a common numerator and unit.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar communication-time model derived from critical-path rounds and payload.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an execution has \(R\) critical-path communication rounds and transmits \(W\) scalar words. Under a homogeneous, nonoverlapped model charging latency \(\alpha\ge0\) once per critical-path round and bandwidth price \(\beta\ge0\) per transmitted word, \[T_{\rm comm}=\alpha R+\beta W.\] Hence executions with crossed pairs \((R_1,W_1)\) and \((R_2,W_2)\) cannot be ranked without the platform prices.

children.title: Cross-Resource Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Regimes where one resource cost dominates gains measured using another resource.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Resource Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued resource accounting and bottleneck identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm's resource vector at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) be \(\mathcal{C}(\varepsilon)=(N_{\nabla},N_{\mathrm{prox}},M,R,W)\), representing component gradients, proximal calls, peak memory, communication rounds, and transmitted words. For platform budgets \(B=(B_{\nabla},B_{\mathrm{prox}},B_M,B_R,B_W)\), feasibility requires every coordinate inequality \(\mathcal{C}_j(\varepsilon)\leq B_j\). The normalized bottleneck factor is \[\beta(\varepsilon)=\max_j\frac{\mathcal{C}_j(\varepsilon)}{B_j}.\] Thus reducing one coordinate cannot establish feasibility or dominance when another coordinate attains the maximum; scalar complexity comparisons require an explicitly chosen cost aggregation or platform model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resource feasibility is coordinatewise; the largest cost-to-budget ratio is the bottleneck, so improving gradients alone may not improve overall feasibility.
assumptions_latex: All compared costs use the same execution and accuracy convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The execution is budget-feasible exactly when \(\beta(\varepsilon)\leq 1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Crossed Resource Vectors Have No Platform-Free Ranking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of scalar method ranking when different methods favor different resource coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c,d\in\mathbb R_+^m\). If \(c_i<d_i\) for some \(i\) and \(c_j>d_j\) for some \(j\), then neither vector Pareto-dominates the other. Moreover, there exist \(p,q\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\) such that \(p^\top c<p^\top d\) and \(q^\top c>q^\top d\). Thus crossed resource vectors admit no platform-independent scalar ranking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive platform prices can reverse the ordering of two methods that trade off different resources.
assumptions_latex: At least one coordinate strictly favors each vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vectors are Pareto-incomparable, and strictly positive price vectors can reverse their weighted-cost order.

children.title: Objective-Gap Measures
children.top_down_role: Performance criteria based on objective-value suboptimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Gap Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-value certificate for finite-sum minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be an objective on \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\), assume the solution set \(X^*=\arg\min_{x\in X}F(x)\) is nonempty, and write \(F^*=\min_{x\in X}F(x)\). The objective-gap measure is \[G(x)=F(x)-F^*,\qquad x\in\operatorname{dom}F\cap X.\] It satisfies \(G(x)\geq0\), and \(G(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\in X^*\). For a random output \(\widehat{x}\), an expected-gap certificate is \(\mathbb{E}[G(\widehat{x})]\leq\varepsilon\); a high-probability certificate must additionally state its confidence level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective gap is current objective value minus the attained optimum; it vanishes exactly at minimizers and supports deterministic or stochastic certificates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probabilistic consequence and reverse-conversion limitation for objective-gap certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(\widehat x)=F(\widehat x)-F^*\ge0\). If \(\mathbb E[G(\widehat x)]\le\varepsilon\), then for every \(\delta\in(0,1)\), \[\mathbb P\!\left(G(\widehat x)>\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right)\le\delta.\] Conversely, a single high-probability bound on \(G(\widehat x)\) need not control its expectation without integrability or tail control on the failure event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expected objective-gap bound gives a confidence-qualified gap through Markov's inequality; the reverse implication needs tail control.
knowledge_statements.title: Expectation-to-Probability Objective-Gap Conversion

children.title: Solution-Distance Measures
children.top_down_role: Performance criteria based on distance to a solution or solution set.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Distance Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-to-solution-set certificate in Euclidean geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X^*\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\) be a nonempty solution set. The solution-distance measure is \[D(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)=\inf_{x^*\in X^*}\|x-x^*\|.\] Its squared variant is \(D^2(x)\). If \(X^*\) is closed, then \(D(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\in X^*\); if the infimum is attained, \(D(x)=\|x-\Pi_{X^*}(x)\|\) for any Euclidean projection \(\Pi_{X^*}(x)\). A stochastic certificate may use \(\mathbb{E}[D^2(\widehat{x})]\leq\varepsilon\), which is distinct from a bound on \(\mathbb{E}[D(\widehat{x})]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solution distance is Euclidean distance to the nonempty minimizer set; its squared and unsquared stochastic certificates must not be conflated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(x)=\inf_{x^*\in X^*}\|x-x^*\|\), and closedness gives \(D(x)=0\iff x\in X^*\).

children.title: Gap-to-Distance Comparability
children.top_down_role: Geometric regimes supporting comparison between value error and solution-space error.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap-to-Distance Comparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided comparison under strong convexity and smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, \(\mu\)-strongly convex, and have \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, with \(0<\mu\leq L\). Then \(F\) has a unique minimizer \(x^*\), and for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\), \[\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-x^*\|^2\leq F(x)-F(x^*)\leq\frac{L}{2}\|x-x^*\|^2.\] Consequently, an objective-gap certificate \(F(x)-F(x^*)\leq\varepsilon\) implies \(\|x-x^*\|^2\leq2\varepsilon/\mu\), while a squared-distance certificate \(\|x-x^*\|^2\leq\delta\) implies objective gap at most \(L\delta/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth strongly convex objectives, objective gap and squared distance to the unique minimizer bound each other with constants μ/2 and L/2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Quadratic Comparability Without the Corresponding Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate failures of the lower and upper quadratic comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F_1(x)=x^4\), no \(c>0\) satisfies \(F_1(x)-F_1(0)\ge c|x|^2\) near zero. For the differentiable convex function \(F_2(x)=|x|^{3/2}\), no \(C<\infty\) satisfies \(F_2(x)-F_2(0)\le C|x|^2\) near zero. Hence convexity alone supplies neither side of a uniform quadratic comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without quadratic growth the lower comparison can fail, and without gradient Lipschitzness the upper comparison can fail.
assumptions_latex: The examples are defined on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Quadratic Comparability Without the Corresponding Regularity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal regularity mechanisms for the two directions of quadratic comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) minimize a differentiable objective \(F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\). If \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, then \[F(x)-F(x^*)\ge \frac\mu2\|x-x^*\|^2.\] Independently, if \(\nabla F\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \(\nabla F(x^*)=0\) and \[F(x)-F(x^*)\le \frac L2\|x-x^*\|^2.\] Thus the lower and upper certificate conversions do not require the other side's curvature assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity supplies the lower quadratic bound, while smoothness at an unconstrained minimizer independently supplies the upper quadratic bound.
assumptions_latex: For the lower bound, \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
For the upper bound, \(F\) is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)-F(x^*)\ge(\mu/2)\|x-x^*\|^2\) under strong convexity and \(F(x)-F(x^*)\le(L/2)\|x-x^*\|^2\) under smoothness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient Stationarity Does Not Imply Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for interpreting a smooth gradient-norm certificate in nonconvex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=(x^2-1)^2\), one has \(\nabla F(0)=0\), but \(F(0)=1\) while \(F(\pm1)=0\). Hence a zero gradient norm certifies first-order stationarity but not local or global minimality for a general differentiable nonconvex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vanishing gradient can occur at a nonoptimal stationary point, so gradient norm alone is not an optimality certificate in nonconvex problems.
