No SARAH-type recursive-estimator source is cited, and the source should resolve whether the failure-boundary leaf should be classified as a property or failure boundary.

children.title: Refresh-Cost Dominance
children.top_down_role: Regimes where reference renewal consumes the dominant computational work.

knowledge_statements.title: Refresh-Cost Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amortized oracle-cost boundary for periodically refreshed reference estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a finite sum \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\). Suppose one reference refresh evaluates all \(n\) component gradients, while each of the \(m\) intervening inner iterations uses \(q\) component-gradient evaluations. The amortized oracle cost per inner iteration is \(q+n/m\). Refresh cost dominates inner-update cost exactly when \(n/m\ge q\), equivalently \(m\le n/q\). In this regime, any advantage measured only by the number of inner iterations is insufficient to establish an oracle-complexity advantage over a method costing \(q\) component gradients per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-gradient refresh dominates cost when epochs contain at most n/q inner steps; iteration savings alone then do not imply oracle savings.
assumptions_latex: A refresh costs exactly \(n\) component-gradient evaluations and each inner iteration costs \(q\).

notation.meaning: component-gradient cost of one inner update

review_flags: exact amortized-cost formulation needs a directly supporting finite-sum variance-reduction source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The amortized-cost calculation is internally consistent and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but the record cites no source. A finite-sum variance-reduction source must support the full-refresh and inner-update cost model at a specific locator.

children.title: Memory-Cost Dominance
children.top_down_role: Regimes where stored estimator state dominates available resources.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the representation and parameter conditions under which the dense-table storage ratio is valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a table implementation stores \(n\) dense vectors in \(\mathbb R^d\), its table alone occupies \(nd\) scalar words. Relative to an alternative whose corresponding persistent state occupies \(cd\) words with \(c>0\), the table-only storage ratio is exactly \(n/c\). This comparison does not apply unchanged to compressed, sparse, scalar-entry, or implicitly represented tables, whose encoded storage must be counted directly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The n-over-c storage ratio requires positive c and dense vector entries; compressed or scalar tables need their own storage count.
assumptions_latex: Each table entry is represented as a dense \(d\)-vector in scalar-word storage.

notation.meaning: Positive number of dense-vector equivalents used by the comparison method
Scalar-word storage of the dense component table

review_flags: Supplies the parameter domain omitted from the deferred seed and limits the conclusion to the stated dense representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Table Comparison Domain
Memory-Cost Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage boundary for gradient-table variance-reduction methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), a method storing one dense component-gradient vector per index requires \(nd\) scalar words, in addition to lower-order state. Let \(M\) be the available scalar-word budget. If \(nd>M\), the gradient table is infeasible. More generally, relative to a memory-light method using \(cd\) words, table storage dominates by a factor at least \(n/c\). Thus table-based variance reduction ceases to be resource-suitable when its stored reference information exceeds the memory budget, regardless of its component-oracle convergence rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense gradient table is infeasible when nd exceeds the memory budget and can dominate the storage of memory-light alternatives.
assumptions_latex: Each of the \(n\) stored component gradients is represented by a dense vector in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
The memory budget \(M\) is measured in scalar words.
review_flags: storage boundary needs a source explicitly treating gradient-table variance-reduction methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dense-table storage boundary is plausible and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but no source is cited. A source must document gradient-table storage, and the comparison parameter c must be assigned a domain before promotion.

children.title: Resource-Balancing Boundary
children.top_down_role: Transitions where reducing refresh work transfers the dominant burden to storage or vice versa.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completes the work-budget cases omitted by the epoch-length rearrangement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(R>0\), \(q>0\), and finite \(m>0\). Since \(q+R/m>q\), no finite epoch length satisfies \(q+R/m\le B\) when \(B\le q\). Thus \(B>q\) is necessary for work feasibility; when \(B>q\), work feasibility is equivalent to \(m\ge R/(B-q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the work budget is no larger than the irreducible inner-update cost, changing the refresh interval cannot make the method feasible.
assumptions_latex: One refresh of cost \(R\) occurs every \(m\) inner updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\le q\Longrightarrow q+\frac Rm>B;\qquad B>q\Longrightarrow\left(q+\frac Rm\le B\iff m\ge\frac{R}{B-q}\right).
knowledge_statements.title: Irreducible Inner-Work Boundary
Resource-Balancing Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint feasibility condition for refresh work and reference-state storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a variance-reduced implementation with refresh cost \(R\), inner-update cost \(q\), epoch length \(m\), and persistent reference storage \(S\). Given an amortized work allowance \(B\) per inner iteration and memory budget \(M\), the implementation is resource-feasible precisely when \(q+R/m\le B\) and \(S\le M\). When \(B>q\), the work constraint is equivalent to \(m\ge R/(B-q)\). Consequently, no epoch length can restore feasibility if \(S>M\), while refresh feasibility requires sufficiently long epochs. The resource-balancing boundary is attained when either constraint holds with equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reference method is feasible only if both amortized refresh work and stored reference state fit their respective budgets.
assumptions_latex: Refreshes occur once every \(m\) inner iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[q+\frac{R}{m}\le B\ \text{ and }\ S\le M;\qquad B>q\Longrightarrow m\ge\frac{R}{B-q}.\]

notation.meaning: amortized refresh work per inner iteration

review_flags: resource model is mathematically explicit but needs finite-sum method-specific sourcing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The budget inequalities follow from the stated cost model, and condition is appropriate for this balancing leaf. The model itself has no cited finite-sum method source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Importance-Model Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Sampling inefficiency caused by inaccurate component-importance estimates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of unbiased recoverability when the implemented distribution omits components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{i:p_i>0\}\), sample \(I\) on \(S\), and set \(Z=g_I/(np_I)\). Then \(\mathbb E Z=n^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}g_i\). Consequently, \(Z\) is unbiased for \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i\) if and only if \(\sum_{i\notin S}g_i=0\). Inverse-probability weighting cannot recover a nonzero uncancelled contribution outside the sampling support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Omitted components preserve unbiasedness only when their total contribution is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(p_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i p_i=1\), and sampling is restricted to \(S=\{i:p_i>0\}\).

notation.meaning: Support of the implemented sampling distribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Misspecification Bias Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Vector Boundary for Optimal Importance Probabilities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment boundary for second-moment-minimizing probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write \(a_i=\lVert g_i\rVert\) and assume \(\sum_i a_i>0\). Over probabilities satisfying \(p_i>0\), the infimum of \(\sum_i a_i^2/p_i\) is \((\sum_i a_i)^2\). It is attained by \(p_i=a_i/\sum_j a_j\) exactly when every \(a_i>0\). If some \(a_i=0\), the infimum is not attained under strict positivity; it is attained on the closed simplex by assigning zero probability only to zero vectors and probabilities proportional to \(a_i\) on the nonzero vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Probabilities proportional to vector norms are an attained strictly positive optimum only when every vector is nonzero; zero vectors create a boundary optimum.
review_flags: corrects the deferred seed's zero-vector optimum ambiguity
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Vector Boundary for Optimal Importance Probabilities
Importance-Model Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance inflation caused by inaccurate importance-sampling probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and sample \(I\) with positive probabilities \(p_i\). The estimator \(Z=g_I/(np_I)\) is unbiased for \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_i g_i\), with second moment \(n^{-2}\sum_i\lVert g_i\rVert^2/p_i\). Its minimum over positive probability vectors is attained at \(p_i^*=\lVert g_i\rVert/\sum_j\lVert g_j\rVert\) for nonzero \(g_i\). If a misspecified model assigns probability \(p_k\) arbitrarily close to zero while \(g_k\ne0\), the second moment and variance become arbitrarily large; unbiased reweighting therefore does not protect against importance-model misspecification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incorrect importance probabilities preserve unbiasedness under exact reweighting but can make estimator variance arbitrarily large by undersampling a nonzero component.

notation.meaning: implemented sampling probability for component i

review_flags: importance-sampling variance identity needs an explicit authoritative locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unbiasedness and second-moment formulas are standard, and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but no source is cited. The optimal-probability claim also needs clarification: with strictly positive probabilities, the displayed minimizer is attained only when every component vector is nonzero; zero vectors generally yield an infimum at zero probability.

children.title: Batch-Size Saturation
children.top_down_role: Regimes where larger batches cease to provide commensurate computational benefit.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary case excluded by the usual finite-population correction formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(n=1\), the only admissible nonempty without-replacement batch has \(b=1\), and \(\widehat g_B=\bar g=g_1\) deterministically. Its variance is zero, but the expression \((n-b)/[b(n-1)]\) is undefined. Thus the displayed finite-population formula requires \(n\ge2\), with \(n=1\) handled separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a one-component finite sum, full batching is deterministic and the standard finite-population correction formula must be replaced by the zero-variance boundary case.
assumptions_latex: The batch is nonempty and sampled without replacement.
review_flags: corrects the deferred seed's missing n>=2 qualification
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Component Degeneracy
Batch-Size Saturation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-population variance boundary for uniform mini-batching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and let \(B\) be a uniformly sampled subset of size \(b\) without replacement. For \(\widehat g_B=b^{-1}\sum_{i\in B}g_i\) and \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_i g_i\), the mini-batch estimator is unbiased and satisfies \(\mathbb{E}\lVert\widehat g_B-\bar g\rVert^2=(n-b)[b(n-1)]^{-1}V\), where \(V=n^{-1}\sum_i\lVert g_i-\bar g\rVert^2\). The sampling variance reaches zero at \(b=n\); increasing the batch beyond \(n\) is impossible, so variance reduction through batch enlargement saturates at the full finite sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without-replacement mini-batch variance decreases by the finite-population factor and vanishes at the full batch, where batch enlargement necessarily saturates.
assumptions_latex: The batch is sampled uniformly without replacement.
review_flags: finite-population variance formula needs a directly supporting source locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-population variance formula is internally correct under uniform sampling without replacement, and property is an acceptable role for the saturation phenomenon. No authoritative source and specific locator are supplied.

children.title: Misspecification-Driven Saturation
children.top_down_role: Batch-scaling limits specifically induced or intensified by poor importance models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Target-Accuracy Feasibility under a Misspecification Floor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility and least-batch test under the assumed additive error model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(E_b=\sigma_{\mathrm{mis}}^2+\sigma_{\mathrm{samp}}^2/b\) for admissible integer \(b\ge1\). If \(\sigma_{\mathrm{samp}}^2=0\), a target \(E_b\le\varepsilon\) is feasible exactly when \(\varepsilon\ge\sigma_{\mathrm{mis}}^2\), and every admissible batch works. If \(\sigma_{\mathrm{samp}}^2>0\), feasibility requires \(\varepsilon>\sigma_{\mathrm{mis}}^2\), and the least batch is \(\max\{1,\lceil\sigma_{\mathrm{samp}}^2/(\varepsilon-\sigma_{\mathrm{mis}}^2)\rceil\}\). With a maximum batch \(B\), the target is feasible exactly when this least batch does not exceed \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The misspecification floor determines target feasibility, while the inverse gap above that floor determines the least required batch.
assumptions_latex: The additive error model holds throughout the admissible batch range.

notation.meaning: Maximum admissible batch size, when present.

review_flags: conditional algebraic certificate under the deferred seed's assumed model
corrects the builder candidate at sigma_samp^2=0 and epsilon=sigma_mis^2
knowledge_statements.title: Target-Accuracy Feasibility under a Misspecification Floor
Misspecification-Driven Saturation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Batch scaling boundary in the presence of irreducible model error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an estimator using batch size \(b\) has mean-square error \(E_b=\sigma_{\mathrm{mis}}^2+\sigma_{\mathrm{samp}}^2/b\), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{mis}}^2\) is a batch-independent misspecification floor and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{samp}}^2/b\) is reducible sampling error. Once \(b\ge \sigma_{\mathrm{samp}}^2/\sigma_{\mathrm{mis}}^2\), the sampling term is no larger than the misspecification term, and \(E_b\le2\sigma_{\mathrm{mis}}^2\). Moreover, \(E_b\downarrow\sigma_{\mathrm{mis}}^2\) as \(b\to\infty\). Hence larger batches cannot reduce error below the misspecification floor, and their relative benefit becomes negligible beyond this crossover.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When estimator error contains a fixed misspecification floor, batch growth saturates once reducible sampling error falls below that floor.
assumptions_latex: The stated additive mean-square-error decomposition holds for all admissible \(b\).

notation.meaning: mean-square estimator error at batch size b

review_flags: additive misspecification model requires method-specific justification and sourcing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The crossover and limiting conclusions follow from the assumed additive error model, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The batch-independent misspecification floor and inverse-batch sampling term require a method-specific source with an exact locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchrony-Induced Staleness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-error boundary for delayed asynchronous component evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every component gradient be \(L\)-Lipschitz, and suppose an asynchronous worker at iteration \(t\) evaluates component \(i_t\) at the delayed iterate \(x_{t-\tau_t}\) rather than \(x_t\). The resulting staleness error obeys \(\lVert\nabla f_{i_t}(x_{t-\tau_t})-\nabla f_{i_t}(x_t)\rVert\le L\lVert x_{t-\tau_t}-x_t\rVert\). If updates satisfy \(\lVert x_{s+1}-x_s\rVert\le\eta G\) and \(\tau_t\le\tau\), then the error is at most \(L\eta G\tau\). Thus variance-reduction guarantees requiring estimator error below \(\varepsilon\) cannot be certified from these bounds when \(L\eta G\tau>\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delayed component gradients incur error proportional to delay and step movement; excessive staleness invalidates any estimator-error tolerance based on the displayed bound.

notation.meaning: delay of the component evaluation at iteration t
uniform bound on one-step iterate displacement

review_flags: asynchronous variance-reduction interpretation needs a direct source beyond the elementary Lipschitz bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Lipschitz and telescoping bounds are plausible, and failure_boundary fits the topic. A direct asynchronous variance-reduction source is required; it should also specify integer delays, valid delayed indices, and the update model supporting the displacement bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Dominated Variance Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wall-clock boundary for distributed reference synchronization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose one distributed variance-reduced round performs \(W\) units of local component-gradient work and communicates \(C\) scalar words. With per-unit times \(t_{\mathrm{comp}}\) and \(t_{\mathrm{comm}}\), its round time is \(T=W t_{\mathrm{comp}}+C t_{\mathrm{comm}}\) under a nonoverlapping cost model. Communication dominates precisely when \(C t_{\mathrm{comm}}\ge W t_{\mathrm{comp}}\). If synchronization occurs every \(m\) local updates, its amortized communication time is \(C t_{\mathrm{comm}}/m\); it dominates per-update computation \(q t_{\mathrm{comp}}\) when \(m\le C t_{\mathrm{comm}}/(q t_{\mathrm{comp}})\). In that regime, component-oracle savings need not produce wall-clock savings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributed variance reduction is communication-dominated when synchronization time exceeds local computation, so oracle savings may not translate into faster execution.
assumptions_latex: Communication and computation do not overlap.
Costs are linear in communicated words and local work units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C t_{\mathrm{comm}}\ge W t_{\mathrm{comp}}\quad\text{or, amortized,}\quad\frac{C t_{\mathrm{comm}}}{m}\ge q t_{\mathrm{comp}}.\]

notation.meaning: local work units per distributed round

review_flags: wall-clock cost model needs a distributed variance-reduction source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dominance inequalities are correct under the stated nonoverlapping linear cost model, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No distributed variance-reduction source supports that wall-clock model or its synchronization interpretation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial Decay under Flat Convex Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-family counterexamples quantifying the loss of geometric contraction at flat convex minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p>2\), \(f_p(x)=|x|^p/p\), and \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta f_p'(x_k)\). If \(x_0>0\) and \(0<\eta x_0^{p-2}<1\), then \(x_k\downarrow0\) and \[\lim_{k\to\infty}k x_k^{p-2}=\frac{1}{(p-2)\eta},\qquad f_p(x_k)\sim\frac1p[(p-2)\eta k]^{-p/(p-2)}.\] Hence \(f_p(x_{k+1})/f_p(x_k)\to1\), excluding a uniform linear objective contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-step gradient descent on a convex power function with a flat minimum converges polynomially, with its one-step objective ratio tending to one.
assumptions_latex: Gradient descent uses the fixed step \(\eta\).

notation.meaning: power controlling flatness at the minimizer

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Decay under Flat Convex Geometry
Loss of Linear-Convergence Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth convex example showing failure of global linear objective contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^4/4\) on \([-1,1]\), whose gradient is Lipschitz there and whose unique minimizer is \(x^*=0\). For gradient descent with fixed \(0<\eta\le1/2\), the update is \(x_{k+1}=x_k(1-\eta x_k^2)\). For every proposed contraction factor \(\rho<1\), the ratio \(f(x_{k+1})/f(x_k)=(1-\eta x_k^2)^4\) exceeds \(\rho\) when a nonzero \(x_k\) is sufficiently close to zero. Thus smoothness and convexity alone do not yield a uniform global linear objective contraction; a growth condition such as strong convexity or the Polyak--Łojasiewicz inequality is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex function x⁴/4 has arbitrarily weak local contraction under fixed-step gradient descent, ruling out a uniform linear rate without stronger geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sup_{x\in[-1,1]\setminus\{0\}}\frac{f(x-\eta f'(x))}{f(x)}=1,\] so no uniform \(\rho<1\) satisfies \(f(x_{k+1})\le\rho f(x_k)\) for all nonzero iterates.
review_flags: counterexample is explicit but requires a source connecting missing growth geometry to variance-reduction linear rates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit x^4/4 example correctly rules out a uniform one-step objective contraction from smooth convex geometry alone, and counterexample is the correct content kind. A source is absent, and the statement that strong convexity or the Polyak--Lojasiewicz inequality is essential should instead be framed as examples of sufficient additional growth geometry, not an exhaustive necessity claim.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbiased Component Noise Can Increase a Stationary Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit smooth two-component finite sum showing that unbiased component sampling does not imply expected descent at a stationary minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_\pm(x)=1-\cos x\pm ax\), where \(a>0\), and let \(F=(f_++f_-)/2=1-\cos x\). At \(x=0\), uniformly sampling a component gradient gives \(v=a\) or \(v=-a\) with probability \(1/2\), so \(\mathbb E[v]=\nabla F(0)=0\). For \(x^+=-\eta v\), \[\mathbb E[F(x^+)]=1-\cos(\eta a)>0=F(0)\] whenever \(\eta a\notin2\pi\mathbb Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a stationary minimizer of a smooth nonconvex finite sum, an unbiased sampled component gradient can strictly increase the expected objective.
assumptions_latex: The two component gradients are sampled uniformly.

notation.meaning: uniformly sampled component gradient at the current point
component-gradient noise magnitude at the stationary point

knowledge_statements.title: Unbiased Component Noise Can Increase a Stationary Objective
Nonconvex Estimator Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-descent boundary for unbiased stochastic directions on smooth nonconvex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) have \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and set \(x^+=x-\eta v\), where \(\mathbb{E}[v\mid x]=
abla f(x)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert v-
abla f(x)Vert^2\mid x]=\sigma^2(x)\). Smoothness gives \(\mathbb{E}[f(x^+)\mid x]\le f(x)-\eta(1-L\eta/2)\lVert
abla f(x)Vert^2+(L\eta^2/2)\sigma^2(x)\). For \(0<\eta<2/L\), this bound certifies strict expected descent only if \(\sigma^2(x)<[2/(L\eta)-1]\lVert
abla f(x)Vert^2\). Near nonconvex stationary regions, failure of this relative-variance condition removes the descent certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbiased estimator need not certify descent when its variance is too large relative to the squared gradient, especially near nonconvex stationary regions.
assumptions_latex: The conditional estimator is unbiased with finite conditional variance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sigma^2(x)<\left(\frac{2}{L\eta}-1\right)\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^2\] is sufficient for the displayed smoothness bound to imply strict expected descent.

notation.meaning: next iterate after one stochastic step

review_flags: descent inequality needs an authoritative nonconvex variance-reduction locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional smoothness inequality and relative-variance threshold are internally consistent, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. An authoritative nonconvex stochastic or variance-reduced optimization source with a precise locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Surrogate with Arbitrarily Large True Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit witness that a surrogate proximal-gradient mapping can vanish while the exact stationarity residual is arbitrarily large.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=1\), \(r\equiv0\), \(f(x)=Mx\) with \(M>0\), and choose \(v=0\). For every \(x\in\mathbb R\) and \(\eta>0\), \[\widetilde G_\eta(x;0)=0,\qquad G_\eta(x)=M.\] Since \(M\) is arbitrary, a zero surrogate mapping alone imposes no finite upper bound on the true mapping norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero estimator-based proximal-gradient residual can coexist with an arbitrarily large exact gradient mapping.

notation.meaning: magnitude of the true gradient mapping

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Surrogate with Arbitrarily Large True Mapping
Surrogate-Certificate Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch between estimator-based and true proximal-gradient stationarity certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+r\), where \(f\) is differentiable and \(r\) is proper, closed, and convex. For \(\eta>0\), define the true proximal-gradient mapping \(G_\eta(x)=\eta^{-1}[x-\operatorname{prox}_{\eta r}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))]\) and the estimator-based mapping \(\widetilde G_\eta(x;v)=\eta^{-1}[x-\operatorname{prox}_{\eta r}(x-\eta v)]\). Nonexpansiveness of the proximal map yields \(\lVert G_\eta(x)-\widetilde G_\eta(x;v)\rVert\le\lVert v-\nabla f(x)\rVert\). Therefore a small surrogate norm certifies true stationarity only when estimator error is also controlled; in particular, \(\widetilde G_\eta(x;v)=0\) can coexist with a large true mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small estimator-based proximal-gradient mapping does not certify true stationarity unless the estimator error is simultaneously bounded.

notation.meaning: gradient surrogate used by the method

review_flags: proximal certificate mismatch requires a supporting source locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proximal nonexpansiveness inequality is correct under the stated convexity assumptions, and failure_boundary fits the certificate-mismatch leaf. No source is cited, and the claim that a zero surrogate mapping can coexist with a large true mapping should be supported by a source or an explicitly stated example.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation-to-high-probability conversion when independent outputs can be validly compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose independent runs produce nonnegative errors X_1,\ldots,X_k with \mathbb E X_j\leq\varepsilon. Markov's inequality gives \mathbb P(X_j>2\varepsilon)\leq1/2. If an output attaining \min_jX_j can be validly selected, then \mathbb P(\min_jX_j>2\varepsilon)\leq2^{-k}. Thus k=\lceil\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil runs suffice for error at most 2\varepsilon with probability at least 1-\delta.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent repetition amplifies confidence exponentially, provided the runs are independent and a valid best-output selection is available.
assumptions_latex: The smallest-error output can be identified exactly or by a separately valid validation procedure.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Restart Confidence Amplification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient tail information for a realized guarantee with an additive confidence penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If X satisfies \mathbb P(X-\mathbb EX\geq t)\leq\exp(-t^2/(2\sigma^2)) for all t\geq0, then for 0<\delta<1, \mathbb P(X\leq\mathbb EX+\sigma\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)})\geq1-\delta. Unlike the expectation-only Markov conversion, the penalty is additive and governed by a verified tail scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verified sub-Gaussian upper tail upgrades mean performance with an additive square-root-log confidence penalty.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb P(X-\mathbb EX\geq t)\leq e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}\text{ for all }t\geq0.
knowledge_statements.title: Concentration Upgrade Condition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expectation Convergence Need Not Give Pathwise Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of vanishing expected error from almost-sure realized convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let independent X_t be Bernoulli with \mathbb P(X_t=1)=1/t. Then \mathbb EX_t=1/t\to0, but \sum_t\mathbb P(X_t=1)=\infty, so X_t=1 infinitely often almost surely. Hence vanishing expected error does not imply almost-sure convergence of realized errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected errors can vanish while unit-sized failures recur infinitely often almost surely.
assumptions_latex: X_t\text{ are independent Bernoulli variables with success probability }1/t.
knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Convergence Need Not Give Pathwise Convergence
Expected-versus-Realized Performance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit of converting expected error guarantees into realized guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\ge0\) denote the realized optimization error of a randomized finite-sum method. An expectation guarantee \(\mathbb{E}X\le\varepsilon\) implies only \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge\varepsilon/\delta)\le\delta\) for \(0<\delta<1\) by Markov's inequality. This dependence is sharp without additional tail information: the random variable taking value \(\varepsilon/\delta\) with probability \(\delta\) and zero otherwise has expectation \(\varepsilon\). Hence an expected convergence certificate does not by itself guarantee that one realized run attains error \(\varepsilon\) with high probability; concentration, bounded increments, or independent repetition is additionally required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected error alone gives only a weak Markov tail bound and cannot ensure comparable accuracy for a single realized run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathbb{P}\!\left(X\ge\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right)\le\delta,\] and this threshold cannot generally be improved using the expectation bound alone.
review_flags: standard probability statement needs an authoritative locator tied to randomized optimization guarantees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Markov bound and sharp two-point construction are mathematically correct, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The record supplies no authoritative probability or randomized-optimization citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Snapshot-Based Method Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection considerations for methods organized around periodically refreshed reference snapshots.

knowledge_statements.title: Snapshot-Based Method Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource-based selection condition for periodically refreshed snapshot estimators of finite-sum gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\). A snapshot-based architecture is admissible when it can store a point \(\widetilde x\) and its full gradient \(
abla F(\widetilde x)\), and between refreshes uses \(v(x,i)=
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(\widetilde x)+
abla F(\widetilde x)\). Given feasible architectures \(\mathcal A\), resource budget \(B\), and predicted total cost \(C(a;\varepsilon)\) for attaining \(\mathbb E[F(x)-F^*]\leq\varepsilon\), select the snapshot architecture \(a_{\mathrm{snap}}\) exactly when \[a_{\mathrm{snap}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A:\,R(a)\leq B}C(a;\varepsilon),\] where its cost includes every full-gradient refresh and intervening component-gradient evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the snapshot architecture when it is feasible and minimizes predicted cost to the requested accuracy after charging for full-gradient refreshes and component evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) is differentiable and has finite optimum value \(F^*\).
The cost model \(C\) and resource usage \(R\) count all snapshot refreshes and component-gradient calls.
At least one architecture satisfies \(R(a)\leq B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_{\mathrm{snap}}\) is selected if and only if it belongs to the resource-feasible cost argmin.

notation.meaning: Predicted cost of architecture a at accuracy epsilon

review_flags: method-selection cost model requires an authoritative finite-sum variance-reduction source
exact refresh-cost convention is architecture dependent

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the snapshot-selection leaf and the estimator formula is recognizable, but no citation supports the proposed exact cost-minimization interface or its refresh accounting. The source inventory does not contain an inspectable finite-sum variance-reduction locator establishing this selection rule.

children.title: Table-Based Method Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection considerations for methods retaining component-level estimator state.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies how a table-based estimator preserves its stored-gradient average after replacing one table entry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If index \(i\) is sampled, let \(g_i^{\mathrm{old}}\) denote its stored vector and set \(g_i^{\mathrm{new}}=\nabla f_i(x)\). The invariant \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n g_j\) is preserved without rescanning the table by the rank-one update \[\bar g^{\mathrm{new}}=\bar g^{\mathrm{old}}+\frac{1}{n}\bigl(g_i^{\mathrm{new}}-g_i^{\mathrm{old}}\bigr).\] Thus maintaining the aggregate requires \(O(d)\) arithmetic and one additional dense \(d\)-vector, beyond the table itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After replacing one stored gradient, update the table average by adding one nth of the entry change; no full table rescan is needed.
assumptions_latex: Every stored entry is a dense vector in \(\mathbb R^d\).
Exactly one table entry is replaced in the stated update.
The previous aggregate equals the average of the previous table.

notation.meaning: Stored component-gradient vector before and after replacement
Average of all stored gradient vectors

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Time Aggregate Maintenance
Table-Based Method Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection condition for methods maintaining component-gradient memories and an aggregate table average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\). A table-based architecture stores vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\) and their average \(\bar g=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n g_j\), uses \(v(x,i)=\nabla f_i(x)-g_i+\bar g\), and replaces \(g_i\) by \(\nabla f_i(x)\) after sampling index \(i\). For feasible architectures \(\mathcal A\), memory budget \(M\), and predicted accuracy cost \(C(a;\varepsilon)\), select a table-based architecture \(a_{\mathrm{tab}}\) exactly when \[a_{\mathrm{tab}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A:\,m(a)\leq M}C(a;\varepsilon).\] Thus the table is excluded whenever its stored-gradient memory \(m(a_{\mathrm{tab}})\) exceeds \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a gradient-table method only when its table fits memory and its predicted accuracy cost is minimal among feasible alternatives.
assumptions_latex: Each component gradient \(\nabla f_i(x)\) is available by indexed oracle access.
The memory measure \(m(a)\) includes all stored component gradients and aggregate state.
At least one candidate architecture satisfies \(m(a)\leq M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_{\mathrm{tab}}\) is selected exactly when it is memory-feasible and cost-minimizing.

notation.meaning: Stored gradient associated with component i

review_flags: table-based selection criterion lacks a directly supporting source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and table-based architecture match the terminal container, but the exact selection condition and storage convention have no cited source. A source must also clarify maintenance of the aggregate after a table entry is replaced.

children.title: Recursive Method Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection considerations for recursively updated variance-reduced estimators.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Method Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection condition for low-memory estimators updated recursively from recent stochastic gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\). A recursive architecture maintains an estimator \(v_t\) without an \(n\)-entry gradient table and updates it, between resets, by \[v_t=v_{t-1}+\nabla f_{i_t}(x_t)-\nabla f_{i_t}(x_{t-1}).\] At designated reset times it replaces \(v_t\) by a prescribed batch or full-gradient estimate. Given feasible architectures \(\mathcal A\), memory budget \(M\), and predicted cost \(C(a;\varepsilon)\), select the recursive architecture \(a_{\mathrm{rec}}\) exactly when \[a_{\mathrm{rec}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A:\,m(a)\leq M}C(a;\varepsilon),\] with reset and paired-gradient costs included in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a recursive estimator when its low-memory state is feasible and its total predicted cost, including resets and paired gradients, is smallest.
assumptions_latex: The same sampled component \(i_t\) can be differentiated at \(x_t\) and \(x_{t-1}\).
The reset rule and all reset costs are specified by the candidate architecture.
At least one architecture obeys \(m(a)\leq M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_{\mathrm{rec}}\) is selected exactly when it is memory-feasible and minimizes fully accounted accuracy cost.

notation.meaning: Recursive gradient estimator at iteration t
Sampled component index at iteration t

review_flags: recursive estimator class admits several inequivalent reset rules
direct source for the selection boundary is missing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is appropriately a condition for recursive-method selection, but recursive estimators have materially different reset and batching rules. No source identifies the intended class or supports the asserted complete-cost comparison.

children.title: Memory–Refresh Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Method-family crossover governed by storage cost, refresh burden, estimator persistence, plus implementation constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Corrects the endpoint and tie conditions under which memory-priced scalarization returns an undominated architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_\lambda(a)=q(a;\varepsilon)+\lambda m(a)\). If \(\lambda>0\), every minimizer of \(D_\lambda\) is undominated in the \((m,q)\) plane. If \(\lambda=0\), an arbitrary minimizer can be dominated by another architecture having the same refresh work and smaller memory; selecting a minimum-memory element among the \(q\)-minimizers restores undominatedness. Even with \(\lambda>0\), varying \(\lambda\) need not recover unsupported undominated points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive memory prices exclude dominated minimizers. At zero price, ties must be broken toward smaller memory, and weighted sums still miss unsupported Pareto points.
assumptions_latex: The compared architectures use a common accuracy target and common units for \(m\) and \(q\).
\(m(a)\) and \(q(a;\varepsilon)\) are finite for feasible architectures.
review_flags: Clarifies that the deferred seed's supported-frontier conclusion requires a positive memory price or Pareto-efficient tie-breaking at zero price.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted-Scalarization Tie Boundary
Memory–Refresh Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto characterization of storage and estimator-refresh costs across reference architectures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each feasible variance-reduction architecture \(a\), let \(m(a)\) be peak stored state and let \(q(a;\varepsilon)\) be the expected number of component-gradient equivalents spent on estimator refreshes before achieving \(\mathbb E[F(x)-F^*]\leq\varepsilon\). Architecture \(a\) is undominated in the memory–refresh plane exactly when no feasible \(b\) satisfies \[m(b)\leq m(a),\qquad q(b;\varepsilon)\leq q(a;\varepsilon),\] with at least one strict inequality. Under a scalarized resource price \(\lambda\geq0\), a compatible selection minimizes \(q(a;\varepsilon)+\lambda m(a)\). Varying \(\lambda\) selects supported points of the lower Pareto frontier, not necessarily every undominated point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An architecture is memory–refresh efficient when no competitor uses both no more memory and no more refresh work, with one strict improvement.
assumptions_latex: All architectures use the same accuracy criterion and component-gradient-equivalent cost unit.
Peak memory and refresh work are finite for every feasible architecture.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Undominated architectures form the memory–refresh Pareto frontier; scalarized minimizers are supported frontier points.

notation.meaning: Expected refresh work to accuracy epsilon

review_flags: Pareto formulation is standard but needs architecture-specific sourcing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the tradeoff leaf, and the supported-versus-undominated Pareto distinction is mathematically sound. Nevertheless, the record supplies no evidence for its architecture-specific refresh-work quantity or common component-gradient-equivalent normalization.

children.title: Accelerated Method Selection
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes where acceleration mechanisms justify their additional structure or overhead.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Order-Level Regime Favoring Accelerated Variance Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic component-gradient regime in which a standard accelerated finite-sum certificate improves on a nonaccelerated variance-reduction certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For smooth strongly convex finite sums, compare certificates of the forms \[Q_{\mathrm{non}}=O\!\left((n+\kappa)\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\right),\qquad Q_{\mathrm{acc}}=O\!\left((n+\sqrt{n\kappa})\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\right).\] If \(\kappa/n\to\infty\), then the accelerated expression is asymptotically smaller by the factor \(\Theta(\sqrt{n/\kappa})\), apart from constants and acceleration-specific overhead. This regime favors an accelerated candidate only when its assumptions hold and its charged overhead does not erase that saving.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the condition number is asymptotically larger than the sample size, the standard accelerated finite-sum complexity improves in order over the nonaccelerated variance-reduction complexity, provided overhead does not erase the gain.
assumptions_latex: Each compared certificate uses the same component-gradient oracle and objective-gap target.
The applicable problem class is a smooth strongly convex finite sum with \(\kappa=L/\mu\).
Acceleration-specific initialization, parameter estimation, and restart costs are charged separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\kappa/n\to\infty\) and charged overhead is lower order than the certified saving, the accelerated candidate has the smaller asymptotic component-gradient cost.

notation.meaning: accelerated and nonaccelerated component-gradient complexity certificates

review_flags: method-specific accelerated and nonaccelerated complexity locators should be supplied before treating hidden constants as operational predictions
knowledge_statements.title: Order-Level Regime Favoring Accelerated Variance Reduction
Accelerated Method Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-complexity selection rule for acceleration in smooth strongly convex finite sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), with condition number \(\kappa=L/\mu\), and target \(\mathbb E[F(x)-F^*]\leq\varepsilon\). Let an accelerated candidate have certified component-gradient complexity \(Q_{\mathrm{acc}}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)\), and let \(Q_j(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)\) denote the certified complexity of each feasible alternative \(j\in\mathcal J\). After including initialization, restart, and parameter-estimation costs in every \(Q\), select acceleration exactly when \[Q_{\mathrm{acc}}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)=\min_{j\in\mathcal J}Q_j(n,\kappa,\varepsilon).\] If acceleration requires unavailable values of \(L\) or \(\mu\), it is feasible only when a certified adaptive procedure supplies the required parameters within the stated cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select acceleration when its complete certified oracle cost is minimal and all required smoothness, strong-convexity, restart, and parameter information is available.
assumptions_latex: Every compared complexity uses the same accuracy and component-gradient oracle convention.
All acceleration overhead is included in \(Q_{\mathrm{acc}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accelerated candidate is selected exactly when it is feasible and minimizes certified total oracle complexity.

notation.meaning: Complete oracle complexity of the accelerated candidate

review_flags: finite-sum accelerated complexity formula is intentionally abstract pending a method-specific source
provided acceleration locator does not establish this selection rule

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition is the correct role for this selection leaf, but no cited finite-sum acceleration result supplies the complexity certificates or overhead model. It is also unclear whether the accelerated candidate belongs to \(\mathcal J\); if \(\mathcal J\) contains only alternatives, equality with their minimum is not the general minimizer condition.

children.title: Nonaccelerated Method Selection
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes favoring simpler variance-reduced methods without acceleration machinery.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regime with No Order-Level Acceleration Gain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strongly convex finite-sum regime where acceleration does not improve the leading asymptotic component-gradient order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose applicable nonaccelerated and accelerated certificates scale respectively as \((n+\kappa)\ell\) and \((n+\sqrt{n\kappa})\ell\), where \(\ell=\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\). If \(\kappa=O(n)\), both expressions are \(\Theta(n\ell)\). Acceleration therefore supplies no order-level oracle improvement in this regime; a nonaccelerated method is selected when its fully charged cost or a declared secondary resource criterion is no worse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the condition number is at most the sample-size scale, accelerated and nonaccelerated finite-sum rates have the same leading order, so overhead or secondary constraints may favor the nonaccelerated method.
assumptions_latex: The compared certificates concern the same smooth strongly convex finite-sum class and accuracy target.
Complexity and overhead are measured in common component-gradient-equivalent units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both certificate families have order \(n\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\); select the nonaccelerated candidate only if its charged total cost or declared tie-break criterion is no worse.
review_flags: method-specific rate locators are required for operational constants
knowledge_statements.title: Regime with No Order-Level Acceleration Gain

assumptions_latex: All candidates are certified for the same finite-sum problem class and target accuracy.
Complexity and overhead are expressed in common component-gradient-equivalent units.
The tie-breaking rule is fixed before selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonaccelerated method is selected when it is a total-cost minimizer after acceleration overhead is charged.

notation.meaning: Certified accelerated oracle cost before overhead

selection criterion is a formal interface rather than a named theorem
LaTeX escape corruption repaired; sourcing remains required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection rule favoring a nonaccelerated method after accounting for acceleration overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed finite-sum problem class and accuracy \(\varepsilon\), let \(Q_{\mathrm{non}}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)\) be the certified component-gradient complexity of a feasible nonaccelerated method, including initialization and refreshes. Let \(Q_{\mathrm{acc}}^{+}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)=Q_{\mathrm{acc}}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)+H_{\mathrm{acc}}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)\), where \(H_{\mathrm{acc}}\) counts restart, momentum-tuning, and parameter-estimation overhead in the same units. Select the nonaccelerated method exactly when \[Q_{\mathrm{non}}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)\leq Q_{\mathrm{acc}}^{+}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)\] and it also minimizes certified cost among the remaining feasible candidates. Ties may be resolved by a declared secondary criterion such as memory or numerical robustness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the nonaccelerated method when its certified total cost is no larger than acceleration with overhead and no other feasible method is cheaper.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonaccelerated Method Selection

children.title: Acceleration Payoff Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Crossovers where conditioning, accuracy targets, or overhead alter the value of acceleration.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition-number-to-sample-size boundary in the standard strongly convex finite-sum complexity comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the comparison \[Q_{\mathrm{non}}\asymp(n+\kappa)\ell,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{acc}}\asymp(n+\sqrt{n\kappa})\ell,\qquad \ell=\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon),\] both costs have order \(n\ell\) when \(\kappa=O(n)\). If \(\kappa/n\to\infty\), then \(Q_{\mathrm{acc}}/Q_{\mathrm{non}}=\Theta(\sqrt{n/\kappa})\to0\). Thus \(\kappa\asymp n\) is the order-level crossover; an exact operational boundary additionally depends on constants and acceleration overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard finite-sum comparison has no order-level acceleration gain when the condition number is at most the sample-size scale, but has a growing gain when the condition number dominates the sample size.
assumptions_latex: Both expressions use the same component-gradient oracle, target, and logarithmic accuracy factor.
The compared rate certificates apply to the same smooth strongly convex finite-sum class.
The displayed crossover is order-level; constants and overhead are not suppressed in an operational comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa\asymp n\) separates the no-order-improvement regime \(\kappa=O(n)\) from the strict asymptotic improvement regime \(\kappa/n\to\infty\).
review_flags: the underlying method-specific complexity certificates require precise scholarly locators
knowledge_statements.title: Order-Level Acceleration Crossover
Acceleration Payoff Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Break-even boundary between accelerated and nonaccelerated certified total costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_{\mathrm{acc}}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{non}}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)\) be certified component-gradient costs for accelerated and nonaccelerated methods on the same problem class, and let \(H_{\mathrm{acc}}\geq0\) be acceleration-specific overhead. Define the payoff function \[\Delta(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)=Q_{\mathrm{non}}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)-Q_{\mathrm{acc}}(n,\kappa,\varepsilon)-H_{\mathrm{acc}}.\] Acceleration has positive predicted payoff precisely on \(\{(n,\kappa,\varepsilon):\Delta>0\}\); the break-even boundary is \(\{\Delta=0\}\); and it is cost-disfavored on \(\{\Delta<0\}\). These regions are meaningful only where both complexity certificates and their parameter assumptions apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration pays off where nonaccelerated cost exceeds accelerated cost plus overhead; equality defines the break-even boundary.
assumptions_latex: Both complexity certificates concern the same oracle, problem class, and accuracy criterion.
\(H_{\mathrm{acc}}\) is measured in the same units as both oracle costs.
The parameters \(n\), \(\kappa\), and \(\varepsilon\) lie in both certificates' validity domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign of \(\Delta\) partitions the parameter domain into acceleration-beneficial, break-even, and acceleration-disfavored regions.

notation.meaning: Condition parameter used by the complexity certificates

review_flags: abstract break-even definition needs specialization to sourced complexity bounds
no supplied locator supports finite-sum payoff boundaries directly

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sign-based break-even condition is internally coherent and fits the payoff-boundary leaf. Its substantive regions cannot be evaluated, however, without sourced accelerated and nonaccelerated complexity bounds having a common validity domain and cost convention.

children.title: Finite-Sum Method Selection
children.top_down_role: Method choices for repeatedly accessible finite component collections.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonrevisitable Observations Exclude Revisit-Dependent Finite-Sum Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Access-model obstruction to full-pass and table methods requiring later indexed queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each observation \(\xi_i\) is exposed once, is discarded after arrival, and cannot be replayed or reconstructed from persistent state. Then any method requiring a later query of \(f_i(\cdot)=f(\cdot;\xi_i)\), a fresh full pass over all components, or post-expiry initialization of an exact component table is inadmissible under this access model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-pass nonrevisitable data cannot support finite-sum methods requiring later component queries or full-data passes.
assumptions_latex: Each observation is available during only one arrival event.
Expired observations cannot be replayed or reconstructed.
The method requires a post-expiry component query, full pass, or exact table construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method is infeasible under the stated one-pass access model.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonrevisitable Observations Exclude Revisit-Dependent Finite-Sum Methods

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive data-access contract under which revisit-dependent finite-sum methods are operationally admissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A run has revisitable fixed finite-sum access when there is a fixed indexed collection \(\{f_i\}_{i=1}^n\) whose identities and query semantics do not change during the run, every index may be queried again at later iterates, a full pass means one permitted query of every index, and state derived from earlier queries may be retained subject to the declared memory budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-sum access is revisitable when component identities remain stable, arbitrary later replays and full passes are permitted, and retained query state obeys the memory budget.
assumptions_latex: The collection contains a fixed finite number \(n\) of indexed components.
Repeated queries to an index retain the same component semantics.
Replay, full-pass, and persistent-state permissions are explicitly declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{stable identities}+\text{replay}+\text{full-pass permission}+\text{permitted persistent state}\) defines the revisitable finite-sum access contract.
knowledge_statements.title: Revisitable Fixed Finite-Sum Access Contract

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Access-and-Resource Feasibility Filter for Finite-Sum Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational selector among finite-sum families after matching their access and storage requirements to the deployment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each candidate method \(a\), declare its required replay pattern, initialization and later full passes, persistent memory \(M(a)\), and predicted target-accuracy cost \(C(a;\varepsilon)\) under one common accounting model. Form \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{feas}}\) from candidates whose access requirements are permitted and whose memory and other resource requirements satisfy the available budgets. If \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{feas}}\ne\varnothing\), select any \(a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{feas}}}C(a;\varepsilon)\); if it is empty, no candidate finite-sum family is admissible under the declared model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First remove methods whose replay, pass, or memory requirements are infeasible; then compare the remaining methods using one declared target-accuracy cost model.
assumptions_latex: Every candidate's replay, full-pass, persistent-memory, and other resource requirements are declared.
All predicted costs use the same target accuracy and accounting convention.
Feasibility is evaluated under the revisitable fixed finite-sum access contract and the available budgets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{feas}}=\varnothing\Rightarrow\) no finite-sum candidate is admissible; otherwise \(a^*\in\arg\min_{a\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{feas}}}C(a;\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: persistent memory required by method a
predicted cost to target accuracy under the common model

knowledge_statements.title: Access-and-Resource Feasibility Filter for Finite-Sum Selection
Finite-Sum Method Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection condition for repeatedly accessible, fixed finite component collections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where the indexed collection \(\{f_i\}_{i=1}^n\) is fixed throughout optimization. A finite-sum variance-reduction method is admissible when it may revisit any index, retain state derived from earlier component queries, and perform any required full pass over all \(n\) components. Given target accuracy \(\varepsilon\), resource budget \(B\), and feasible methods \(\mathcal A\), select a finite-sum method \(a_{\mathrm{fs}}\) exactly when \[a_{\mathrm{fs}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A:\,R(a)\leq B}C(a;\varepsilon),\] where \(C\) charges repeated component access, stored state, and full passes according to the declared computational model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use a finite-sum method when components remain fixed and revisitable, required passes and memory are feasible, and total predicted cost is minimal.
assumptions_latex: The number \(n\) and component identities remain fixed during the optimization run.
Indexed components can be revisited under a stable oracle semantics.
At least one candidate satisfies the resource budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite-sum method is selected exactly when it is access-feasible, resource-feasible, and cost-minimizing.
review_flags: data-access suitability rule needs a direct finite-sum variance-reduction source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role matches finite-sum method selection, but the admissibility and cost interface are uncited. None of the supplied local locators specifically supports revisitable finite-sum variance reduction, full-pass feasibility, and the declared resource accounting.

children.title: Streaming Method Selection
children.top_down_role: Method choices for sequential, transient, or continually arriving observations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-Memory Nonreplay Streams Exclude Exact Full Gradient Tables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection boundary for exact table methods under one-pass access and an explicit storage budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a one-pass stream of \(n\) observations whose component-gradient records are arbitrary vectors in \(\mathbb R^d\). If expired observations cannot be replayed and an exact independently addressable record must be retained for every component, then the standard explicit-storage representation requires \(nd\) scalar words. Hence a method with an \(o(nd)\) auxiliary-storage budget cannot maintain an exact full component-gradient table for arbitrary streams without additional reconstruction or compression structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-memory nonreplay stream cannot support an arbitrary exact full gradient table unless extra structure permits reconstruction or compression.
assumptions_latex: Component-gradient records are arbitrary vectors in \(\mathbb R^d\).
Every record must be preserved exactly and support indexed retrieval.
Storage is measured in scalar words under explicit representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact arbitrary full table requires \(nd\) scalar words and is infeasible under an \(o(nd)\) budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Memory Nonreplay Streams Exclude Exact Full Gradient Tables

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Taxonomy separating arrival assumptions from replay constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\xi_t,\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge1}\) be an adapted stream. It is i.i.d. from \(P\) when \(\mathcal L(\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P\); stationary dependent when its joint law is shift-invariant but conditional laws may depend on the past; drifting when \(P_t:=\mathcal L(\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})\) varies with \(t\); and adversarial when no probabilistic law is assumed beyond a declared nonanticipation rule. Independently, a nonreplay stream forbids later access to expired observations, whereas replayable access explicitly charges storage or external replay.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Streaming selection must separately declare the arrival law and whether expired observations can be replayed.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_t\) contains observations and algorithmic information revealed through time \(t\).
Any adversary obeys the declared anticipation rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Arrival law and replay capability are independent coordinates of a streaming regime.}
knowledge_statements.title: Streaming Arrival Taxonomy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection among methods compatible with a declared streaming regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an arrival model \(\mathcal P\), replay rule \(\mathcal R\), state budget \(M\), performance criterion \(Q\), and resource cost \(C\). A method \(a\) is streaming-admissible when \(m(s_t)\le M\), its update is measurable with respect to currently available information, and every access obeys \(\mathcal R\). Among admissible methods satisfying \(Q(a)\le\varepsilon\), select any \[a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_a C(a).\] If no candidate has a guarantee matching \((\mathcal P,Q)\), no selection is justified by transferring a theorem from another arrival model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the least-cost bounded-state method whose guarantee matches the declared arrival and replay model.
assumptions_latex: Arrival, replay, memory, accuracy, and cost conventions are declared.
Candidate guarantees are evaluated under those same conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Streaming Method Admissibility and Selection
Streaming Method Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection condition when observations arrive sequentially and cannot reliably be revisited.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose data arrive as a sequence \(\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots\), and the objective is \(F(x)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P}[f(x;\xi)]\). A streaming method is admissible when its update at time \(t\) uses the current observation and a state \(s_{t-1}\) of size at most \(M\), without requiring later access to \(\xi_t\). For feasible methods \(\mathcal A\), select a streaming method \(a_{\mathrm{str}}\) exactly when \[a_{\mathrm{str}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A:\,m(a)\leq M}C_{\mathrm{stream}}(a;\varepsilon),\] where the cost model prohibits full passes and component-index revisits unless an external replay mechanism is explicitly available and charged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a streaming method when samples are sequential or nonrevisitable and it minimizes predicted cost using only feasible bounded state.
assumptions_latex: Observations are supplied sequentially from a specified data-generating process.
Past observations are unavailable unless replay storage is explicitly included.
The accuracy criterion and streaming cost model are fixed across candidates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_{\mathrm{str}}\) is selected when it respects one-pass access and memory limits and minimizes streaming cost.

notation.meaning: Persistent algorithmic state after time t
Predicted cost under streaming access constraints

review_flags: streaming selection interface requires a source distinguishing finite-sum and online regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement fits the streaming-selection container, but it combines an objective under a fixed distribution \(P\) with a merely specified sequential data-generating process. A source is needed to determine whether the intended regime is i.i.d., stationary dependent, or drifting and to support the one-pass selection condition.

children.title: Hybrid Data-Arrival Regimes
children.top_down_role: Selection issues for partially reusable data mixed with continuing sample arrivals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Wholly Stale Reuse Is Biased After Objective Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of an estimator that substitutes historical component gradients for current component queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F_t(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_{i,t}(x)\), let \(s_i<t\), and fix stored references \(\alpha_i\). For a uniformly sampled index \(I\), define \(\widetilde v_t=
abla f_{I,s_I}(x)-\alpha_I+n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_j\). Conditional on the stored state, \[\mathbb E_I[\widetilde v_t]-
abla F_t(x)= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n igl(
abla f_{i,s_i}(x)-
abla f_{i,t}(x) igr).\] Thus wholly stale reuse is biased unless the average historical-to-current gradient drift vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing current component queries by historical gradients generally introduces average drift bias.
assumptions_latex: Every current and historical component is differentiable at \(x\).
The sampled index is uniform conditional on the stored state.
At least one component may change between its storage time and time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde v_t\) has the displayed drift bias, which vanishes only when the average gradient drift is zero.

notation.meaning: time associated with historical component i
estimator using a historical sampled gradient

knowledge_statements.title: Wholly Stale Reuse Is Biased After Objective Drift
Hybrid Data-Arrival Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal access model combining a revisitable core with newly arriving observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At time \(t\), let \(D_t=R_t\cup N_t\), where \(R_t\) is a stored, revisitable set and \(N_t\) is a batch of newly arriving observations. A hybrid method is admissible if its estimator \(v_t\) may reuse component information indexed by \(R_t\), processes each element of \(N_t\) before its expiry, and obeys a storage budget \(|R_t|\leq M\). Given candidates \(\mathcal A\), choose a hybrid architecture exactly when \[a_{\mathrm{hyb}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A}C(a;\varepsilon)\quad\text{subject to}\quad |R_t(a)|\leq M\ \text{and all expiry constraints}.\] The cost must include insertion, eviction, refresh, and new-data processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a hybrid method when some data are revisitable and others expire, and it minimizes cost while respecting storage and processing deadlines.
assumptions_latex: Each observation has a declared revisitation or expiry rule.
The storage budget \(M\) applies at every time \(t\).
All candidates use the same accuracy and data-processing cost conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hybrid architecture is selected when it minimizes total cost subject to storage and expiry feasibility.

notation.meaning: Revisitable data retained at time t
Newly arriving data at time t

review_flags: hybrid arrival model is one formalization among several
source needed for variance-reduction guarantees under insertion and eviction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition is a plausible role for this hybrid-regime leaf, but the proposed retained/new partition, expiry semantics, and estimator guarantees are one unsourced formalization among several. The record also does not state whether \(R_t\) and \(N_t\) are disjoint.

children.title: Reuse–Freshness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Crossovers governed by the relative value of component reuse versus newly arriving information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decomposition of mean-square estimator error used in reuse-versus-refresh comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_t\) be a conditionally square-integrable estimator of \(g_t=\nabla F_t(x_t)\), and let \(\mathcal H_t\) denote the information fixed before its internal randomization. With \(b_t=\mathbb E[v_t\mid\mathcal H_t]-g_t\), \[\mathbb E[\|v_t-g_t\|^2\mid\mathcal H_t]=\|b_t\|^2+\mathbb E[\|v_t-\mathbb E[v_t\mid\mathcal H_t]\|^2\mid\mathcal H_t].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean-square reuse error is squared conditional bias plus conditional variance.
assumptions_latex: \(g_t\) and \(\mathcal H_t\) are fixed before the estimator's internal randomization.

notation.meaning: conditional bias relative to the current gradient

knowledge_statements.title: Bias–Variance Decomposition of Reuse Error

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact action certificate under the declared two-action loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(\Delta_t=J_t(\mathrm{refresh})-J_t(\mathrm{reuse})\). Then \(\Delta_t<0\) certifies refresh, \(\Delta_t>0\) certifies reuse, and \(\Delta_t=0\) certifies indifference. Equivalently, refresh is preferred exactly when \[c_t(\mathrm{refresh})-c_t(\mathrm{reuse})<\lambda_t\bigl(e_t(\mathrm{reuse})-e_t(\mathrm{refresh})\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sign of the declared loss difference exactly classifies refresh, reuse, and indifference.
assumptions_latex: Reuse and refresh are the complete feasible action set.
The declared scalar loss is the decision objective.
Costs and errors use the conventions of the declared decision model.
knowledge_statements.title: Reuse, Refresh, and Indifference Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision model making refresh cost and estimator error commensurate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a\in\{\mathrm{reuse},\mathrm{refresh}\}\), let \(c_t(a)\) be its declared cost and let \(e_t(a)=\mathbb E[\|v_t^a-\nabla F_t(x_t)\|^2\mid\mathcal H_t]\). Given \(\lambda_t>0\), define \(J_t(a)=c_t(a)+\lambda_t e_t(a)\). A reuse–freshness boundary is a state satisfying \(J_t(\mathrm{reuse})=J_t(\mathrm{refresh})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A declared loss prices access cost and conditional estimator error in common units; equality of action losses defines the boundary.
assumptions_latex: Both estimators target the same current aggregate gradient.
Both costs and errors use common conditioning and accounting conventions.

notation.meaning: declared one-step loss of action a
price converting squared estimator error to cost units
information available when the action is selected

knowledge_statements.title: Declared Reuse–Refresh Decision Model

assumptions_latex: Both estimators target the current gradient \(\nabla F_t(x_t)\).
Refresh cost and squared estimator error are converted to common utility units by \(\lambda_t>0\).
The expectations use the same information available at time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign of \(c_t^{\mathrm{ref}}+\lambda_t(e_t^{\mathrm{fresh}}-e_t^{\mathrm{reuse}})\) determines refresh, indifference, or reuse.

notation.meaning: Mean-square error of the reused estimator
Cost of refreshing at time t

review_flags: utility scalarization and drift model need authoritative support
boundary is decision-theoretic rather than a convergence theorem
LaTeX escape corruption repaired; sourcing remains required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Break-even condition comparing estimator reuse against refresh under data drift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At time \(t\), let \(v_t^{\mathrm{reuse}}\) reuse stored component information and let \(v_t^{\mathrm{fresh}}\) be obtained by a refresh costing \(c_t^{\mathrm{ref}}>0\). Let \(e_t^{\mathrm{reuse}}=\mathbb E\|v_t^{\mathrm{reuse}}-\nabla F_t(x_t)\|^2\) and \(e_t^{\mathrm{fresh}}=\mathbb E\|v_t^{\mathrm{fresh}}-\nabla F_t(x_t)\|^2\). For a declared error price \(\lambda_t>0\), refresh is preferred exactly when \[c_t^{\mathrm{ref}}+\lambda_t e_t^{\mathrm{fresh}}<\lambda_t e_t^{\mathrm{reuse}}.\] Equality is the reuse–freshness boundary; on the reverse strict inequality, reuse is preferred. The comparison includes drift-induced bias in each mean-square error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refresh when its cost plus residual estimator error is smaller than the priced error from reuse; equality is the boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Reuse–Freshness Boundaries

children.title: Centralized Method Selection
children.top_down_role: Method choices for shared-memory or single-coordinator execution environments.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit feasibility certificate for a coordinator-mediated finite-sum architecture before cost-based method selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be the available communication graph with coordinator \(0\), and let \(E_{\mathrm{req}}(a)\) be the directed worker-to-coordinator and coordinator-to-worker links required by a centralized architecture \(a\). If \(m_0(a)\) is its coordinator-state requirement and \(M_0\) is available coordinator memory, define \[\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cen}}^{\mathrm{feas}}=\{a:E_{\mathrm{req}}(a)\subseteq E,\ m_0(a)\le M_0\}.\] Cost minimization over centralized candidates is valid only over \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cen}}^{\mathrm{feas}}\); an empty set certifies that centralized deployment is infeasible under the declared architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A centralized method is admissible only if every required coordinator link exists and its shared state fits coordinator memory; selection must be restricted to this feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The available communication graph and coordinator are declared.
Each candidate declares its required directed links and coordinator-state size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Centralized selection is restricted to \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cen}}^{\mathrm{feas}}\), and \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cen}}^{\mathrm{feas}}=\varnothing\) certifies centralized infeasibility.

notation.meaning: communication links required by centralized candidate a

knowledge_statements.title: Centralized Topology and Memory Admissibility
Centralized Method Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection condition for variance reduction coordinated by one shared state and aggregator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let workers \(k=1,\ldots,K\) hold component subsets and communicate with a central coordinator maintaining shared state \(s_t\). A centralized architecture is feasible when every required worker-to-center message and center-to-worker broadcast fits the communication graph, while \(s_t\) fits coordinator memory \(M_0\). For candidate architectures \(\mathcal A\), select the centralized method \(a_{\mathrm{cen}}\) exactly when \[a_{\mathrm{cen}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A:\,m_0(a)\leq M_0}T(a;\varepsilon),\] where \(T\) includes local gradient computation, aggregation, synchronization, message latency, and bandwidth costs required to reach the common accuracy criterion. A central bottleneck is therefore charged rather than treated as free.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose centralized coordination when the coordinator and communication pattern are feasible and yield the smallest predicted end-to-end time.
assumptions_latex: The coordinator can communicate with every participating worker as required by the method.
Coordinator memory and communication costs are explicitly modeled.
All candidates target the same optimization accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The centralized method is selected exactly when it is topology-feasible, memory-feasible, and minimizes predicted end-to-end time.

notation.meaning: Shared coordinator state at iteration t
Predicted wall-clock time to accuracy epsilon

review_flags: centralized finite-sum selection rule needs distributed-optimization sourcing
latency and bandwidth model is deployment dependent
